## 2026-11-14: an attempt that errored is no trial of pass@k

An attempt ends as `passed`, `failed` or `errored`, so that an infrastructure failure never becomes a score of zero. The summary of a run did not keep to that: `Result.summarize` took every ended attempt of a task as a trial of pass@k, and an attempt that ended without a verdict, as a `verifier`, `agent`, `environment`, `budget` or `cancelled` error, lowered pass@k exactly as a failed one. Nothing in the line said so.

**Found** on directory slots under local workerd, with a scripted model whose answer to each attempt was planned: one `claude` agent, 8 small tasks, 3 attempts each, one slot.

- A run cancelled after 10 of its 24 rows had ended. `status` printed `finished` and `passed 3/24, errored 17, mean reward 0.429, pass@1 25.0%, pass@2 25.0%, pass@3 25.0%`. By hand: 6 tasks have a first attempt with a verdict and 2 of them passed, 33.3 %. One task has two attempts with a verdict, and both passed. No task has three. The 14 rows that never ran were counted as three attempts that did not pass.
- The same run left to finish, where the plan made the verifier of one task write no reward, the model endpoint refuse every request of a second and one request of a third: `passed 7/24, errored 7, pass@1 25.0%, pass@2 37.5%, pass@3 50.0%`, over 8 tasks of which 2 never had a verdict.

**The rule.** The trials of a task are its scored attempts, the ones that passed or failed, in the order of their attempt numbers. An agent timeout keeps its verifier reward and stays a trial. pass@k is over the tasks that have at least k scored attempts, for every k that some task has, and `AgentSummary.rated` holds how many tasks each pass@k rates. The CLI writes that count behind a pass@k that rates fewer tasks than the run has, `pass@2 100.0% of 1 task`, and nothing where it rates them all, so a run without errors reads as before. `pass_at_k` of an exported job follows, and its `metrics.mean` stays Harbor's, which counts a trial without a reward as 0.

**Why not keep the count over all tasks.** A task whose three attempts errored is not known to be unsolved, and `run --rerun RUN --errored` exists to find out. Counting it as unsolved made the pass@k of a run depend on the health of the machine, and made a cancelled run print the pass@3 of attempts it never made.

**Checked.**

- Unit tests in `test/Result.test.ts` and `test/Summary.test.ts`: a run cut short, a task whose attempts all errored, an errored attempt before a passed one, and the line the CLI prints.
- The two runs above read again from the same Worker state with the change: the cancelled one prints `pass@1 33.3% of 6 tasks, pass@2 100.0% of 1 task`, and the finished one `pass@1 33.3% of 6 tasks, pass@2 50.0% of 6 tasks, pass@3 60.0% of 5 tasks`, each equal to the figure by hand. A run of 3 tasks and 2 attempts with no error prints `pass@1 33.3%, pass@2 66.7%` before and after.
- `npm run lint`, `npm run check:types`, `npm test`, and the plain lane on directory slots.

**Not verified.** krun and ns slots, a real model, a deployed Worker: the change is in the summary, which no slot sees. A CLI of this commit against a Worker of the one before prints pass@k without the count of tasks.

## 2026-11-14: pass@k is estimated from every scored attempt of a task

pass@k came from gakonst/nanoeval as "any of the first k attempts passed". With more attempts than k that reads k of them and drops the rest: a run with `--attempts 3` printed a pass@1 that one attempt in three decided, and which attempt it was depended on the attempt number alone. It is an estimate of the right quantity, the chance that k attempts of a task include a pass, with more noise than the run had paid for.

**Found** on directory slots under local workerd, with a scripted model whose answer to each attempt was planned.

- 3 tasks, 2 attempts each, no error: the outcomes were passed and passed, failed and passed, failed and failed. `status` printed `passed 3/6, pass@1 33.3%, pass@2 66.7%`. Half of the attempts passed, and the mean pass rate of the three tasks is (1 + 1/2 + 0) / 3, 50.0 %.
- 8 tasks, 3 attempts each, the run of the entry above: after that entry it printed `pass@1 33.3% of 6 tasks, pass@2 50.0% of 6 tasks`. By hand over the same scored attempts, pass@1 is (0 + 1 + 2/3 + 0 + 1/3 + 1/2) / 6, 41.7 %, and pass@2 is (0 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 2/3 + 1) / 6, 61.1 %.

**The rule.** A task with n scored attempts of which c passed counts 1 − C(n−c, k)/C(n, k) towards pass@k: the share of the ways to draw k of its attempts that include a pass. This is the estimator of Chen et al., "Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code" (2021), unbiased for every k up to n, and equal to the earlier figure when a task has exactly k scored attempts. pass@1 is the mean pass rate of the tasks. Tasks may have different numbers of scored attempts, after errors or in a run that is under way, and each is rated with its own. Nothing else of the entry above changes.

**Checked.**

- A unit test in `test/Result.test.ts`: four tasks of three attempts against the figures by hand, the same outcomes in another order, all passed, none passed, and tasks with 2 and with 4 attempts.
- The runs above read again from the same Worker state: `pass@1 50.0%, pass@2 66.7%` for the first, and `pass@1 41.7% of 6 tasks, pass@2 61.1% of 6 tasks, pass@3 60.0% of 5 tasks` for the second. pass@3 is under pass@2 there because it rates one task fewer, which the line says.
- `npm run lint`, `npm run check:types`, `npm test`, and the plain lane on directory slots, whose two agents pass every attempt or none and read 100 % and 0 % as before.

**Not verified.** A run with a real model, where attempts of one task are not independent draws when a cache or a seed ties them. An interval around the figure: the summary prints a point estimate, and with a few attempts on a few tasks two runs of one agent can differ by more than a change between them.

## 2026-11-14: compare counts a row once when a rerun retried it

`nanoeval compare` is the one command that reads several runs together, and a run with its reruns is the first thing to give it: a rerun is a run of its own, whose summary covers only the rows it retried, and the results of the earlier run are never changed. The table added the attempts of all its runs, so a row that was retried counted twice, as the attempt that did not pass and as its retry.

**Found** on directory slots under local workerd with the scripted model: the run of 8 tasks and 3 attempts of the entries above, 7 passed, 10 failed and 7 errored, then `run --rerun RUN --failed`, 10 rows of which 4 passed, and `run --rerun RUN --errored`, 7 rows of which 1 passed. `compare` of the three printed 41 attempts, 12 passed, 16 failed and 13 errored, and for one task `failed, passed, failed, passed, passed`. The 24 rows stand at 12 passed, 6 failed and 6 errored. The same run named twice printed 48 attempts.

**The rule.** `Compare.standing` takes each run once, by its id, and leaves out every attempt that an ended attempt of another run of the table names as the one it retries. What a retry of a retry replaces goes the same way. An attempt whose retry has not ended stands until it has. The line of a run says how many of its attempts were left out, and outcomes, time, tokens and cost are those of the attempts that stand, so the cost of a retried attempt is in the table of its own run and not in this one. Two reruns of the same rows both stand: they are two further attempts of those rows.

**Checked.**

- A unit test in `test/Compare.test.ts`: a run and its rerun in either order, the run named twice, and the rerun alone.
- The three runs above read again: 24 attempts, 12 passed, 6 failed, 6 errored, 2,535 input tokens of which 1,560 cached and 273 output tokens, each equal to the sum by hand over the attempts that stand, and `24 attempts ended, 17 of them retried by a run of this table and left out` on the line of the first run.
- `npm run lint`, `npm run check:types`, `npm test`.

**Not verified.** A rerun that is still running beside its run, and a rerun of a rerun, outside the unit test. The table still has no pass@k, and two unrelated runs of one agent still share a row.

## 2026-11-14: a rerun says which options it does not take

`run --rerun RUN` builds its rows from the attempts of `RUN` and takes the eval version, the agents and the attempt numbers from it. The command line took every option of `run` beside it and dropped the ones a rerun does not follow, without a word.

**Found** on directory slots under local workerd, on a run of 8 tasks and 3 attempts with 10 failed and 7 errored attempts:

- `run --rerun RUN --failed --errored` made a run of the 10 failed attempts. The usage names the two as alternatives, and the command took the first: the 7 errored attempts were not retried, and nothing said so.
- `run --rerun RUN --attempts 5 --agent b=claude:x --limit 1 --eval other --only t2` made a run of one row, the failed attempt of `t2` by the agent of `RUN` on the eval of `RUN`: `--only` narrowed it, and the other four were ignored. That was before `--agent ID` narrowed a rerun to agents of its run: it now does, and refuses an id the run does not have.

**The rule.** `--failed` and `--errored` together select what they name together, every attempt that did not pass, which is the selection with neither. `--only` narrows a rerun to tasks, as it did, and the usage now says so. A rerun with `--attempts`, `--oracle`, `--eval`, `--task` or `--limit` is refused before anything is asked of the Worker, with the options to leave out. `--agent` is not among them: with a rerun it names agents of the run to keep. `--attempts` lost its default in the option table for that, and a run without it has one attempt as before.

**Checked.** Unit tests in `test/Selection.test.ts`. On the run above: the second command without its `--agent` is refused, and `--rerun RUN --failed --errored --only t2 --only t6` made the 3 rows of those two tasks that had not passed, one failed and two of the other task, one errored and one failed. `npm run lint`, `npm run check:types`, `npm test`.

**Not verified.** The sandbox settings of a rerun, which still come from the command line and not from its run.

## 2026-11-14: the spend of a run says what it leaves out

`status` prints `spend: model $…`. Through the gateway that is what each response reported. With a key of a provider or a plan login no response carries a cost, and the figure is the one nanocode publishes when a turn ends, `cost_usd` with `cost_status: estimated_from_usage`: tokens at list prices. The line did not say which of the two it was, and the estimate has a hole.

**Found** on directory slots under local workerd, with a scripted Messages endpoint that reports tokens and no cost: 20 uncached input tokens, 40 read from the cache, 5 written to it and 7 output tokens a response, which nanocode prices at $0.00006525 for `claude-haiku-4-5`. A run of 24 rows got 37 responses: 14 attempts with two, 3 attempts of a task with an agent timeout of 3 s whose only command sleeps 30 s, with one each, and 3 attempts whose verifier wrote no reward, with two. `status` printed `spend: model $0.0022`, the exported job `cost_usd: 0.0022185`, which is 34 responses. By hand the 37 are $0.00241425. The three attempts that timed out have their tokens in every total, 65 input and 7 output, and `cost_usd: null`: the turn was cancelled, and nanocode ends a cancelled turn with `run.failed`, `cost_usd: null` and `cost_status: other`. `compare` showed it as `$0.0022 for 17 of 24`, which also counts 4 attempts that never reached the model.

An attempt that runs into its timeout is the one that used the most tokens of its task, so on a benchmark this is the larger part of the estimate and not the smaller. Through the gateway each response carries its cost and an attempt has the sum of them, whatever ended its turn: read in `worker/Run.ts`, not run here.

**What changed.** The cost itself is not repaired here: the prices are in the brain, nanocode-ts exports no table, and a second table in this repository would be a magic constant that drifts. `Result.uncosted` counts the attempts whose usage has model calls and no cost, the run reports it as `spend.uncostedAttempts`, and `status` prints `spend: model $0.0022 estimated from tokens, without 3 attempts whose model calls have no cost`. `estimated from tokens` is printed when the run has no gateway key and a response came without a cost. `--model-budget-usd` on such a run bounds the same estimate and does not see those attempts either.

**Checked.** A unit test in `test/Summary.test.ts`. The run above and a run cancelled while one such attempt had ended, read again: 3 attempts and 1 attempt. A run with neither prints `estimated from tokens` alone. `npm run lint`, `npm run check:types`, `npm test`.

**Not verified.** A gateway run, where the line is unchanged unless an attempt has no cost. A `codex` session. Whether nanocode can price a cancelled turn from the usage it already has: that is the repair, in nanocode, and the count here goes to zero with it.

## 2026-11-14: the summary names a cancelled run

A run that is cancelled ends its unfinished rows as `cancelled` errors and is then `finished`. `status` printed that word alone on its first line, so a run cut short after 10 of 24 rows read as one that had run to its end with 17 errors. And a failure whose message holds a line break, such as the last output of a verifier that wrote no reward, broke the list of rows with an empty line after it.

**What changed.** The first line of the summary of a run with cancelled rows is `finished, cancelled with 14 rows not finished`. The count is of the rows whose failure is `cancelled`, so a `cancel` sent to a run that had already finished changes nothing. The message of a failure is printed with its whitespace folded to single spaces before it is cut to 160 characters.

**Checked.** A unit test in `test/Summary.test.ts`. The cancelled run of the entries above read again, and a finished run that was sent `cancel` afterwards, which prints `finished`. `npm run lint`, `npm run check:types`, `npm test`.

**Not verified.** A run cancelled while a leased sandbox held its rows.

## 2026-11-14: a refusal is one line

Every command that was refused ended in an uncaught rejection: Node printed the source line of the `throw`, a caret, the message, the stack and its version. What the Worker said came inside the JSON of its answer, `Error: /v1/runs answered 400: {"error":"the eval audit cannot be read: the eval has no task typo"}`, and a missing run id read `--RUN is required`, as if it were an option. The checks themselves are right, and were tried on an eval of 8 tasks on directory slots: `--only` with an id the eval does not have, `--limit 0`, `--attempts 0`, an eval or a version that does not exist, no agent, two agents of one id and an unknown option are all refused before a run exists. So this is how they read, not what they do.

**What changed.** `main` is awaited with a handler that prints `nanoeval: ` and the message on standard error and exits 1. An answer of the Worker is printed as what it said, with the route and the status behind it: `nanoeval: the eval audit cannot be read: the eval has no task typo (/v1/runs answered 400)`. A refusal is a plain `Error`, one of this repository's named errors, or an error of the option parser. Anything else, a `TypeError` of a mistake in the code, keeps its stack. A positional that is missing is named without dashes. Exit statuses are unchanged: 1 for a refusal, 2 for an unknown command.

**Checked.** Unit tests in `test/Refusal.test.ts`, one of which runs the command. The refusals above read again. `npm run lint`, `npm run check:types`, `npm test`, and the plain lane and the lane `machine` on directory slots, whose runner exits with what its machine said.

**Not verified.** A runner in a leased sandbox, whose log is where its last words go: it now ends with one line where it had a stack.

## 2026-11-14: a comparison says what the numbers support

`compare --baseline` printed `gained` and `lost` for a task as "some attempt passed on one side and none on the other". With a few attempts a task that passes half the time changes sides by chance, an attempt that errored counted as one that did not pass, the pass@k of the two sides was over each side's own tasks, and nothing said how sure the answer was.

**Found** on directory slots under local workerd with a scripted model whose answer to each attempt was planned, 8 tasks and 3 attempts a side.

- A run cancelled after 10 of its 24 rows, against the same run left to finish: `lost: t2 (2/3 to 0/3), t4 (1/3 to 0/3)`. Each of the two tasks had one scored attempt in the cancelled run, which failed, and two rows that never ran.
- Two runs of the same agent on the same builds, 3 tasks and 2 attempts against 8 tasks and 3: `compare` put them in one row of 30 attempts, and `pass@1 41.7% of 6 tasks` stood beside `50.0%` of 3 other tasks.

**The rule.**

- A side is a run with the reruns named beside it, each row once, as `compare` counts them. `--baseline` may be given several times, and the runs given after the options are taken apart into a run with its reruns each.
- The score of a task on a side is its passed attempts over its scored ones, `2/3`, with the errored ones beside it, `0/1 +2 errored`. A task with no scored attempt on a side has no verdict there and is not compared: it is listed as such and left out of the verdict.
- pass@k is printed for each side as its summary prints it, and again over the tasks that both sides rate at that k wherever the two differ, so a figure is never set against one over other tasks.
- A task is `lost` or `gained` when Fisher's exact test of its two pass counts, one-sided, gives 0.05 or less: the chance, if the attempts of both sides came from one pass rate, that the passes fall this unevenly or more. Otherwise a task whose rate changed is `moved, within noise`, with that chance printed. Three attempts a side reach 0.05 only as 3/3 against 0/3, four reach 0.014, and one or two cannot reach it at all (0.5 and 0.167), which the output then says: one task that flips is not evidence.
- The verdict is the same test over all tasks together: the passes of the run summed over the tasks both sides scored, against the exact distribution of that sum when each task keeps its own total of passes (the test stratified by task, of which the sign test is the case of one attempt a side). It is a `regression` or an `improvement` at 0.05 or less in that direction, else `no change beyond noise`, with both chances printed.
- The error rate: an agent that did not change is called a regression in at most 1 comparison of 20, and an improvement in at most 1 of 20. Each task is held to the same line by itself, with no correction for the number of tasks, so over many flaky tasks a false `lost` is expected now and then (at three attempts at most 1.6 % a task, the chance of 3/3 against 0/3 at a pass rate of one half), and the verdict is the line to gate on. The tests are exact and conservative: the true rates are lower with few attempts.
- What it assumes: the attempts of a task on a side are independent and share a pass rate. A cache or a seed that ties attempts together breaks that, and so does a task whose outcome depends on the machine.
- In the table of `compare`, runs of one agent on one revision share a row only while they hold different rows: two runs of the same task and attempt number are two measurements and get a row each, named by its run. A run and its reruns are one row, as before.

**Why not an interval around pass@k.** An interval for each side says how well each is known, and two intervals that overlap are not a test of their difference. The question of a comparison is whether the difference is more than chance, and the paired test answers it with the tasks as their own controls, which is where most of the variance is.

**Why not a correction over tasks.** With three attempts a side no single task could then be called at all. The overall verdict already answers for the whole comparison at one error rate, and the task lines say which tasks to read.

**Checked.**

- `test/Stats.test.ts`: the chances of single tasks against counts of the ways by hand (3/3 against 0/3 is 1 of 20, 2/3 against 1/3 is 10 of 20, 5/5 against 1/5 is 6 of 252, unequal sides), the test over tasks against the sign test (5 flips one way 1 of 32, 4 flips 1 of 16, 3 against 1 5 of 16), and two tasks whose joint figure is 52 of 400.
- `test/Compare.test.ts`: three attempts a side with a task lost, one gained, one moved, one that errored on a side and tasks only one side ran; one attempt a side where five flips are a regression and four are not; a baseline with its rerun; pass@k over the tasks both sides rate; two runs of the same rows as two rows of the table.
- On directory slots with the scripted model, a run of 8 tasks and 3 attempts against one whose plan broke one task, lowered one and raised two: `lost: t1 (3/3 to 0/3, p = 0.050)`, `moved, within noise: t2 (2/3 to 1/3, p = 0.500), t4 (1/3 to 3/3, p = 0.200), t6 (1/2 +1 errored to 3/3, p = 0.400)`, two tasks not compared, pass@1 41.7 % against 38.9 % on the 6 tasks both sides rate, and `no change beyond noise` at 0.534 for worse and 0.768 for better: every count by hand from the rows, the two chances of the verdict by a separate enumeration of all outcomes. The same run against the baseline with its two reruns, where the reruns had passed every retried row of two tasks: `regression` at 0.010, which is 1/20 times 4/20 by hand. Two runs of 6 tasks and one attempt where five tasks flipped down: no task called, `regression` at 0.031, and the line that one flip is not evidence. The cancelled run of the first finding now reads `moved, within noise: t2 (2/3 to 0/1 +2 errored, p = 0.500)`.
- `npm run lint`, `npm run check:types`, `npm test`.

**Not verified.** A real model, where the assumption of independent attempts is the open question. Runs of many tasks: the test was read on 8 tasks here and on fixtures. Agents are matched by their id, so a comparison of two models has to give them one id.

## 2026-11-14: an exit status that gates a script

`run --wait` exits 1 when an attempt errored and 0 otherwise, and `compare` always 0, so a script could stop on a broken machine and not on a lower pass rate: it had to read the summary. That status is kept as it is, because scripts read it, and a gate is asked for by name.

**The rule.** `--fail-on` takes `regression`, `lost` and `any-failure`, repeated or as a list, on `run --wait`, `revision` and `compare`.

| Status | When |
| --- | --- |
| 3 | `regression`: the verdict of the comparison against the baseline is a regression, for any agent. `lost`: that, or one task is lost |
| 4 | `any-failure`: an attempt failed or errored. For `compare`, an attempt of the runs named that stands after their reruns, not of the baseline |
| 1 | As before: an attempt errored or was cancelled, for `run --wait` and `revision`. And a gate that cannot be judged is refused: no `--baseline`, an agent the baseline does not have, or no task that both sides scored |
| 0 | Nothing of the above |

3 goes before 4 and 4 before 1: the status names the strongest thing the command found. `run --wait` takes `--baseline`, repeated for a baseline with its reruns, and prints the comparison under its summary, as `revision` did, so that one command runs a selection and gates on it. `--baseline` or `--fail-on` without `--wait` is refused, since there is nothing to read yet.

**Which gate.** `regression` has the error rate of the verdict: a run of an agent that did not change fails it at most 1 time in 20. `lost` also fails on a single task at 0.05 or less, which finds a task that broke beside many flaky ones that dilute the verdict, and fails more often by chance, each flaky task adding its own small rate. A gate that fails on every lower pass rate was not added: with a few attempts that is a coin.

**Checked.**

- `test/Gate.test.ts`: the names and a wrong one, every status with and without a gate, noise that does not fail `regression`, one task lost beside one gained that fails `lost` and not `regression`, and the order of 3, 4 and 1.
- From a shell on directory slots with the scripted model, the runs of the entry above: `compare --baseline` with no gate 0; `--fail-on regression` 0 where the verdict is noise and one task is lost, and 3 against the baseline with its reruns, where it is a regression at 0.010; `--fail-on lost` 3; `--fail-on any-failure` 4; both gates 3. `run --eval ... --only ... --attempts 3 --baseline RUN --baseline RERUN --baseline RERUN --fail-on regression --wait` on five tasks printed its summary, the comparison and exited 3. A gate without a baseline, a gate with another word, and `--baseline` without `--wait` each printed one line and exited 1 before anything was run or printed.
- `npm run lint`, `npm run check:types`, `npm test`.

**Not verified.** `revision --fail-on`: it shares the code of `run --wait` and was not run, since it builds nanocode. A gate in a CI job.

## 2026-11-14: tasks are chosen by name, by pattern and by subset

`--only` took task ids, one a flag. `status` and `compare` print task names, a selection of ten tasks was ten flags on every command, and the same ten had to be typed again for the baseline, the run and the rerun.

**The rule.**

- `--only` takes an id, a name as `status` prints it (`terminal-bench/fix-git`), the last part of a name as `compare` prints it, or a pattern. A pattern is a word with `*` (any characters) or `?` (one character), matched against the whole id, the whole name and its last part, and it takes every task it matches. Nothing else is special: a bracket or a dot is itself.
- `--only-file FILE` holds such words one a line, with `#` comments. `--subset NAME` reads `{"EVAL": {"SUBSET": ["task", ...]}}` from `subsets.json` at the root of the checkout, or from `--subsets FILE` or `NANOEVAL_SUBSETS`, and takes the list under the eval of the run. The three add up, and `--limit` takes the first N of the result in the order of the eval, as before.
- Refused before a run exists, with one line: a name that no task has, a pattern that matches none, a last part that two tasks share (it names them), a subset the file does not have for that eval (it names the ones it has), and a file that is not there or does not have that shape.
- The CLI resolves the words against the tasks of the eval version and sends ids, so a Worker of an earlier commit takes them. A rerun resolves `--only` against the eval of its run.
- In a lab (`nanoeval revision`) a word is resolved against the tasks the lab holds, and one that is not there is imported by its id as before. A pattern or a name that matches nothing in the lab is refused, since nothing says which task to import.

**Why a file in the checkout and not a table with the eval.** A subset is a choice of the people who run an eval, it changes more often than the eval, and it wants review. A file is versioned with the commands that use it, works against a deployed Worker and a lab alike, and needs no deploy. A table in the eval index would need a route, a migration and a protocol change to hold a dozen names.

**Checked.**

- `test/Subset.test.ts`: an id, a full name, a last part, patterns over ids and names, the union in the order of the eval, each refusal with its text, the file of words with comments, and the subsets file with four wrong shapes.
- On directory slots with the scripted model, an eval of 8 tasks, one attempt each: `--only audit/t1 --only 't?' --limit 3` ran t1, t2, t3; a file with a name, an id and `*low` ran slow, t3, t4; `--subset smoke` ran its two tasks; two subsets and an `--only` ran five; a rerun with `--only audit/t5 --only 'e*'` retried the two errored rows of two tasks. Seven refusals each printed one line and exited 1 with no run created, and `nanoeval eval` printed the two subsets with their tasks.
- `npm run lint`, `npm run check:types`, `npm test`.

**Not verified.** `subsets.json` ships one subset, `smoke` of `terminal-bench-2.1`, with the four task ids that the revision command was run on: the ids were read from an import of that eval, and no run was made through `--subset smoke`. The lab path was not run: it needs a build of nanocode.

## 2026-11-14: a baseline is found by rule

A comparison needed the id of its baseline typed by hand, and a baseline whose errored rows had been retried needed the ids of its reruns too. The run to compare against is nearly always the same one: the last full run on the pins.

**The rule.** `--baseline latest`, on `run --wait`, `revision` and `compare`, is the newest run in the list of runs that

- has finished, was not cancelled, and is not a rerun of another run,
- is of the same eval and the same version digest,
- ran on the builds this checkout pins: the Worker named the pinned nanocode-ts release, and every runner reported the pinned hand and no other,
- has every agent of the run it is set against, with the same id, harness, orchestration, model and thinking,
- holds every task of that run. It may hold more: a full run is a baseline for every subset, and the comparison is then over the tasks both have,
- is not one of the runs it would be set against.

The command prints the id it took. When none fits it is refused before a run is created, with the count of runs it read by the first reason each did not fit. A rerun cannot ask for `latest`: its selection is the rows of its run, and its baseline is named. `--with-reruns` adds the reruns a run lists, and theirs, to the baseline and, for `compare`, to each run named: a rerun that is still under way counts with the rows it has ended.

**Why the pins and not "the latest run".** The latest run of an eval is often the one made a minute ago on the change under test. A baseline has to be what the change is measured against, and the pins are the one build every checkout agrees on. A run on another build is named by its id.

**Why not the same number of attempts.** The comparison handles sides of different sizes, and a baseline with more attempts is a better one. The line that names the baseline is followed by the table with both counts.

**Checked.**

- `test/Baseline.test.ts`: a run that fits, each reason a run does not fit, the order of the search, that it stops at the first fit, and the refusal with its counts.
- On directory slots with the scripted model, a Worker with 16 listed runs of one eval: `compare --baseline latest RUN` for a run of 8 tasks took the earlier full run, past 11 newer runs of fewer tasks, a cancelled run and three reruns, and printed the comparison of the entry on comparisons; with `--with-reruns` the baseline was that run with its two reruns and the verdict the regression at 0.010. A run of 6 tasks took the latest run that held those 6. `run --subset smoke --attempts 2 --baseline latest --with-reruns --fail-on regression --wait` took the latest run that held the two tasks with its rerun, and exited 0 on no change. An agent no run had was refused with `of the runs listed, 3 a rerun, 1 cancelled, 11 without these agents` and no run was made; a rerun with `latest` and an id that is no run were each refused in one line.
- `npm run lint`, `npm run check:types`, `npm test`.

**Not verified.** A deployed Worker with many runs: the search reads the config and the status of each listed run of the eval version, newest first, until one fits. A lab, where `revision --baseline latest` would take the last run on the pins: not run, it needs a build. A run whose runners reported two hands is never a baseline by rule, which is intended and was only unit tested.

**The rule.**

## 2026-11-14: an attempt that hit its agent timeout has no cost, and the change that gives it one is nanocode's

`status` says `spend: model $0.0022 estimated from tokens, without 3 attempts whose model calls have no cost` for a run in which three attempts ran into their agent timeout. This entry records why nanoeval cannot fill that in, and the change upstream that does.

**What happens.** A session reports the cost of a turn in the event that ends it, `run.completed` or `run.failed`, and `Atif.usage` reads `cost_usd` there. The tokens come from the `model.call.completed` events before it. When the agent timeout ends a turn, nanoeval cancels it, and the brain ends it with `run.failed {"status": "cancelled", "cost_usd": null, "cost_status": "other"}`, read from the events of such an attempt on directory slots, though the model calls of the turn completed and were counted: one call of 65 input and 7 output tokens, where the same call in a turn that completed is priced at $0.00006525. The attempt keeps its tokens and has no cost, the spend of the run and `--model-budget-usd` leave it out, and the line above says how many attempts that is.

**Why not price it here.** The prices are in nanocode (`crates/core/types-core/src/pricing`), compiled into the brain. nanocode-ts exports a model catalog without prices, and nanoeval sends models nothing of its own and keeps no table of theirs: a second price list here would drift from the one that prices every other turn of the same run. Through a gateway key each response carries what it was charged, and those attempts are priced already.

**The change, in nanocodexyz/nanocode**, `crates/backends/claude/src/agent.rs` at master `86c465b4dca2`: `emit_run_finished` (lines 4948 to 4989) takes the usage of a turn from its result, which only a completed turn has, at line 4970. The usage of the turn so far lives in a local of `run_rounds` (line 7125) and is lost when the turn ends in an error. The patch keeps that usage in the caller (line 5914), passes it down through `run_locked` (7037) and `run_rounds` (7053), and lets `emit_run_finished` fall back to it, so a turn that was cancelled or failed reports the cost of the model calls it completed, as `estimated_from_usage` or `reported_by_provider`. A turn that ended before its first model call still reports no cost. **It is not tested and was not compiled**: it was written against the source and is recorded here for whoever lands it there.

## 2026-11-14: a slot whose process is still ending is gone

**The defect.** The entry on a row whose slot ends under it gives the row back when the process of its slot is gone, and `slot.sh gone` asked that with `kill -0`. A process that was killed answers `kill -0` until it has finished ending and has been reaped. A microVM lets go of its guest's memory first and closes its files after that, so the socket of the guest refuses connections while the process still exists. On a faster machine the runner asked in that window: the verifier's command had already ended with 125, "the guest connection ended", `gone` still said that the slot runs, and the row ended as a `verifier` error where it should have gone back to the run. The lane that kills a microVM under its verifier (`NANOEVAL_E2E_SCENARIO=gone`) failed that way.

**The rule.** A slot is gone when its process is gone or has given up its memory: `/proc/PID/status` of a process that is ending, and of one that waits to be reaped, has no `VmSize` line. The kernel releases the memory of a process before it closes its files, so by the time a command in the guest fails for a closed socket, the line is gone.

**Measured** on a second, faster machine (Linux, 24 cores, 48 threads, kernel 7.0, libkrunfw 5.5.0), the lane alone, at `2244c58` with two changes that machine needed for other lanes and that are not in this repository, and then with this one.

| | The lane |
| --- | --- |
| Before, alone | passed 0 times of 4: "errored verifier: the verifier exited with 125 and wrote no reward: nanoeval-krun: the guest connection ended" |
| Before, in runs of every step of the workflow at three commits that hold the lane | passed 1 time of 3 |
| With the rule, alone | passed 4 times of 4 |

On the 32-core machine of the entries above, at a load average above 55, the lane without the rule passed 5 times of 5 in the runs and the proof of this day's entries, and then failed the same way once, in a run of every step of the workflow for a later change. With the rule it passed there once, alone.

**Not verified.**

- ns slots, whose process is the first of the slot's namespaces: the same test of the same file, not run with a kill.
- A microVM that the kernel kills for memory, which the entry on the row leaves open as well.

## 2026-11-14: `nanoeval watch`, the evals run as nanocode changes

Until now an eval ran when someone started it. This entry adds `nanoeval watch`: it follows a branch of nanocode and one of nanocode-ts, runs the newest pair of revisions through `nanoeval revision` on a subset of an eval at K attempts, sets the result against the last accepted baseline, and keeps a ledger and a scoreboard. The README section [Following nanocode](README.md#following-nanocode) says how to use it. It adds `src/Watch.ts`, `cli/Watch.ts`, `test/StubRevision.ts`, `test/Watch.test.ts`, `test/WatchCommand.test.ts`, `test/WatchRecovery.test.ts`, `test/WatchWorld.ts` and two unit files under `scripts/`, and changes three places of `cli/nanoeval.ts`: an import, the end of the usage text and the last line, which hands `watch` to `cli/Watch.ts`. No table, route, dependency or option of another command changes.

**A subcommand in files of its own.** The watcher is installed, configured and found like the rest: `nanoeval watch`, in `nanoeval --help`, with the environment that the installed command reads. It parses its own arguments, so the option table of the command line is not touched, and its rules are in `src/Watch.ts`, which uses no Node API and is tested without a process. A separate script would have been a second entry point to install and document for no gain. Two starts of `nanoeval --help` took 355 and 372 ms with the change and 423 and 430 ms without, on the machine below: the import costs nothing that shows.

**It starts `nanoeval revision` as a process and reads the job.** That command was not in this tree when the watcher was written, so every call goes through `invoke` in `cli/Watch.ts` with the arguments of `Watch.invocation`, and a stand-in, `test/StubRevision.ts`, plays it in the tests: it holds `flock` on the lock of its lab, keeps builds by revision, fails a build, refuses a missing credential before it builds, ends rows as errors, and writes its job with `Harbor.files`, the code a run exports with. The watcher reads no text the command prints. What a run scored is read from the Harbor job, whose layout `src/Harbor.ts` fixes: the task, the agent and the attempt of each trial, its reward, its exception and its usage, with the outcome rule of `Result.outcome`. A build is a call of its own, `--build-only`, so a build that failed is told from a run that failed by the exit status of a call that does nothing else, and a cached build costs a few seconds. Each run is given `--out` under the state directory and a `--name`, and where no job is there the one new directory under `LAB/runs` is taken, by that name if several are new. Before a call the watcher asks `flock --nonblock LAB/lock` whether another evaluation holds the lab, and comes back later if one does. The README lists what is assumed of the command.

**The state is a ledger and one file for each evaluation in flight.** `watch.jsonl` is the only record: the baseline, the passes it holds, what was tried and what the day spent are all read from it, and the scoreboard is written from it. A line is appended whole and synced, and a last line that was cut off is removed, under the lock, by the next start. An evaluation in flight is a file under `intents/`, rewritten by rename before every call and after it: open, in a step with the process id of its command, failed, or final with its line. Started again, the watcher finds a step whose command still runs (its process names the run in its arguments) and waits, finds a job where the command ended without the watcher and takes it, and otherwise ends the evaluation as `interrupted`, charged the whole budget of the run because what it spent is not known. A final line is appended once, by its id, and its hook is run again after a restart with `repeat` set: an alert twice is better than none. The lock of the state is `flock` held by a child whose pipe the watcher holds, so it ends with the watcher however that ends.

**The rule for lost and gained.** The suggestion was: lost when the baseline solved a task in at least K-1 of K attempts and the revision in none of K, confirmed by none of K more. Enumerated for a task whose pass rate did not change, that rule calls it lost with probability up to 0.148 at K = 2 (at a pass rate of 0.18) and 0.028 at K = 3, for each task, agent and revision: a subset with a few flaky tasks would raise a false alarm most days. The rule here is a one-sided Fisher exact test on two counts, the passes of the task among the scored attempts of the last `baseline.window` accepted revisions and among those of the revision. It is exact for any pass rate, so its false alarms are bounded by `baseline.alpha` without a guess about the task. Three things follow from two attempts being little:

- A task is never lost or gained on one run. Attempts of one run share a time and a machine, and whatever broke them together breaks the test's assumption. So a task that moved is rerun once, K more attempts, when those could bring it to alpha, and is judged on all of them. One that could not get there is listed as within noise and costs nothing more.
- The baseline pools accepted revisions, because one run of two attempts cannot be told from anything: 2 of 2 against 0 of 4 is p = 1/15. The default window is the fewest revisions at which a task that always passed and now never does reaches alpha, and the first baseline runs window times K attempts so the first comparison can find one.
- A revision that lost a task is not accepted and its attempts do not enter the window, so a regression is not averaged into the baseline, and a task that was gained, or lost in a revision that someone accepted, starts its history again at that revision.

Each row is exact, by enumeration over the binomial outcomes with `Watch.judge` itself, at alpha 0.05. "Called lost" is the largest probability over pass rates from 0.01 to 0.99 for a task that did not change. The last four columns are the probability that a change is found, for a task that goes from the first pass rate to the second.

| Attempts | Window | First baseline | Unchanged task called lost | Under the suggested rule | 1 to 0 | 1 to 0.25 | 1 to 0.5 | 0.75 to 0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 5 | 5 attempts | 0.015 | not defined | 1.000 | 0.563 | 0.250 | 0.237 |
| 2 | 2 | 4 | 0.004 | 0.148 | 1.000 | 0.316 | 0.063 | 0.316 |
| 2 | 3 | 6 | 0.013 | | 1.000 | | 0.313 | 0.534 |
| 2 | 5 | 10 | 0.017 | | 1.000 | | 0.313 | 0.776 |
| 3 | 1 | 3 | 0.015 | 0.028 | 1.000 | 0.534 | 0.109 | 0.422 |
| 4 | 1 | 4 | 0.011 | 0.005 | 1.000 | 0.679 | 0.145 | 0.738 |

What the table says plainly: a task that stops passing is always found, a task that becomes flaky is mostly not found at these sizes by any rule, and a longer window buys detection on tasks the baseline only mostly solved, at the price of a first baseline with more attempts. The suggested rule finds 0.75 to 0 more often at K = 2 (0.938) because it is looser, which is the same looseness that gives it the false alarms. Not corrected for: the number of tasks and agents compared at once, so with T tasks and A agents the chance of some false loss in a revision is at most T x A times the column, and a slow drift within noise, which the window follows.

**Newest first, and the search.** The newest pair stands for the commits behind it: a pass for it is taken as a pass for them, and its line records how many it covers. When it lost tasks, the commits of both branches since the baseline are put in one line by commit date, each point a pair that both branches once were, and the line is bisected: a point is bad when it loses one of the lost tasks by the rule above, rerun included, and good when it ran them all and lost none. Only the lost tasks and the agents that lost them run. Results are read as monotone along the line, so earlier evaluations count where they lie on it, and a point whose build fails past its retries is passed over: if the points between the last good and the first bad one are all like that, the answer is the list of their commits. A search on noisy attempts can name the wrong commit. Each of its lines keeps the attempts it saw.

**Budget and retries.** A run is admitted only while the runs of the UTC day are below `daily_runs` and the day's spend plus one more `run_usd` is within `daily_usd`, so the cap holds even if the run spends all it may. The spend of a run is the cost of its rows where every metered row has one, and its whole `run_usd` otherwise, as for a run that left no job. Builds are free of the cap. `[retries]` has three counts, each 1: a build that failed is tried once more, since the failures seen so far were of the network and the registry, and a second failure is taken as the revision's own; an evaluation that did not complete (no job, interrupted, tasks without their attempts) likewise; and errored attempts are run again once inside an evaluation. After that the revision is left, its last line says why, and `--retry` forgets the count. A pass over the branches ends at the first evaluation that did not complete.

**Checked** on a 5-core Linux machine without KVM, Node 24.22.1, git 2.43.0, with the stand-in for the command unless a line says otherwise. No model was paid for.

- `test/Watch.test.ts`, 17 tests: the configuration, the exact test against hand-computed values, the window, the rule, the rows of a job written by `Harbor.files`, pass@1 and pass@k equal to `Result.summarize`, the arguments of the command, the first baseline, the rerun, errored attempts, the window and where it starts again, the line of pairs, the search over six and two commits in three evaluations, a build that fails beside it, the caps, and the scoreboard.
- `test/WatchCommand.test.ts` and `test/WatchRecovery.test.ts`, 11 tests that start `nanoeval watch` itself over two local repositories: commits that arrive while it repeats, each evaluated once; seven commits on two branches, the newest run first, the first losing commit found in three evaluations on the lost task and its agent alone, and the hook called twice; an accepted regression; the watcher and its run killed with SIGKILL in a run, which leaves an `interrupted` line charged the whole budget and one more run; the watcher killed alone, which waits for the run and takes its job with no second run; a build that fails twice and is left until `--retry` or a new commit; an errored attempt run again; a credential that expired, 12 rows errored and no rerun; a credential that is missing; the lab held by another process; both daily caps; a checkout with uncommitted changes on demand, which lost a task, exited with 1 and left the checkout and the baseline as they were; a job written under `LAB/runs` instead; and a ledger line cut off.
- `npm run lint`, `npm run check:types`, `npm run dry-run` and `npm test`: 187 tests, 183 passed, 4 skipped, the four that need KVM. The two files that start the command take about a minute each and run side by side.
- Against GitHub, fetch only: `watch --dry-run` on the two repositories named the heads of both master branches as the first baseline in 2,992 ms the first time, and the mirrors it keeps, commits without trees, are 4.9 MB for nanocode (4,393 commits on the first-parent line) and 0.5 MB for nanocode-ts.
- Over `nanoeval revision` itself, taken from the commit that adds it with this change on top, on directory slots, with both sides `pinned` so that nothing is built, one task (`tasks/write-greeting`) at three attempts and a scripted Messages endpoint for the model, one run of each: `watch --once` wrote a first baseline of 3 of 3 in 12 s and read its job from `--out`. With the endpoint answering the wrong command, `watch --nanocode pinned --nanocode-ts pinned` got 0 of 3, ran three more attempts of the task, reported it lost at p 0.012 and exited with 1 in 18 s, and the baseline stayed. With an endpoint that answers 401 to every request the three rows errored, nothing was rerun, and the line was `incomplete` with the message of the endpoint. With no credential the build call passed, the run was refused, and the line was `run failed` with the refusal.
- Read in the source of that command and not run: that it stops its runner and its Worker and releases the lock on SIGTERM, and that a second evaluation waits on the same `flock`.

**Not verified.**

- A model, a build of a real revision through the watcher, krun slots, a `codex` agent, two agents in one run of the command, and the options a real machine adds (`--ca-bundle`, `--slot-forward`, a plan login).
- That a SIGKILL of the watcher outside systemd leaves no Worker or runner of the evaluation behind: the command starts them in process groups of their own. Under systemd the control group of the unit ends them, which was not run either.
- The two unit files under systemd: `systemd-analyze verify` needs a user manager, which the machine has not.
- The search on real revisions, where a revision of nanocode-ts may not build against the nanocode it is paired with by date.
- A daily cap across midnight, a hook that fails, a hook that does not end, and a ledger of months.
- CI on GitHub.

## 2026-11-14: `nanoeval watch` over `nanoeval revision` itself, with a model

The entry above wrote the watcher against a description of `nanoeval revision` and a stand-in. This entry is what happened when it ran over the command itself, with real builds and a model, and what changed because of it. Nothing changed in how the command is called: every assumption the README lists held. What changed is the unit file, a limit for the hook, the texts of a few lines, and the README, which now says what was run.

**Where.** A 32-core Linux machine shared with other work, at a load average of 90 to 140 during all of it, with KVM. krun slots, two at a time, 8 GiB of guest memory admitted. `codex:gpt-6-luna` paid by a ChatGPT plan login (`--codex-login`). Terminal-Bench 2.1 from a store that already held its converted disks, so an import took one to two seconds a task. The host policy of the machine, `--ca-bundle` and `--slot-forward`, in `[revision] options`, so it reached builds and runs alike. The watcher ran as a systemd user service with `MemoryMax=12G`. About 65 scored rows in all, $0.12 at list price as the Worker estimates it.

**What held, each seen once or more.**

- `--build-only` with `pinned` on both sides builds nothing and exits with 0 in a second. With two full commit ids and both repository options it built the hand and the package in an empty lab in one piece: 1,194 s, of which the hand 262 s and the package 910 s. The next revision of nanocode on the same nanocode-ts took 188 s and about 190 s, later ones 76 to 88 s for the hand. A revision built before returns in a second.
- The run call with `--eval`, `--only`, `--agent`, `--attempts`, `--model-budget-usd`, `--slots`, `--name` and `--out` wrote the Harbor job to `--out` every time, and the rows, tokens and costs the watcher read from it are those the summary of the command printed.
- `flock --nonblock LAB/lock` answers 1 while a build or a run of the command holds the lab. A pass of the watcher during a 20-minute build printed that another evaluation holds the lock, recorded nothing, and ran the evaluation on the next pass.
- On SIGTERM the command gave its two rows in flight back, took its slots down, stopped its runner and its Worker and freed the lock, within a second.
- A hand that does not compile (a checkout with one line that has the wrong type) ended the build call with 1 after 3.5 minutes, the checkout was left as it was, and the line said `build failed` with the last lines of the compiler.
- A login whose token expired (a file made for the test, with a token that is none) passed the credential check of the command, and the row ended as an error, "ChatGPT authorization must be refreshed by logging in again": the line was `incomplete`, nothing was run again, and the run counted as its whole budget. With no login the command refused before it built, and the line was `run failed` with the refusal.

**The runs.** Two tasks at two attempts unless a line says otherwise.

- A baseline on the pins, with both sides `pinned`: 7 of 8, $0.0150, 224 s with the import. Then two revisions of nanocode master on demand against it, each with the head of nanocode-ts master, the commit that was newest and the one four commits before it: 4 of 4, `ok`, and 2 of 4, `ok` with both tasks listed as within noise (p 0.33 and 0.60), since two more attempts could not have brought either to 0.05.
- The branches followed, on local copies of the two repositories whose branch was moved from the older commit to the newest. The service was stopped by systemd 50 s into the run of the first baseline. Started again, the watcher wrote the `interrupted` line, charged the budget of the run, and ran the baseline again. When the branch moved it started the evaluation of the newest commit, and the watcher alone was killed with SIGKILL 15 s into its run: the command went on. A start during the run said that the step still runs as its process and did nothing, a start after it took the job that the command had written, and the line was `ok` with one run. A third start said it was up to date.
- A regression end to end, three tasks at three attempts, window 1. After a baseline of 9 of 9 on the newest commit, two commits made for the test arrived on the local copy: one that changes a line of a README, and after it one that makes every shell command of the hand run `/bin/false`. The first run of the newest pair met the port race of the command (below) and was recorded as `run failed`. The next pass ran it: 0 of 9, then the rerun of the three tasks, 0 of 9 again, and `REGRESSION, lost` the three tasks at `3/3 -> 0/6 (p 0.012)`, with the hook called. The search then built and ran the commit before it on the three tasks, 9 of 9, and named the second test commit as the first losing commit, with the hook called again. From the push to the name: 23 minutes, of which builds about 13, three runs for $0.05.

**The port race of the command.** `nanoeval revision` finds a free port and then starts its Worker on it, and on a machine where other Workers start all the time the port can be taken in between: the command then ends with wrangler's "Address already in use" and no job. It happened once in 12 runs here. The watcher did what it does for any run without a job: `run failed`, the budget of the run counted, the same revision run once more on the next pass. That costs a pass and one `run_usd` of the daily cap for a run that spent nothing, so `daily_usd` should leave room for one or two of them.

**What changed.**

- `scripts/nanoeval-watch.service` stops the watcher alone (`KillMode=mixed`, `TimeoutStopSec=120`), so that the command it runs gives its rows back and takes its slots down, as it did in a second here, and what is left after that is killed. The watcher exits with 143 when it is stopped, which the unit takes as success, and `OOMPolicy=continue` keeps an evaluation when the kernel kills one microVM for memory.
- A hook that has not ended after `hook.timeout_sec` (60) is killed and the line says so. A hook that hangs would otherwise hold the lock of the state, and every later pass would do nothing.
- The lock of the lab is asked about for a second before another evaluation is taken to hold it. The child that holds the lock for the command can outlive it by a moment, and a watcher that asked in that moment said the lab was busy and ended its pass: one test of the watcher failed that way, once, in a run of the whole suite at a load average of 70.
- The detail of a failed call no longer repeats the command line, the colour codes of wrangler or its stack lines, and keeps 300 characters of an error instead of 200, which cut the message of an expired login in the middle.
- Wording: "1 task has", "the last accepted revision", one pass@1 column where K is 1, and no empty tables when no attempt ran.
- One exact test. `src/Watch.ts` had its own Fisher test. It now calls `Stats.task` of `src/Stats.ts`, the function that `nanoeval compare` judges its tasks with, so a watcher and a comparison of the same counts give the same p. The tables of the entry above and the one below were enumerated again with it and did not change.

**Which window at three attempts.** The default window at K = 3 is 1: a task that always passed and now never does is found, and little else is. A subset that has tasks the agent solves only sometimes needs more history to say anything about them. Exact, by the enumeration of the entry above:

| alpha | Window | First baseline | Unchanged task called lost, worst case | 1 to 0 | 1 to 0.25 | 0.75 to 0 | 0.67 to 0 | 0.5 to 0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.05 | 1 | 3 attempts | 0.015 | 1.000 | 0.534 | 0.422 | 0.296 | 0.125 |
| 0.05 | 2 | 6 | 0.019 | 1.000 | 0.831 | 0.831 | 0.680 | 0.344 |
| 0.05 | 3 | 9 | 0.025 | 1.000 | 0.956 | 0.951 | 0.855 | 0.500 |
| 0.02 | 2 | 6 | 0.003 | 1.000 | 0.534 | 0.534 | 0.351 | 0.109 |
| 0.02 | 3 | 9 | 0.006 | 1.000 | 0.831 | 0.834 | 0.650 | 0.254 |

For ten tasks of which six pass 95 times in 100 and four pass 70 times in 100, the chance that an unchanged revision loses some task is 0.015 at the default, 0.047 at alpha 0.05 with window 2, and 0.020 at alpha 0.02 with window 3, which finds a task that fell from 0.7 to nothing 73 times in 100 where the default finds it 34 times. The price is a first baseline of nine attempts a task. A regression that stays is tried again at every later revision, since the baseline does not move, so these are chances for one revision.

**Not verified.**

- Two agents in one evaluation, and a `claude` agent, over the command itself.
- The search where a revision of nanocode-ts does not build against the nanocode it is paired with by date. Here nanocode-ts stood still.
- The daily cap across midnight, and a ledger of months: the scoreboard lists every evaluation.
- A plan that reaches its usage limit in a run. None did in these rows.

**Proof.** Every `run` step of `.github/workflows/ci.yml` from a fresh clone, on the three commits of this change on the main they landed on, before this paragraph was added to the last of them, which is the only difference. On a clean 48-thread Linux machine with KVM, with no lane skipped: 77 of 79 steps passed at once, the `check` job in 984 s of its 20 minutes, `npm test` with 252 tests and none skipped, the watcher's among them. The two that did not: "directory slots, two leased sandboxes of which one dies during the run" failed once with "the rows of the sandbox that died lost their claims" and passed twice alone, and fails the same way on main without this change on that machine, where every row is done before the sandbox dies; "ns slots, slot networks" fails on main on that machine every time, for a reason of its network stack, and passed on the shared machine of the runs above in 137 s, on the same commit, after `npm ci`. Main moved twice while this was proved, by three commits, one of which changed `cli/nanoeval.ts`, so the whole proof was run again on the last tip. A first proof of the same three commits, three main commits earlier, was stopped at step 49 of 79 with all 49 passed, when the machine ran out of its pull quota at the registry. Lint, the type check, the dry run and `npm test` passed on the shared machine on each of the rebased tips.

## 2026-11-14: a codex session runs without web search and subagents, as codex-cli does

The `codex` agents (`nanox` in Code Mode and `nanoxd` with direct tools) are the nanocode arm beside `codex-cli`, which `src/Installed.ts` runs as `codex exec` without `--search`: its model has no web search tool and no tool that starts another agent. A nanocode codex session had both. The nanocode-ts WebAssembly host turns web search on for a provider unless the turn body says `web_search: false` (`WebSearch` defaults to enabled in `src/wasm.rs`), and the `App` gives every session its subagent tools. A task that one arm solves by a search or by children then measured a tool that the other arm did not have.

Decided (Georgios, 2026-11-14): the codex sessions match codex-cli. `src/Turn.ts` builds the body of a turn, and a `codex` turn carries `web_search: false` and `subagents: false` under both orchestrations, also for a codex judge. A `claude` turn carries neither: Claude Code has WebSearch and Task, so `claude` beside `claude-code` keeps both.

`subagents` in a turn body is new in nanocode-ts build-b8158fd (b8158fd), which binds it at the first accepted turn of the session as it binds `codex_orchestration`. `package.json` moves from build-f3aa94f to build-b8158fd, which also pins nanocode 0bbcb64a0. An older build ignores the field and keeps the subagent tools, so a Worker on an older build does not run this decision. In the same change the hand moves to `nanocode-cli-0bbcb64` (nanocode 0bbcb64a0: Codex requests keep up to 500 images instead of 8, and Code Mode's Bash description says that `&` and `nohup` jobs are not followed).

**Checked.** `test/Turn.test.ts` holds the body of a codex turn in both orchestrations and of a claude turn. On dev-georgios (32 cores, Node 24.22.2): `npm run lint`, `npm run check:types`, `npm test` (254 tests, all passed) and `npm run dry-run` on the working tree, then the directory lanes listed in the commit from a fresh clone.
