## 2026-11-14: the host relay of a slot always reads what its guest sends

**The stall.** The entry "a verifier that could not install what its test.sh installs" left 22 attempts whose downloads stalled for 30 s, uv's wheels from the registry proxy behind `--slot-forward`, which reach the machine through the slot's forward, a vsock port of libkrun and `nanoeval-net host`. Read on dev-georgios from a krun slot built as `slot.sh` builds one (`--relay net/relay.sock --forward`), with the launcher of the pinned libkrun `8ce363e` and the deployed `nanoeval-net`: a guest program that sends 300 MiB through the forward to a TCP echo server on the machine's loopback while it reads the echo stalled, and from then on the microVM answered nothing on vsock, not even `nanoeval-krun exec -- echo`. The threads of the VMM at that moment: one blocked in `sock_alloc_send_pskb`, a write to `relay.sock`, the vsock muxer idle in `ep_poll`, and the connection on `relay.sock` full both ways (233,152 bytes queued to the relay, 238,336 from it). 20 MiB went through in 0.1 s.

**The cause.** libkrun's proxy for a guest-initiated vsock port (`src/devices/src/virtio/vsock/unix.rs`) switches its host socket to blocking once connected and writes what the guest sends with a blocking `send` on the thread that processes the guest's transmit queue. That queue also carries the guest's credit updates, without which the muxer stops reading the host socket for the guest. `nanoeval-net host` copied each direction with one thread and a blocking write, so a relay whose upstream had stopped reading stopped reading `relay.sock` too. Once the upstream waits on its own writes back, which an echo does and an HTTP/2 or TLS peer does when the guest is slow to read, every party waits on the next: the VMM on the relay, the relay on the upstream, the upstream on the relay's way back, that on the muxer, and the muxer on a credit update queued behind the VMM's blocked write. The VMM's thread is shared by every vsock connection of the slot, so the slot's commands stall with it.

**The rule.** `nanoeval-net host` reads what the guest sends as soon as it arrives and queues it for the upstream on a thread of its own (`drain` in `krun/net/src/forward.rs`), so the VMM never waits on the relay and the cycle cannot close. The queue holds what the guest sent and the upstream has not yet taken; it is not bounded, since bounding it is what deadlocks, and the guest's own TCP window toward the forward bounds how fast it grows. The direction toward the guest and the guest side of the forward are unchanged. A libkrun that writes without blocking would remove the cause; it is not changed here.

**Checked** on dev-georgios (one run each, load average about 50): `forward::tests::a_guest_that_writes_before_it_reads_is_echoed_in_full` writes 64 MiB through `serve` to an echo server before it reads any of it, as the VMM does; with the old relay it does not finish in 60 s, with this one it passes in about a second. End to end, krun slots of `bin-base` (the launcher of `8ce363e`), 2 vCPUs, the guest sending 300 MiB in 1 MiB writes while reading the echo: with this relay 4 of 4 slots echoed all 300 MiB in 1.9 to 2.9 s and answered `exec` after; with the deployed relay 3 of 3 stalled until killed at 100 s, and none answered `exec` again. The script is `trial.sh` of the scratch directory, not committed: `vmup.sh` boots the slot, a Python client sends and reads through the forward. `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings` and `cargo test --locked` in `krun/` pass. The passt path was stressed too, 4 slots with 8 parallel 2 GiB downloads each, from a server on the machine and through a network namespace with 60 ms of round trip, also with the guest's vCPUs kept busy: no download stopped for more than 200 ms, with the launcher of `8ce363e`.

**Release.** `nanoeval-net` is part of the launcher's directory: a machine takes it when its `NANOEVAL_KRUN` binaries are rebuilt from this commit, and a slot when its relay starts. dev-georgios runs `~/nc-live/krunfull`, built on libkrun `df85b8b` (lane 3's entry above), which lacks `8ce363e`'s fix of a credit request that never raised the guest's interrupt, the other vsock stall of these slots; rebuilding it from this commit takes both. The retry of 3fc0515 stays for downloads that fail upstream.
## 2026-11-14: two local Workers that start at the same moment

**The defect.** An end-to-end lane sometimes ended within a few seconds with `wrangler dev did not start`, and its `wrangler.log` said `Address already in use. Please check that you are not already running a server on this address or specify a different port with --port.` Earlier entries met it and took it for the port of the Worker: the entry on the credit request counts 6 of 120 and 4 of 80 runs that ended "on the port", "because two copies had taken the same port for their Workers". The port of the Worker was not the one. `wrangler dev` 4.151.1 also opens an inspector for workerd, on the first port from 9229 upwards that it finds free, and it looks before workerd binds. Two that start in the same moment find the same port free, and the second workerd cannot bind it. Read from the listening sockets of three Workers on one machine: each had one port from the kernel for the Worker, and they had 9229, 9230 and 9231.

So it takes two Workers that start together on one machine: two lanes of two checkouts, two runs of the workflow's steps side by side, two installations of `scripts/install-linux.sh` that systemd starts at login, or two `nanoeval worker` of a script. A hosted CI job runs one lane at a time and does not meet it.

**The rule.** `nanoeval worker` and the end-to-end test start `wrangler dev` with `--inspector-port 0`. wrangler passes the 0 on, workerd binds port 0, and the kernel hands each a port of its own. Nothing here reads the inspector, and whoever wants it finds the port among the listening sockets of the workerd process.

**Measured** on a Linux machine with 24 cores and 48 threads (kernel 7.0, Node 24.22.2, wrangler 4.151.1), beside an oracle run of Terminal-Bench 2.1 on 12 krun slots and two runs of the workflow's steps, at a load average between 13 and 25. One run of each line, at `da2a0d4` and at `da2a0d4` with this change.

| | Lost a Worker |
| --- | ---: |
| Two `wrangler dev` of this checkout started together on free ports, 20 rounds | 17 of 20 rounds, each with `Address already in use` |
| The same, each with an inspector port of its own that was free a moment before | 0 of 20 rounds |
| The same, each with `--inspector-port 0` | 0 of 20 rounds |
| Two oracle lanes on directory slots started together in one checkout under two labels, 10 rounds, before the change | 10 of 20 lanes, each with `Address already in use` in its `wrangler.log` |
| The same with the change | 0 of 20 lanes |

A port that `bind(0)` returned and released is not what is taken again: with 6,000 loopback connections opened in the second after its release, it could be bound again in 40 of 40 trials. So the lanes' way of choosing the Worker's port stays as it is.

**Not verified.**

- Other versions of wrangler. The flag is read from `wrangler dev --help` of 4.151.1.
- A deployed Worker, which has no inspector.

## 2026-11-14: an invalid segment from the uplink no longer resets the connection of an ns slot

**The defect.** The lane on ns slots that asks what a private slot reaches (`NANOEVAL_E2E_BACKEND=ns NANOEVAL_E2E_SCENARIO=network`) passed on the machine of the earlier entries and failed on a second one, every time: `wget -q -T 20 -O /dev/null https://example.com/` in the slot ended with "download timed out". In that slot a name resolved, and no TCP connection got an answer to its first request, to any address, over HTTP or HTTPS. The guest that carries the slots reached the same addresses from its own sockets.

Read from a capture in the guest (`tcpdump -ni any -vv`, one HTTP request from the slot):

1. The slot's SYN leaves the guest masqueraded, and the uplink, passt on that machine, answers SYN-ACK. The slot acknowledges and sends its request, 89 bytes.
2. passt sends a segment with no flag at all: a sequence number, a window, no ACK.
3. Connection tracking calls a TCP segment without flags invalid. An invalid packet is not translated back, so it does not go to the slot. It is delivered to the guest itself, on the port the masquerade had chosen, where no socket listens.
4. The guest answers with a reset. passt ends the connection.
5. The slot sends its request again, five times in three seconds in the capture, and nothing answers.

A socket of the guest itself is not hurt by the same segment: TCP discards a segment that has none of ACK, RST and SYN. UDP is not concerned, which is why the name resolved. krun slots are not concerned either: nothing stands between their own stack and passt.

So the fault that shows is the reset, and it is ours: a machine that masquerades for its slots answered, in a slot's place, a packet that it could not attribute to the slot.

**The rule.** The `input` chain of the `nanoeval` table drops TCP that connection tracking calls invalid, `meta l4proto tcp ct state invalid drop`, after the rule that drops what comes from a slot. The machine then says nothing to such a segment, the uplink goes on, and its next segment carries the ACK. `setup` writes the table again when that rule is missing, so a machine that holds the table of an earlier `slot.sh` gets the rule the next time a runner sets it up. The table is replaced in one transaction, and the translations of connections that are open stay with connection tracking.

The rule is on the machine's own input, not only on what answers a slot: a packet that is invalid cannot be told apart by where it was going. What it drops there is what the machine would have answered with a reset or dropped itself.

**Measured** on the second machine: Linux with 24 cores and 48 threads, kernel 7.0, libkrunfw 5.5.0, passt `0.0~git20240220.1e6f92b-1` as its distribution packages it, the lane run by a user who is not root, so its ns slots are in a guest.

| | The lane |
| --- | --- |
| Before, in runs of every step of the workflow at three commits of this day, and run again alone | failed 4 times of 4, each after 33 s, at "a slot resolves a name and reaches it over HTTPS" |
| With the rule, the lane alone | passed 3 times of 3 |

**Every step.** Every `run` step of `.github/workflows/ci.yml` ran from a fresh clone of this change together with the one on the inspector port above, on the machine of this entry, by a user who is not root, beside one other run of the steps each time, three times. On `9c869c3` and on `614bbac`, with the change on a slot whose process is still ending, which went to main on its own: 79 steps each, all passed at once. On `2fd69f5`: 79 steps, 78 passed at once, and the lane on directory slots with two leased sandboxes of which one dies failed once and passed twice when run again alone, as it does on that machine without these changes, where it failed 2 times of 4 at `614bbac`. The 25 lanes on krun slots and the 11 on ns slots ran each time and none was skipped. The `check` job took 15.5 to 16.1 minutes of its 20 and `krun` 22 s. Beside the second run, the same steps of `614bbac` without these changes failed this lane and no other. The commit that holds this paragraph differs from the one that ran last in Markdown only.

**Not verified.**

- Why passt sent that segment there and not on the machine of the earlier entries: its version, the kernel of the machine, 7.0 there against 6.8, and the speed of the connection may all differ, and none was varied.
- A machine that is the root of its ns slots without a guest, and a leased sandbox: the rule is the same table there, and no such machine had the fault to show.

## 2026-11-14: the lane where a leased sandbox dies no longer races its rows

**The defect.** The lane on directory slots with two leased sandboxes of which one dies (`NANOEVAL_E2E_GATEWAY=1 NANOEVAL_E2E_SCENARIO=fleet`) ended the first sandbox when it saw a row of that sandbox's runner in flight, and failed with "the fleet happened during the run" when it never saw one. It reads the status every 100 ms. A sandbox is `ready` only at the tick after its runner said hello, and ticks are half a second apart. On a fast machine the 12 rows of the run were done 1.8 s after it began, so a run could end before one reading had both a ready sandbox and a busy row. The lane was a race against the speed of the machine, and the faster machine lost it.

**Two ways that did not work.**

- Holding back a model response in the model endpoint of the test, as the lanes with a standing runner do. A gateway lane does not use that endpoint: its model requests go to the scripted gateway. The lane failed 6 times of 6.
- Holding the response back in the scripted gateway and answering it after the sandbox had died. The run takes the row from the dead sandbox and halts its session while the request is out, so the gateway charged for a response that the run never read, and the lane failed at "the model spend of the run is what the gateway reported as charged". Once in two runs on a loaded machine.

**The rule.** The scripted gateway can leave a model request without an answer: its `model` returns nothing, the request stays open, nothing is charged for it, and the gateway ends it when the lane closes it. The fleet lane leaves the first model request of the run unanswered. That is the request of the first row of the first sandbox, because a run opens a second sandbox only when the runner of the first has no slot free. The row stays in its `run` phase until the lane has seen it there and ended its sandbox, however fast the machine is. The run then takes the row away, which halts the session and ends the request, and the row is claimed again in another sandbox, where the model answers. The gateway charged nothing that the run did not record.

What the lane no longer does: end a sandbox under a row in any phase it happened to be in. The row is now always waiting for its model.

**Measured.** On directory slots, one run of each line.

| | The lane |
| --- | --- |
| Before, on a machine with 24 cores and 48 threads that did little else: in a run of every step of the workflow, in another as a user without KVM on four of its cores, and alone | failed 2 of 2, 2 of 4 and 2 of 6 times, each with "the fleet happened during the run" |
| Before, on the 32-core machine of the entries above at a load average of 58 to 74, where a row takes seconds | passed 6 of 6 |
| With the change, on that 32-core machine at a load average of 76 to 94 | passed 6 of 6, and 6 of 6 more with the change to leases of the entry below |
| With the change, on a 5-core machine without KVM at a load average of 16 to 21 | passed 2 of 2, and 4 of 4 more with the change to leases. A third run of the first two lost its Worker to the inspector port, before the entry above was under it |

**Not verified.**

- The lane with the change on a machine as fast as the one it failed on. None could be had on the night of the change. On such a machine the row waits as it does on a slow one: nothing answers its model.
- A sandbox that dies while its row is in the environment or the verifier phase. The lane on krun slots where a microVM is killed under its verifier covers the slot, not the sandbox.

## 2026-11-14: the restart lane and a tool call that the restart cut before it left

**The defect.** The lane that kills the Worker during a run and starts it again (`NANOEVAL_E2E_BACKEND=dir NANOEVAL_E2E_SCENARIO=restart`) kills it as soon as a row is active. When the kill falls between the first response of the model and the dispatch of its tool call, the turn that resumes reports that call with an unknown outcome, though it never left the Worker: the pinned nanocode-ts writes the row of the session before it records the request for the hand, and a kill between the two leaves nothing to recover the call from. The scripted model then answers that the task is complete, and a right agent's row is scored `failed`. The lane allowed for that where it counts the rows that passed, and not where it asks every trajectory for a tool call: a row whose only call was cut has none. So the lane failed whenever the kill fell in that window, 2 times in about 12 runs on a 48-thread machine, with one and with three rows cut.

**The rule.** In the restart lane an attempt whose events carry `"outcome_unknown":true` is one whose call the restart cut. A right one may be scored failed, as before, and it need not have a tool call in its trajectory. Every other attempt must, as before. The lane prints how many attempts were cut, so that a run of it says whether it met the window.

**To tighten.** nanocode-ts `ac29d32` with nanocode `67e6a187d` records the request for the hand before the row, and a call that never left is dispatched when the turn resumes. No release that this repository pinned when this was written had it. When the pin carries it, no attempt of this lane may have an unknown outcome: the set `cut` in `test/e2e.ts` goes, with `interrupted`, and the lane asks that every right attempt passed and that every trajectory has a tool call.

**Measured.** With the change, on directory slots, on a 5-core machine without KVM at a load average of 11 to 12: a copy of the lane that kills the Worker 0, 30 and 80 ms after the first answer of the model, in place of the moment a row is active, passed 2 of 2 runs each. Every one of the six printed that the kill cut a tool call of 0 of 8 attempts. The window was not met on that machine, also not when the kill was aimed at it, so the change is not shown on a run that meets the window: the two runs that did are the failures above, on the 48-thread machine, before it.

## 2026-11-14: a lease is renewed while a sandbox is closed

The entry on a lease that is renewed while a runner starts fixed one wait of a tick. The lanes that lease sandboxes for 3 s still failed now and then on a busy machine: a sandbox ended as `lapsed` where the lane asks that every sandbox was terminated, or a run counted three sandboxes where two were expected.

**The defect.** A tick does one thing after another, and renews leases in one of its steps. Three other steps end a sandbox and wait for the provider to have killed it: the one that closes a sandbox with no row left, the one that fails a sandbox whose runner stopped or whose renewal was refused, and the one that closes a sandbox whose lease is over. While a tick waited for such a kill no lease of the run was renewed, as it was while a runner started. A renewal leaves a lease between one and two lease times long, so with leases of 3 s a kill and what else the tick did had about 3 s before the next lease was over, and the tick after it found that lease ended, closed the sandbox and took its rows. A renewal that was refused made it worse inside one pass: the sandbox was killed before the leases after it in the table were renewed.

Read from the timeline of a run of the lane with two leased sandboxes, before this change, on a 5-core machine that other work kept at a load average of 27. The run renewed the lease of its last busy sandbox, 3 s long, and 1.8 s later began to kill the other sandbox, which had no row left. The scripted gateway answered that kill after 3,389 ms. The renewal that followed came 9 ms before the end of the lease by the run's own record, the gateway had ended the sandbox, answered `404`, and the sandbox ended as `failed` where the lane asks `closed`. In another run there the kill of an idle sandbox took 4.3 s with its price, the lease of the busy one ran out during it, and the tick after it closed that sandbox as one whose lease had ended and took its row: the gateway counted it as `lapsed`.

For real a lease is 300 s and is renewed with 60 s left, so a kill would have to take a minute. The lanes lease for 3 s to end in seconds, and a kill through the scripted gateway takes that long when the machine is busy: it ends a runner and removes its directory.

**The rule.** A kill that a tick waits for is attended like the start of a runner: the run renews once every tick period while it waits, one renewal at a time, and goes on when the last one was answered.

- A sandbox is written as `closed` or `failed` before its kill is asked for, so a renewal that runs meanwhile does not renew what is being killed. An idle sandbox was written as closed only after the kill.
- A renewal reads a sandbox again before it asks and after it was answered. What a kill decided meanwhile stands: a sandbox that was closed or failed is not renewed, not moved back to `ready`, and a renewal that was refused for it is not counted as a second failure.
- A pass of renewals renews first and kills afterwards: a sandbox whose renewal was refused is written as failed at once, and killed when every lease of the pass was asked for. When the pass ran beside a kill or a start, it is killed when that has ended.
- The steps that go through the sandboxes read each one again when they come to it, because a kill they waited for may have let a renewal change it.

**Checked.** The lanes that lease sandboxes for 3 s, on directory slots, on the 5-core machine without KVM while other work kept it at a load average of 15 to 27. One run of each line.

| | Before | With the change |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Two leased sandboxes of which one dies | failed 2 of 4: a kill of 3.4 s and one of 4.3 s, each with the lease of the other sandbox over at its end | passed 4 of 4 |
| A sandbox kept warm for a second run | passed 3 of 3 | passed 3 of 3 |
| Model requests whose payment is refused in passing | passed 2 of 2 | passed 3 of 3 |

The "before" of the first line is the lane as it was, with its race against its rows, which a machine this slow does not lose: both failures are the lease. The other two lanes passed before the change as well, in the few runs there were: on this machine they say that the change breaks neither, and nothing more.

On the 32-core machine at a load average of 60 to 90, with the change: the three lanes passed 6 of 6, 3 of 3 and 3 of 3, and the lane with tasks through the gateway 2 of 2. Before the change the same lanes passed there, 6 of 6, 4 of 4 and 4 of 4, the last two with the whole process tree of the lane held to half a CPU (`systemd-run --scope -p CPUQuota=50%`): a quota did not make a kill slow there, a machine with five cores and four times as many runnable processes did.

**Not verified.**

- A real gateway and a deployed Worker, as in the entry on a lease renewed while a runner starts.
- The other waits of a tick: a row that is taken away halts its session and reads its events before the tick goes on, and the pool is asked about a sandbox that is kept. Neither was seen to take long, and neither is attended.
- A runner or a standing member that a busy machine keeps silent for longer than a lease is lost, as the protocol says, and the lanes with leases of 3 s then fail for the machine and not for the code. No lease was made longer to hide it.

## 2026-11-14: a registry that limits pulls is an error, and the lanes read images through the machine's layer cache

**The defect.** Two things met when the steps of the workflow ran more than once in an hour on one machine.

- Every lane on krun and ns slots converted its fixture images with a layer cache of its own, under the directory of the lane. So each lane asked Docker Hub for the same images again, `alpine:3.21`, `python:3.12-alpine` and the base of the guest: about 40 pulls for one run of the steps. Docker Hub gives an address without a login 100 an hour, counted in a window that starts with the hour.
- A registry that answered `429` was waited for. The launcher asked again every minute, for as long as the window the registry names, which is six hours for Docker Hub, and said so on its standard error, which the converter shows only when a build fails. A lane then stood still without a word: on a 48-thread machine one took 310 s where it takes 10, and later lanes waited for the hour to turn.

**The rule.**

- A `429` fails the build at once, with the registry, the request, the limit the registry names in `ratelimit-limit` and the option that waits. `nanoeval-krun image build --pull-wait SECONDS` waits that long for the registry first and asks again after `Retry-After`, or every minute. `nanoeval import --pull-wait SEC` and `NANOEVAL_PULL_WAIT_SEC` pass it on. Without it nothing waits: how long an import may stand still is for the operator to say, and the six hours were nobody's choice. What was read stays in the layer cache and a conversion that ended is recorded, so an import that is started again asks only for what is missing.
- The lanes and the unit tests that convert an image read through the layer cache of the machine, the one an import uses: `NANOEVAL_LAYERS`, or `oci` under `~/.cache/nanoeval`. The guest of the ns lanes already did. The cache keeps layers, configs and manifests by digest with one lock and one download for each, so lanes and runs of the steps side by side share it. On a machine that holds the images a conversion asks the registry only which digest a tag names, a `HEAD` request, which Docker Hub says it does not count.

**Checked.**

- `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings` and `cargo test --locked` in `krun/` on the 32-core machine with KVM: all passed, with a test of what a refused pull says, and the two tests of the launcher that build an image in a microVM.
- A unit test of the policy: `NANOEVAL_PULL_WAIT_SEC` is passed on as whole seconds, and anything else is refused.
- `npm test` on a machine without KVM: 254 tests, 250 passed and the 4 that need KVM skipped.

**Not verified.**

- A `429` from a registry, with and without `--pull-wait`. The wait it replaces ran for the first time in the lanes of this day. The error has not been met.
- The lanes on krun and ns slots and the four unit tests that convert an image, with the layer cache of the machine: the machines with KVM were out of reach when the change was finished. The change in each is one expression, the one the guest of the ns lanes had.
- How many requests a second run of the steps makes on one machine, and that Docker Hub does not count a `HEAD`: the first follows from the cache, the second is what Docker Hub documents, and neither was counted here.

## 2026-11-14: the workflow made ready for hosted runners with KVM

The workflow has never run on GitHub: Actions is disabled for the repository, `GET /repos/nanocodexyz/nanoeval/actions/permissions` answers `"enabled": false` and the repository has no run. Its steps were run on machines at hand instead. This entry changes the workflow so that a hosted runner would run every lane, and says what of that could be checked without one.

**What a hosted `ubuntu-24.04` runner lacks.** It has `/dev/kvm`, and its user may not open it. It has none of libkrunfw, passt and `x86_64-linux-musl-gcc`. So the 25 lanes on krun slots, the 11 on ns slots, four unit tests and the two integration tests of the launcher printed that they were skipped, and the job was green without one attempt in a microVM. One job ran all 76 steps under a limit of 20 minutes: with every lane running they took 15.5 to 16.4 minutes on a machine with 48 threads, and a hosted runner has four.

**The rule.**

- `scripts/ci-machine.sh` gives a machine that is thrown away after a job what it lacks: a udev rule that opens `/dev/kvm` to every user, passt, `musl-tools` and e2fsprogs from the distribution, and libkrunfw 5.5.0 from its release, checked against its SHA-256. It ends with `cargo --version` in `krun/`, which makes rustup install the toolchain that `krun/rust-toolchain.toml` pins, once: the unit tests run their files at the same time, several of them build the launcher, and on a machine that has rustup and not that toolchain each first `cargo` started an install of its own. On a new user with 4 CPUs of a 24-core machine that failed one unit test of 255, 2 times of 2, with `could not rename 'component' file` from rustup, and with one such call made first the 255 passed, once. The composite action `.github/actions/machine` runs it. It is a `uses` step, so a run of "every `run` step of the workflow" on a machine that is kept does not execute it: there the machine is prepared once, by hand, as the README lists.
- Five jobs instead of two. `check`: lint, types, unit tests, the deploy dry run. `e2e-dir`: the 35 lanes on directory slots, which need no KVM and so say something on any runner. `e2e-krun`: the 25 lanes on krun slots. `e2e-ns`: the 11 lanes on ns slots. `krun`: format, clippy and the tests of the launcher. Every job but `e2e-dir` prepares the machine first. Each job installs with `npm ci` itself, so the workflow has 82 `run` steps where it had 79, and each stays one line with its variables on the step, which the scripts that run the steps elsewhere rely on.
- Limits by job: 20 minutes for `check`, `e2e-dir` and `krun`, 45 for `e2e-krun` and 30 for `e2e-ns`. On a machine with 48 threads the steps took 66 s for the checks, 361 s for the directory lanes, 326 s for the krun lanes, 186 s for the ns lanes and 22 s for the launcher, and the directory lanes took 354 s on four of its cores. How long the lanes with KVM take on a hosted runner, which has four cores and nests its virtualization, is not known: the limits leave them about eight times what they took there.
- Two caches for the jobs with KVM, each under a key of its own job. The build of the launcher: `~/.cargo/registry`, `~/.cargo/git` and `krun/target`, by `krun/Cargo.lock` and the pinned toolchain. The layer cache of the lanes, `~/.cache/nanoeval/oci`, by the Dockerfiles of the fixtures, the sample tasks and the guest: with it a job pulls nothing from Docker Hub, whose limit a hosted runner shares with whoever else has its address, and without it a pull that is refused fails its lane with what the registry said, see the entry above.
- A push to main no longer cancels the run of the push before it. Main moved eight times in one morning, and a workflow that cancels on every push would have finished for none of them. A pull request still cancels its own earlier run.
- Actions are named by commit, with the version beside it, and the checkout keeps no credential.

**The one setting.** Actions is switched off for this repository in one of two places, and the answer above does not say which. In the repository: Settings, Actions, General, "Actions permissions", which an administrator of the repository changes. Or in the organization `nanocodexyz`: Settings, Actions, General, Policies, where it is allowed for all repositories or for selected ones that `nanoeval` would have to be among, which only an owner of the organization changes. `gh api repos/nanocodexyz/nanoeval/actions/permissions` reads the first and `gh api orgs/nanocodexyz/actions/permissions` the second. The workflow uses actions of GitHub's own (`actions/checkout`, `actions/setup-node`, `actions/cache`, `actions/upload-artifact`) and one of this repository, so a policy that allows the actions of GitHub and of the repository itself is enough.

**Checked.** `actionlint` 1.7.12 reports nothing for the workflow and its action. The `run` steps of the five jobs were run in order from a fresh clone on machines at hand, without the `uses` steps: which, where and with what result is in the entry on the proof of this day's changes, at the end of this file.

**Not verified.** A run on GitHub. So nothing here says that `scripts/ci-machine.sh` does on a hosted runner what it does on a machine at hand, that the two caches are restored and saved, that the limits of the jobs with KVM hold there, or that the logs of a failed lane are uploaded.
## 2026-11-14: a tool call and an instruction that a session publishes again are counted once

The entry of this day on a turn that goes on after its Worker was killed made the usage and the trajectory of such a session those of the responses it was given: a model call that nanocode reads back from its log carries `timing.replayed` and is not a call, and an instruction accepted again under the same `item_id` is one step. Two more things are published again that it did not cover. This entry changes `src/Atif.ts` and `test/Telemetry.test.ts` only.

**What was measured.** A separate harness around nanocode-ts `build-7968b53` (a minimal Worker on `nanocode-ts/cloudflare` under local workerd, the hand `nanocode-cli-3f97ab0`, a scripted model endpoint for the Messages and the Responses shape) recorded every event handed to `published` while the Worker was killed in a turn of six cells, and `Atif.usage` and `Atif.fromEvents` were run over those events before and after this change. One run of each:

| Session and kill | Before: tool calls, steps | After | Without a kill |
|---|---|---|---|
| `claude`, killed in the fourth cell | 15, 9 | 13, 9 | 13, 9 |
| `claude`, killed while the `wait` is out | 15, 9 | 13, 9 | 13, 9 |
| `claude`, killed in the fourth cell and again while the `wait` is out | 16, 9 | 13, 9 | 13, 9 |
| `codex` on `gpt-right`, killed in the fourth cell | 14, 11 | 13, 9 | 13, 9 |

- **A tool call in flight is published a second time.** When the session goes on, nanocode publishes `tool.call` again for the call of the step that was in flight, with the same `call_id` and no mark, and again for a nested call whose result arrives under a later `wait`. `tool.result` comes once. `Atif.usage` counted every `tool.call`, and `Atif.fromEvents` listed the call twice in its step. Both now keep the first `tool.call` of a `call_id`.
- **A `codex` session accepts its instruction under a new `item_id`.** A `claude` session names the item after the request (`<request>:prompt`), so the rule of that entry held. A `codex` session names it after its own turn id, which is new after a recovery, so the instruction was a second user step and the tool result that followed opened a second agent step: 11 steps for a turn of 9. An accepted prompt is now one step for each `request_id`, which both kinds of session carry. An input of another kind keeps its `item_id`.

Model calls and tokens were already right in all four: 8 calls for 8 responses.

**What the same harness found in nanocode-ts, which this repository cannot fix.** On `build-7968b53`, five runs of each lane unless a count is given:

- A `codex` session killed in a cell, while the model is asked and while a `wait` is out goes on as a `claude` session does, for `gpt-6-luna` and for a model nanocode does not know: 8, 9 and 8 requests, and 8 when it is killed twice. A session on a ChatGPT plan uses the Responses WebSocket for `gpt-6-luna` and sends the whole input again after the Worker is back: 8, 9, 8 and 8 there as well.
- A `claude` session runs the tool calls of one reply one after the other, and every lane with two cells or a cell and a `wait` in one reply passes. A `codex` session on a model nanocode does not know runs them together, and a cell that had finished while another was still running came back as "outcome unknown" in 5 of 5 runs (the command did not run twice). The reply of the finished cell is recorded without the nested calls that its updates carried, and nanocode-ts cannot read it back. A TypeScript change to nanocode-ts that keeps them makes the lane pass 5 of 5 times on the same hand and WebAssembly module; it is not in a release, so the pin here does not have it.
- A turn that spawned a subagent does not go on cleanly: the cell of the parent that waits in `wait_agent` fails, and the cell of the child that was running is reported with an unknown outcome while it keeps running on the hand (0 of 5 runs passed for each of three kills, and 5 of 5 without a kill). Both are in nanocode.
- A Worker killed within a few milliseconds of a model answer: at 0 ms the answer is lost, the request is sent again, and the lost response is in no usage count (9 answered, 8 counted, 5 of 5 runs); at 3 ms the same happened in 13 of 15 runs, and in 2 the row of the cell was written and the frame had not reached the hand, and the model read "outcome unknown" for a command that never ran.
- The usage of a subagent is not in `Atif.usage`: it reads the events of the session's own agent, and a child's model calls arrive as `subagent` events. Seen without any kill (4 calls counted for 9 answered). Not changed here.

**Checked.**

- `test/Telemetry.test.ts`: the events of `build-81eada9` with the instruction, `run.started`, the model call as replayed and the two `tool.call` events of the second cell published a second time give the usage and the trajectory of the events without them, and so do the same events with the instruction under another `item_id`. Without the change to `Atif` the test fails on 6 tool calls for 4.
- `npm run lint`, `npm run check:types` and `npm test`: 149 tests, 145 passed and 4 skipped on a machine without KVM.

**Not verified.** The end-to-end lanes of this repository were not run with the change, and no lane here kills a `codex` session: the numbers above are from the separate harness. A second `tool.result` for one `call_id`, which a recovered cell can publish, is still two results in a step. A deployed Worker and a real model, as in the entry before this.

## 2026-11-14: a lane for a cell that answered beside a running one, and what the next nanocode-ts pin must hold

The entry on the tool calls that a session publishes again listed what a separate harness found in nanocode-ts `build-7968b53` and this repository could not fix. One of those was fixed in nanocode-ts on this day: when the tool calls of one reply run side by side and the Worker is killed after one cell has answered and while another still runs, the cell that had answered came back to the model as "Tool execution interrupted by a host crash; outcome unknown". This entry adds the kill that shows it to the lane `midturn`, checks the tool calls in the three kills that were there, and records why the pin of nanocode-ts was not moved and what the next pin must hold. It changes `test/e2e.ts` and README.md. `package.json`, `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, `worker/` and `src/` are unchanged.

**The cause and the fix, in nanocode-ts.** A hand answers a cell with a compact reply: a call inside the cell whose end the hand had already sent as an update is listed as delivered, and the hand keeps the whole reply only until the brain acknowledges the compact one. The session stored the compact reply alone, in its table `hand_requests`, and nanocode cannot read that back without the updates. A session whose calls run one after the other never has to: since `build-7968b53` the result of a cell is in a row of the log before the next request leaves. A `codex` session runs the calls of one reply together, so a cell that answered while its neighbour ran had its result in no row. nanocode sends `parallel_tool_calls: true` for a model it does not know and `false` for `gpt-6-luna`, and runs two calls together for either when the model sends them. The fix (nanocode-ts 4f2f8f9 on its master) keeps the update frames of a hand request, writes them to a new table of the session object, `hand_updates`, when the reply names a delivered call, and reads the reply back whole. It is TypeScript only.

**The builds that hold the fix.**

| Build | What it is | Holds |
|---|---|---|
| `build-fab71ba` | nanocode-ts master at 4f2f8f9 and its two commits of lanes and notes, nanocode 86c465b | this fix. Not `codex_orchestration` |
| `build-ac29d32` | nanocode-ts master at ac29d32, nanocode 67e6a187d | this fix, and the fixes for a turn that spawned a subagent and for a cell whose frame never left (nanocode 8f70c4a72, eb707662a, 16217ef97). Not `codex_orchestration` |
| `build-0f8ae19` | `build-f3aa94f` and the one commit of this fix, on the nanocode-ts branch `feat/codex-orchestration-hand-updates` | this fix and `codex_orchestration`. Not the other three |

`build-0f8ae19` has the four WebAssembly modules of `build-f3aa94f` byte for byte. The package differs in `dist/cloudflare/App.js`, the new `dist/cloudflare/internal/Replies.js` and the Pyodide snapshot, which every build writes anew. Its tarball has SHA-256 `0af3f1a5935c09b6ed2dba58c3ed347c57c40c38a6020ed960332630f4dc102e` and the integrity `sha512-P1RVlUTLhfdIUG+uBf2sJWDdgpCdV6VHkpvgPbXepBVQtvipaHfVj6TeKqRqdkVckvbOFD8+YJiX3RY85b22XQ==`.

**Why the pin stays at `build-f3aa94f`.** The `codex-direct` agent needs `codex_orchestration`, which is nanocode-ts f3aa94f and nanocode 0e428f673, each on a branch and on neither master. On a build of master, a turn whose body says `codex_orchestration: "direct"` is a Code Mode session, so a pin of master would change that agent without a word. `build-0f8ae19` keeps the option and was measured below, but it holds one of the fixes and not the other three, and a pin is moved once: a run records its pins, and the baseline of a comparison is the latest run on the pinned builds, so every move starts the baselines again. Bringing the other three onto the branch line was tried and stopped. The two nanocode commits for subagents apply to 0e428f673. The third, 16217ef97, conflicts in `crates/backends/claude/src/agent/durable.rs` with changes that master has and the branch has not, and a merge by hand of the recovery of a call is not a thing to ship unread by its author.

**What the next pin must hold**, all of it in one build:

1. `codex_orchestration`: nanocode-ts f3aa94f (`src/cloudflare/App.ts`, `src/Contracts.ts`, `src/wasm.rs`) and nanocode 0e428f673.
2. nanocode-ts 4f2f8f9, the fix of this entry.
3. nanocode-ts ac29d32 with nanocode 8f70c4a72, eb707662a and 16217ef97.

The plain way is that `codex_orchestration` lands on both masters and the pin goes to the first release of nanocode-ts master after it. That move is a large one: from 2aad477 it takes 13 commits of nanocode-ts and, from the base of 0e428f673, the nanocode of master, 67e6a187d or later. What a session of this repository sends on a build of master is under the next heading. The move needs the request check below again and, for a `codex` agent, a paired arm. With it, the kill `pair` joins the lanes of `midturn` in `ci.yml`, six lines after the step of the kill `wait` with `NANOEVAL_E2E_KILL: pair`, and the README rows of the harness sessions and of the orchestrator restart name the build.

**What a session sends on the builds with the fix.** Every model request of the kills `cell` and `pair` below, and of `pair` with `gpt-6-luna` in the place of `gpt-right`, was written out under `build-f3aa94f`, `build-0f8ae19` and `build-fab71ba`, on directory slots with the same hand, `nanocode-cli-3f97ab0`.

- **`build-0f8ae19`**: the 8 requests of the `claude` session are byte for byte those of `build-f3aa94f` in the first five, and differ in the last three only in the wall time that the cell which was waited for reports. The 5 requests of each `codex` session are the same but for ids, the directory of the slot, and the one output that the fix is for.
- **`build-fab71ba`**: the `claude` requests and the `gpt-6-luna` requests are the same in that sense. For `gpt-right`, `prompt_cache_key` is the id of the session where it was a digest of the prefix. Not seen in a request and in the brain of that build: a streaming turn is admitted without a row of its own, a model without remote compaction compacts locally at 90% of its window, a reply without visible text is nudged once, and a 402 of the gateway's payment layer is retried.
- **`build-ac29d32`**: every session sends other text for its two tools. The description of `exec` is 12,101 bytes where it was 11,426 for a `claude` session, and 31,821 where it was 31,398 for a `codex` session, in its sentences on the token budget, on work that is not awaited, on `audio`, `notify` and `exit`, and on a name missing from `ALL_TOOLS`. `wait` and the two budget fields say "no budget of its own" where they said "unlimited output". A `claude` request also carries `metadata.user_id` and the header `x-claude-code-session-id`, and a `gpt-right` request the id of the session as `prompt_cache_key`. Scores on that build do not stand beside earlier ones without a paired arm.

**The kill.** `NANOEVAL_E2E_SCENARIO=midturn NANOEVAL_E2E_KILL=pair`, on directory slots: one row of `write-greeting` and one `codex` session on `gpt-right`, a model nanocode does not know, paid with a key so that its Responses requests reach the scripted endpoint without the gateway. The model answers `exec 1`, then two cells in one reply, `exec 2a` and `exec 2b`, of which the second sleeps 20 s, then a `wait` for the cell that still runs, then `exec 3`, which writes the greeting and prints `steps.log`, then its final message. The Worker is killed 5 s after `steps.log` in the slot holds `step-2a` and `step-2b`: the first cell has answered, the second runs, and its yield of 10 s has not passed. It asks what the three kills before it ask, for five requests and four commands, and that no output the model was sent reads `outcome unknown`. All four now also ask that the tool calls of the attempt are the distinct `call_id` values of the `tool.call` events it kept, and the three whose cells run one at a time that they are 13.

| Kill `pair` | `build-7968b53` and `build-f3aa94f` | `build-0f8ae19` and `build-fab71ba` |
|---|---|---|
| the model is asked | `exec 1`, `exec 2a+exec 2b`, `wait`, `exec 3`, final | the same five |
| the output of `exec 2a` in the request after the kill | the unknown outcome | the result of the cell |
| the lane | fails: the model did not read the result of a cell that had answered | passes |

**What the kept events of that attempt hold**, on the builds with the fix: 10 `tool.call` events for 8 ids, where 9 calls ran. The two `exec` calls of the reply are published again when the session goes on, which the entry before this counts once. The Bash call inside the cell that was in flight has its `tool.result` and no `tool.call`: the event of its start was handed to the session before the kill and was in no row of the log, and nanocode does not publish it again. So that attempt shows 8 tool calls, and its trajectory has the result of that call without the call. The kills whose cells run one at a time keep all 13. Not changed here: which events a session keeps is nanocode's.

**Checked** on a machine with 5 cores and no KVM, with the hand `nanocode-cli-3f97ab0`. No model was paid for.

- **The kill `pair`**: fails on `build-7968b53` and on the pinned `build-f3aa94f` (3 runs each, one of them with `gpt-6-luna`), each time on the result the model did not read. Passes on `build-0f8ae19` 7 of 7, five of them in a row in 38 to 53 s with the Worker back 5.4 to 7.7 s after the kill beside two other lanes on the machine, and once more with `gpt-6-luna`. Passes on `build-fab71ba` and on `build-ac29d32`, one run and one with `gpt-6-luna` each.
- **The kills `cell`, `model` and `wait` with the check of the tool calls**, on the pinned build: passed, each with 13 tool calls. Also on `build-0f8ae19`, three runs each.
- **nanocode-ts's own lanes**, the harness that its `bench/resume` was written from, five runs a lane. On `build-7968b53` the lane of this fix, `pairDone` on a `codex` session on `gpt-right`, failed 5 of 5. On a package of the commit of `build-0f8ae19` with the modules of that release, and on the tarball of `build-fab71ba`, it passed 5 of 5, and so did eleven other lanes on each: `cell`, `model`, `wait`, `twoKills`, `pairDone` and `clean` on a `claude` session, `cell`, `pair`, `pairWaits` and `waitExec` on `gpt-right`, and `cell` on `gpt-6-luna` over the Responses WebSocket.
- `npm run lint`, `npm run check:types`, `npm run dry-run` and `npm test`: 224 tests, 220 passed and 4 skipped on a machine without KVM.
- The proof of this change, every `run` step of `.github/workflows/ci.yml` from a fresh clone, is in the entry on what was run for the changes of this day, at the end of this file.

**Not verified.**

- A deployed Worker and a real model. A real `gpt-6-luna` is sent `parallel_tool_calls: false`, so the case needs a model that is not in nanocode's catalog, or one that answers two calls all the same.
- The `codex-direct` agent on `build-0f8ae19`. Its option is in the package (`codex_orchestration` is in `dist/cloudflare/App.js` as often as in `build-f3aa94f`), and no lane here runs it.
- A cell whose calls are tools of the brain, which nanocode-ts names as not covered by its fix, and two cells that had both answered.
- The kill on krun and ns slots: it reads `steps.log` in the directory of a slot, and the change is in the session object.
- `hand_updates` in a real session: its rows go when the request they belong to is pruned, and their size was measured by nanocode-ts only (11 rows and 3.5 KB more for a turn of six cells).
- A build with all of what the next pin must hold: none exists.

## 2026-11-14: a sandbox whose runner left before the run saw it start is closed

**Found** with the lane of two leased sandboxes of which one dies (`NANOEVAL_E2E_SCENARIO=fleet` through the scripted gateway, directory slots), on a 5-core machine, at `438f2a9`: the lane did not end. The run had opened a sandbox for the rows that waited. A tick that opens a sandbox stays in it until the runner was started, and the rows ended in the other sandbox meanwhile. The new runner said hello, was told that the run had no row left, and left, 43 ms after its hello and between two ticks. The next tick found a sandbox in state `starting` whose runner had `left`. That was neither a runner that is ready nor one that is lost, so the sandbox stayed `starting`, its lease was renewed, and the run did not finish, until `--setup-sec` had passed and the sandbox was failed with "the runner did not start within 600 s". On a deployed Worker that is up to `--setup-sec` of lease, 1,200 s in the paid runs of this day, for an empty sandbox at the end of a run, and a run that ends that much later.

**The rule.** A sandbox has started once its runner said what its machine can do, whatever the runner did next: it is ready, it was refused, or it left. A started sandbox whose runner holds no row is closed, or kept warm, by the tick as soon as no row waits, so one whose runner has left goes in the tick that sees it.

**Checked.** The lane of the next entry holds the start of a runner back until every row of the run has ended, and asks that its sandbox is closed with a runner that left and ran no row, and that the run ends inside `--setup-sec`. With this rule taken out of the tree of that entry the lane kept that sandbox `starting` for the 600 s of its `--setup-sec`, failed it with "the runner did not start within 600 s", ended after 643 s and recorded $0.2641 for its sandboxes, where it ends after 78 to 147 s and records $0.047 to $0.088 with the rule, and failed on the count of sandboxes that were closed. The lane of two leased sandboxes, which hung once in one run before, passed 1 time of 1 after on the same machine.

**Not verified.** A deployed Worker and a real gateway. A sandbox kept warm whose runner left before the tick: the same branch, read and not run.

## 2026-11-14: a sandbox that could not be opened is asked for again

**Found** in a paid run of 54 rows on this day, which asked a gateway for 8 sandboxes. The provider behind the gateway lets 20 sandboxes run at once, for all who pay it together, and others held 14: the creates of sandboxes 7 and 8 were answered `429 rate_limited`, "you have reached the maximum number of concurrent E2B sandboxes (20)", two minutes into the run. A run counted the sandboxes that failed, opened none once two had failed in a row, and forgot the count only when a sandbox started. The six sandboxes worked on, and five were closed as their rows ended. An hour in, the sixth stopped answering under a row. The count still stood at two, and the sandbox that had died made it three, so the row, on the first of its three claims, ended at once as `environment: Gateway.RefusedError: the gateway refused create with 429`. Two things were wrong: a refusal that passes was counted like a failure that does not, and a sandbox that had worked for an hour was counted as one that could not be opened. A third was the money: the key was charged $0.12664 for each of the two refused creates, and the run had written both back.

**Reproduced** with the scripted gateway on directory slots, in the lane `capped` below: two sandboxes allowed, a cap of one, and the sandbox ended under its row once two creates were refused. On the code before, 12 of 12 rows ended as that `environment` error the moment the sandbox ended.

**The rule.** `src/Opening.ts` holds it, and the run keeps what it needs beside its other state.

- **What a failure to open is.** A sandbox that never started: its create failed, or its runner did not start in it. A sandbox that started and ended later, by its provider, by its lease or by a runner that stopped answering, is none: its rows go back, each counts a claim, and the run opens another as it does for any row that waits.
- **Refused for now.** A create that the gateway answered `402`, `408`, `429`, or at `5xx` with a problem of its own, before or after it was priced. These are the answers that say no sandbox was opened and that time may change: a cap, a rate, a gateway that cannot pay a fee right now, a payment that a top-up settles. Everything else is a failure that does not pass by itself: another `4xx`, a create whose outcome nothing proves, a sandbox budget that is spent, a runner that does not start.
- **When it asks again.** After the first failure with the next tick, then after the notice of the run (`--lease-sec`, 60 s), then after twice that, and so on up to `--setup-sec`. A `Retry-After` on the refusal is kept when it is the longer of the two. A sandbox that starts ends the pauses. The sandboxes the run has work on meanwhile, and no row ends because another sandbox could not be opened. At `--lease-sec 60 --setup-sec 1200` a provider that refuses for a whole hour is asked 8 times in it, at 0, 2, 62, 182, 422, 902, 1,862 and 3,062 s.
- **With no sandbox left.** When a row waits and no sandbox of the run serves, the run asks at once and starts the pauses over. From that moment the rows wait `--setup-sec`, the time a row waits for a runner everywhere else in a run. Then they end as `environment` errors that say for how long, in how many tries and with what last answer no sandbox could be opened, and `run --rerun RUN --errored` takes them. At the same figures that is five more creates, at 0, 60, 180, 420 and 900 s.
- **Failures that do not pass.** Two in a row close the opening, as before: rows that no sandbox can take end at once with the failure, as `budget` errors when it was the budget. New is that it is closed for `--setup-sec` after the last of the two and not for the rest of the run, so a run whose sandboxes end an hour later asks again.
- **What the run says.** `status` has a line while rows wait: `sandboxes: 6 open; another could not be opened 2 times since +128 s, and is asked for again at +190 s: Gateway.RefusedError: the gateway refused create with 429: …`, and with none left `sandboxes: none open; one could not be opened 3 times since +3665 s, and is asked for again at +3728 s; the rows that wait end as errors at +4865 s unless one starts: …`. The run's JSON has the same as `opening`.

**What it costs.** The provider is paid before it answers: its payment proxy takes the price of the lease and then asks for the sandbox, so a create that is refused for the cap has been paid for, and nothing returns it. A refusal that says what was kept, as a number of USD in `meta.kept` of its problem, is recorded at that: the rest of the price is written back, and `payments` holds a row `compute.create refused with 429, of which the provider kept $0.12664`. A `429` to a paid create that names nothing keeps the whole price, which is what the key showed on the day. Every other refusal is written back as before. So the sandbox spend of a run and `--sandbox-budget-usd` count the creates that bought nothing, and the pauses above bound them: at the price of the day an hour of refusals is at most $1.01, and nothing once the gateway refuses before it pays.

**What was weighed.** Asking with every tick, as a run did after one failure, is 1,800 creates an hour against a provider that said no, each of them paid for. A fixed number of tries is the defect. Ending the rows at the first refusal with no sandbox left gives up what a minute later may be there, and waiting without an end leaves a run that never finishes: `--setup-sec` is the wait a run already names.

**Checked.** Unit tests in `test/Opening.test.ts`: which answers pass, the pauses, an hour of refusals beside sandboxes that work, the five creates and the end of a run that is alone, a pause the provider names, two failures that close the opening and what `--setup-sec` later does to them; in `test/Gateway.test.ts`: what is kept and what is written back for a refused create with and without `meta.kept`, and the `Retry-After` of a refusal before and after the price. The lane `capped`, in `ci.yml` on directory slots: beside a sandbox that works, a cap of one refuses three creates, the second at once and the third one notice later; the scripted gateway keeps the price of the first, as a provider that is paid first does, and of no other; it then ends the sandbox under a row and allows none, and the status says until when the rows wait; then it allows two, the row is claimed again in a new sandbox, and no row errors. It passed 5 times of 5 on a 5-core machine without KVM at a load average of 12 to 20, in 78 to 147 s. The other lanes through the scripted gateway on directory slots, whose first create is refused with `503`, passed as before.

**Not verified.** The real gateway and the real cap: nothing was paid for this change. A `402` and a `408` on a create, and a gateway that refuses before it prices: classified from the status and unit tested, not met. The `meta.kept` of a refusal is the gateway's to carry, and no deployed gateway was seen to send it. A warm sandbox of the pool taken while creates are refused: the pool is asked when the run is about to open a sandbox, so it is not asked during a pause. krun and ns slots: the rule is the run's and does not know the slot, and the lane runs on directory slots only.

## 2026-11-14: a gateway sandbox lives an hour

**Found** in the paid run of the entry above. The run named a lifetime of 43,200 s for its sandboxes, the gateway took it and answered an `expiresAt` twelve hours ahead, and the run renewed the lease of its first sandbox four times, the last time 3,547 s after it was created. The sandbox stopped answering 3,597 s after it was created, with its lease paid for another 14 minutes. E2B ends a sandbox 3,600 s after it starts, whatever timeout it was asked for and whatever is paid, as it does for a sandbox paid over MPP directly (the entry on the 3,600 s of `E2b.maxTimeoutSec`): its own record of two renewed sandboxes of the same account showed an end exactly 3,600.000 s after their start. The run had planned its rows against twelve hours, so a row whose timeouts no hour covers was claimed 20 minutes into the sandbox and lost with it.

**The rule.**

- `Gateway.maxTimeoutSec` is 3,600, where it was 86,400. A lifetime named above it with `--sandbox-timeout-sec` is refused before a run exists, with the figure, and a lifetime the run computes is cut to it. A sandbox then takes a row only while the timeouts of the row end before the hour does, stops claiming once no row that is left does, and the run opens another for those, as the entry on a runner that knows its end describes.
- The end of a sandbox is the sooner of what the gateway answers and what the run asked, counted from before the create was sent: a gateway that answers `now + timeout` after the sandbox has started names an end some seconds after the provider's.
- A sandbox that ends sooner than both is a sandbox that died: its rows go back and another is opened, by the entry above.

**Checked.** The unit test of the provider refuses 3,601 s before any request. The lane `capped` ends a sandbox by its provider under a paid lease. The lanes through the scripted gateway name 3,600 s and passed.

**Not verified.** Nothing was paid for this change: a run of more than an hour on the real gateway with this rule was not made. A gateway that answers a sooner `expiresAt` than asked is taken by the same line that takes a later one, which no lane exercises. A renewal that the gateway refuses with `409` because it would pass the end still marks the sandbox as ending, as before.

## 2026-11-14: a deploy restarts the pool at once, and the pool says which commit it runs

**What was promised.** The entry on a standing runner with several runs says, under "State of an existing deployment": "Members 'with a run' whose runners are gone are closed and removed one notice after the deploy, at the first alarm." The notice of a standing runner is 60 s.

**What the deployment did.** The Worker was deployed from the commit before that change to `2244c58`. Its pool held five members "with a run" of standing runners that had been stopped hours before, some closed members, and one member of a runner that stood by. The runner was started again from the new commit half a minute after the deploy. The five members and the closed ones were still listed 3 min 20 s after the deploy and were gone 7 min 48 s after it: between 3 min 20 s and 7 min 48 s, not one notice.

**The cause is not in the table.** With the change, such a member is due at once: `wakeAt` answers a time hours in the past for it, `schedule` sets the alarm to now with every request that ends, and nothing a live runner does keeps a member of no machine. The pool did not run the change. Cloudflare lets a Durable Object that is active keep the code before a deploy until it hibernates, for up to 300 s by default ([Durable Objects code updates](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/deployments/durable-objects-code-updates/): "By default, Durable Objects defer code updates for up to 300 seconds (5 minutes) to give in-flight requests time to finish. An active object can keep running its current code until it hibernates or reaches this delay."). A standing runner holds a request for a third of its lease and asks again when it ends, so the pool never hibernates, and `wrangler.jsonc` named no strategy. 300 s after the deploy lies inside what was seen. Until then the pool was one without the change, which is the case "Order of a deploy" of that entry warns of: the runner of the new commit enrolled in it.

**Measured** under local workerd on 2026-11-14, on a Linux machine with 5 cores, kernel 6.18, at a load average of 9 to 20, once each. `wrangler dev --persist-to` at `da2a0d4`, the commit before the change, with `HOLD_MS` 50000: eight members enrolled over HTTP with a notice of 60 s, two of them left, one held by a script that asks as a runner does, for 20 s at a time. The Worker was stopped, five members were made "with a run" and last seen 3 h before in the pool's SQLite file, and a Worker was started on the same directory.

| What ran on that state | When the five members and the closed ones were gone |
| --- | --- |
| `438f2a9`, the runner still asking | 20.2 s after the Worker started, when its first held request ended |
| `438f2a9`, the runner leaving 23 s after the start | 20.6 s |
| `438f2a9`, nobody asking | 31.7 s, at the alarm the code before had set |
| `da2a0d4` again for 200 s, with the runner stopped and one of the new commit enrolled, as on the deployment | never: listed at every one of 20 readings 10 s apart, and the member of the runner that left was listed as closed |
| `438f2a9` after those 200 s | 20.6 s after it started |

Local workerd defers no update: the Worker that is started is the code that runs. So the minutes appear only while the object runs the code before, and there the listing is the one the deployment showed.

**The rule now.**

- `wrangler.jsonc` asks for `"code_update_strategy": { "mode": "immediate" }`: a deploy restarts every object of the Worker, the runs and sessions as well as the pool. A restart ends the requests an object holds and nothing it has written. A runner asks again, and a run whose Worker restarts under its attempts finishes, which the lanes that kill the Worker ask. A test in `test/Pool.test.ts` reads the setting, since no test of the table can fail for it.
- The pool says the commit its object runs: `commit` of `GET /v1/pool`, and the first line of `nanoeval pool`. `GET /v1/version` cannot say it, the Worker answers that without an object. A pool of a commit before this one says none, and the command prints that.
- The promise, corrected: members "with a run" whose runners are gone are closed and removed at the first alarm after the pool object starts on the change, which is due at once: 20 s later while a runner stands by, when its held request ends, and 32 s later with none. Without `immediate` an active pool starts on it up to 300 s after the deploy.
- The order of a deploy stays "the Worker first", and now ends when the pool names the deployed commit: `node cli/nanoeval.ts pool` after `wrangler deploy --var COMMIT:$(git rev-parse HEAD)`. The README says so.

**Checked.** `node --test test/Pool.test.ts` with the test and the `wrangler.jsonc` before: 7 passed, 1 failed. With the setting: 8 passed. `npm run dry-run` with wrangler 4.151.1 takes the setting. `nanoeval pool` against a Worker at `da2a0d4` printed "commit not said: its object runs the code of a commit before the pool said one". Every end-to-end lane now reads the commit of the lane from the pool, and the lane `standing` passed with it on directory slots.

**Not verified.**

- What `immediate` does on a deployed Worker: not deployed. That an object which still runs the code before also answers with the commit before is how Cloudflare describes a version, code and variables together, and was not seen either.
- That the pool of the deployment ran the code before for those minutes was not read from it. It follows from Cloudflare's default, from the missing setting, from the times, and from the same listing under the code before.
- The five members were made in the file of the pool, not by a run whose runner was stopped.
- Runs in flight at a deploy on Cloudflare: each of their objects is now restarted at the deploy where it was restarted within 300 s before.

## 2026-11-14: a member that a run took and handed nothing goes back to the pool

**The defect.** The entry on a standing runner with several runs left it open: "a member that a run took but never assigned (the run died between the two pool calls) stays 'assigned' while its runner keeps asking". A run gets a runner from the pool in two calls. `take` marks a member as the run's. The run then writes a runner of its own for it, and `assign` hands the member the configuration of that runner, which answers the request the standing runner holds. When the second call never comes or fails, because the run's object was restarted between the two, the run was cancelled or deleted, or the pool did not answer, the member is "with a run" and has nothing to give its runner. The runner is answered that there is no run yet and asks again, for good:

- The pool closes a machine member only when no member of its machine asks any more, and this one asks.
- No other run takes it, since it is not idle. The run that took it is not handed another member of the same machine, since it has one.
- The runner enrols one more member only when a member of it is handed a run. So a standing runner in this state serves nothing until it is started again, and the rows of every run that waits for it end as `environment` errors after `--setup-sec`.

A deploy restarts every object at once since the entry before this one, which makes a run that is restarted between the two calls more likely than it was.

**The rule.** A take is the run's for one notice of the member, the time the pool already gives a runner to say a word.

- The pool keeps when a member was taken (`members.taken_at`). A machine member that is "with a run", has no assignment, and was taken more than its notice ago goes back: idle, with no run, and with one run less in its count, since the run that handed it nothing is no run of it. Its runner notices nothing, and the request it holds is the one the next run answers.
- `wakeAt` names that moment, and the pool sets its alarm when a member is taken. Before, a take set no alarm.
- A member whose runner asks no more is closed as before, taken or not: that rule is asked first.
- An `assign` that comes after the member went back is refused, as it was for any member that is not the run's. `adopt` in `worker/Run.ts` already calls its runner lost then and takes again at a later tick. The ticks of a run are one at a time, so a run has one take in flight.
- A run that is alive and lost its `assign` waits one notice for the member, 60 s for a standing runner with the default lease, which is inside the default `--setup-sec` of 600. Handing the member again to the same run at its next tick would be faster, and was left out: the pool cannot tell a run that asks again from the same take arriving late.
- A kept sandbox (`--warm-sec`) is not given back. A run that is alive finds the runner of such a sandbox by the lease and ends the sandbox, which would then end under the run that took it next.

**State of an existing deployment.** The column is added when the pool object next starts. A machine member that is "with a run" and has no assignment then is taken to have been taken when its runner last asked, so it goes back one notice after that, or is closed when its runner is gone. Runs are not touched, and `Protocol.version` stays: nothing between a runner and a Worker changes.

**The lane `taken`**, new in `ci.yml` on directory slots. Nothing in the Worker that is deployed lets an operator lose a call between two objects, and none was added: the lane starts `wrangler dev` on `test/worker/Taken.ts`, a Worker of the lane that exports the objects of `worker/index.ts` and extends the pool with one route, `POST /v1/pool/lose-assign`, after which the pool answers the next `assign` with `503`. The take is the real one, of a real run. The lane stands a runner with a lease of 10 s, asks the pool to lose an assign, creates a run, waits until the pool lists the member with that run, cancels the run and asks that the member is still listed with it. It then creates a second run with `--setup-sec 30`, and asks that the pool hands it the same member with a count of one run, no sooner than one notice after the first run was asked for, that it ends as every lane's run, and that the runner exits with status 0 and leaves the pool empty when it is stopped.

**Measured** on 2026-11-14 on a Linux machine with 5 cores, kernel 6.18, at a load average of 17 to 32, scripted model, 3 tasks and 2 agents.

| | The lane |
| --- | --- |
| At the commit of the entry before, with the lane and its Worker | failed, once of once, after 127 s: "the second run ended with no member of the pool", its 6 rows `environment` errors, "no runner of the run could take the row for 30 s: the run has no runner, and opens no sandbox itself" |
