Standard output is unchanged, and so is everything a script reads: the watcher reads no text of the command.

The same run after the change, the times of the machine in front:

```
09:29:05 [0:00] worker: starting under local workerd on the state in LAB/worker
09:29:13 [0:08] worker: http://127.0.0.1:32891, log in LAB/logs/worker.log
09:29:13 [0:08] import: 3 task directories
09:29:14 run RUN: 9 attempts of local@59cb6b725a72
09:29:14 [0:09] runner: started on the rows of the run, log in LAB/logs/runner-RUN.log
09:29:14 [0:09] rows: 0 of 9 ended, 0 running, 9 waiting
09:29:22 [0:17] rows: 0 of 9 ended, 2 running, 7 waiting
09:29:33 [0:28] rows: 2 of 9 ended (2 passed, 0 failed, 0 errored), 2 running, 5 waiting
09:30:10 [1:05] rows: 9 of 9 ended (9 passed, 0 failed, 0 errored), 0 running, 0 waiting
```

**Rejected.** A progress bar or a percentage: rows take from seconds to an hour each, so a share of rows says nothing about the time left. A line every N seconds where nothing changed: a log would fill with the same line, and the interval would be a number nobody measured. The time of each phase at its end instead of the clock at its start: a phase that hangs would then print nothing, which is the defect.

**Checked.** A unit test of the lines and their clock, of the counter in a file (a line a change) and on a terminal (one line rewritten, erased before another line), and of `--quiet`. The lane of the entry below reads the lines of the Worker, the import, the runner, both builds and the rows from the command itself, and nothing but the baseline's line from a command with `--quiet`.

**Not verified.** The line on a real terminal was read by nobody: the test asks for the bytes. The steps of the package build were read from a build of two small local repositories, not of nanocode-ts.

## 2026-11-14: evaluations take a lab in the order they were started, and name a baseline before it exists

Several `nanoeval revision` commands in one lab waited on `flock`, and the kernel gives a lock that is freed to whichever waiter it wakes first. Reproduced on the commit before this change, on directory slots with a scripted model: four commands started half a second apart behind a running one got the lab first, third, second and fourth. And `--baseline` took the id of a run, which an evaluation that waits behind its baseline's evaluation cannot know: three revisions to compare meant three commands typed one after another, each after reading the id the one before printed.

**The queue.** An evaluation takes a ticket before it waits: a file `queue/N.json` in the lab, N one more than the highest there, written under a lock that is held for that moment only, and it holds a lock on its ticket for as long as it lives. It then waits for the lock of every ticket with a lower number, in order, removes each when it gets it, and takes the lock of the lab. So the order is the order of the tickets, a command that was killed while it waited frees its ticket with its last process and is passed over, and nothing is polled. The line that says an evaluation waits names what is ahead: "lab: waiting in LAB for 2 evaluations that came first: nanocode 0a9ed13f2337 (process 4711), nanocode pinned, the-name (process 4712)".

**The names of a baseline.** `--baseline` takes, beside an id and `latest`:

- `previous`: the run before this one. It is the newest finished run of the eval, on any builds, that is not a rerun, was not cancelled, has the agents of this run, paid for and reached as they are, and holds at least one of its tasks unchanged.
- a revision, as `--nanocode` takes it, or `pinned`: the newest such run whose one hand is that revision. A commit, a branch or a tag is resolved in the lab's build tree, a directory is read as a checkout with its changes, so the name a revision was built under is the name that finds its run.

Each is looked up when the evaluation has the lab, after the evaluations ahead of it ended, which is what makes the names useful to a command that waits. Anything that is not `latest`, `previous` or the id of a run is a revision, in `nanoeval revision` only: `run` and `compare` have no lab to resolve it in. The command prints the run it took and its builds.

**Rejected.** A `--after RUN` option that waits for another run: it still needs an id. Tickets named by time: two commands in one millisecond, and clocks that step. A daemon that owns the lab: every command of this repository ends when its work does. Holding the lab's lock in ticket order by passing a token through a pipe: the kernel's lock on a file is released when its holder dies, which a token is not.

**Checked.**

- Unit tests: five holders started in a row get the lab in that order, each told who is ahead; a ticket whose holder is gone is removed and not waited for; the tickets are gone when the holders are; the rule for `previous` and for a revision, and the search and its refusal for each.
- The lane starts three evaluations as fast as their tickets appear, the second and third with `--baseline previous`: the lab recorded the runs in the order of the commands, the second against the first and the third against the second, and each printed the run it took. A later command names a checkout with changes as its baseline and is set against the run of that checkout.

**Not verified.** Evaluations queued for hours, a machine that restarts with tickets in the lab (their locks are gone with their holders, so they are passed over, which was tested with one ticket), a lab on a network file system, where `flock` is not this lock, and two machines on one lab.

## 2026-11-14: a lab is read while evaluations run in it

`revision --serve` took the lab's lock, so it waited for every evaluation, and an evaluation waited for it. A run of an hour could be read only from the log of its runner, and a served lab left running stopped every evaluation and the watcher. Reproduced on directory slots: started twelve seconds into an evaluation, the command printed "waiting for another evaluation in LAB" and nothing else until it was killed.

**The rule.** A served lab is one address that forwards reads to whichever Worker has the tables of the lab at that moment, and it takes no ticket and no lock of the lab.

- The tables have one writer. Whoever runs a Worker on them holds `worker.lock` and writes its address to `worker.json`.
- An evaluation writes `worker.wanted` before it asks for that lock, for its own Worker on the built package, and removes it when its Worker stopped.
- `revision --serve` keeps a Worker of its own, on the pinned package, only while `worker.wanted` names no live process: it stops it, or gives up starting it, when an evaluation asks, and starts one again when the lab is left alone, which includes the minutes an evaluation spends building.
- The served address answers `GET` and `HEAD` from the Worker that `worker.json` names, its own or the evaluation's, with the token of the lab, which both Workers take. Anything else is answered 405, and the moment between two Workers 503 with `retry-after`.

So `runs`, `status`, `compare`, `attempt` and `export` work at one address across the Workers of many evaluations, and nothing that changes a run goes through it.

**Rejected.** A second Worker on the tables beside the one of the evaluation: two workerd processes on one SQLite file. Printing the address of the evaluation's Worker: it changes with each evaluation and ends with it, and it takes writes. A copy of the tables for the served Worker: the run under way is not in a copy. Holding a request until a Worker is there: a build takes a quarter of an hour, and a client that waits that long has no line to print.

**Checked.**

- A unit test against a stand-in Worker: reads are forwarded with their authorization, a 404 stays a 404, `POST`, `PUT` and `DELETE` are refused, no Worker and a Worker whose process is gone are 503.
- The lane keeps one served lab for its whole length: it lists the runs of an empty lab from the served command's own Worker, reads a run that is under way and its status while the first row waits for its model, is refused a cancel, reads the same run finished after the evaluation's Worker stopped, lists eight runs at the end and runs `compare` through it. The served command answered from a Worker of its own 7, 11 and 16 s after it started, in three runs of the lane.

**Not verified.** A served lab beside an evaluation on krun slots or with a model, a served lab that is killed with SIGKILL while its own Worker runs (its lock is freed, its workerd may live on and must be stopped by hand), two served labs on one lab, and a client that streams: the answer is read whole and then sent.

## 2026-11-14: a nanocode that a slot cannot start is refused when it is named

`nanoeval revision` built any revision of nanocode and ran it, and every row of a revision before `5f8b457de` ended as an error. The cause is the entry of 2026-11-12 on a command that exhausts a slot's memory: `sandbox/slot.sh` starts the hand with `--own-processes`, which nanocode has from that commit on. A hand of an earlier commit prints the usage of `hand` and exits, the session waits for a hand that never dials in, and the row is an environment error after the build of the hand had taken its minutes. Checked with a hand built two days before that commit: `nanocode hand --help` names no such option.

**The rule.** When a revision of nanocode is named as the hand, the command looks for the option in the sources of that commit, `git grep` for `own-processes` in the lab's build tree, or in the uncommitted change of a checkout, and refuses the revision before it builds anything: "nanocode 0123456789ab cannot be the hand of a slot: a slot starts its hand with --own-processes, so that a command that exhausts the memory of the slot ends alone, and nanocode knows that option from 5f8b457de on. A hand without it ends at once and every row is an error: name a revision from 5f8b457de on".

**Why refused and not supported.** Leaving the option out for an old hand would run it as the entry of 2026-11-12 measured: a command that exhausts memory takes the hand with it and the row waits 30 s for an outcome that is unknown. Rows of such a hand would be compared with rows of a hand that has the option, as if the revisions differed in what they solve. A revision that old also speaks an older protocol with the brain. The sources are asked, not the ancestry of the commit: a fork or a branch that carries the option is accepted, and the two local repositories of the lane are no descendants of nanocode's history.

**Checked.** A unit test over a repository with a commit before the option, one with it, and a checkout of the first whose uncommitted change adds it. In the lane the command for the earlier commit exits with 1 and that line, with no hand and no build tree output in the lab.

**Not verified.** The refusal against nanocode's own repository: its commits were read (`bin/nanocode/src/cli.rs` names the option from `5f8b457de` on), the command was not run against them. A package built on a nanocode that old is not refused: only the hand is started by a slot.

## 2026-11-14: a baseline of another version of an eval is compared on the tasks both hold

A lab imports the tasks a run names, and each import makes a version of its eval. `--baseline latest` looked for a run "of the same eval and the same version digest", so a baseline from before any import was never found, and a comparison with a baseline named by its id set tasks side by side by their names, whatever each version held under a name. Reproduced on the commit before this change: a lab ran three sample tasks, a fourth was imported, and `--baseline latest` for a run of one of the first three was refused, "no finished run of samples@a8862a3a8052 on nanocode-ts build-f3aa94f, hand nanocode-cli-3f97ab0 holds this task with a: of the runs listed, 1 without these tasks": the run that held the task was of the version before and was not among the runs listed.

**The rule.** The unit of a comparison is the task, and a task is the same on both sides when its digest in the version of each run is the same: the digest covers its instruction, its tests, its solution, its limits and its environment as it was converted.

- `compare`, `run --baseline` and `revision --baseline` read the entries of each run's eval version and compare the tasks whose digests agree. A task with one name and two digests is left out of the verdict and of the pass@k "on the tasks both sides rate", and named: "left out, the task is another in the eval version of the baseline: write-greeting". Tasks that only one side ran are named as before.
- `--baseline latest` takes a run of any version of the eval that holds every task of the run at the same digest. A run that holds a task of that name at another digest is counted in the refusal as "with another version of these tasks".
- A result read without its entries, in a test or from an older caller, is compared by the checksum of the task's files, which every attempt carries.

**Rejected.** The checksum alone: it is the task's files and not the environment that was converted from them, and a second import of one task on another day can convert another image. Refusing a baseline of another version: that is the defect. A version that only grows by its new tasks staying "the same version": a version is its digest, and a reader verifies it.

**Checked.**

- Unit tests: a comparison with a task that changed, one only the baseline has and one only the run has, by digests and by checksums; the rule of `latest` with a run of another version that holds the tasks unchanged, and with one that holds a task at another digest.
- In the lane the lab's eval gets a second version, one task with a changed instruction and one new task. A run of those two against a run of the first version, named by its id, names the changed task as left out, the new one as not in the baseline and the two others as only in the baseline. A run of the two unchanged tasks with `--baseline latest` takes a run of the first version on the pinned builds, past a newer run of the second version that does not hold them.

**Not verified.** A deployed Worker with many versions: each run of the search costs one more read, of the entries of its version, once a version. Two imports of one dataset whose environments converted differently, which is the case the digest is for: no such pair was at hand.

## 2026-11-14: a package that does not build on its nanocode is built on the one it names

The two branches the watcher follows move apart: on 2026-11-14 nanocode-ts master did not compile on nanocode master for some hours, and the watcher recorded `build failed` for two pairs of heads in a row and would have for every commit until the branches fit again. It went on only because the installed watcher called a script in place of `nanoeval revision` that tried a failed build again with `--sdk pinned`. That script was in no repository and had no test.

**The rule.** `revision --sdk-fallback pinned` is what the script did, in the command. When the package of a nanocode-ts revision does not build on the nanocode it was given, it is built on the nanocode that revision names itself, `sdk-revision.json`. The command says so on standard error, with the log of the build that failed. The failure is written beside the packages of the lab, so the next command for the same pair, the run after a `--build-only`, goes to the fallback at once and builds nothing twice. Without the option a failure is as it was, and a remembered failure is tried again.

The hand is still the one of the nanocode that was named, so such a run tests the new hand with the brain of an older nanocode, and says so wherever a run says what it ran on: "nanocode-ts A on nanocode B, hand nanocode C". The watcher needs one line, `options = ["--sdk-fallback", "pinned"]` in `[revision]`, and now records the builds of every evaluation in `watch.jsonl`, from the version each trial of the job names, and says in its line when the package was built on another nanocode than the hand.

**Rejected.** The fallback as the default: a pair that does not build is a finding, and whoever evaluates one revision by hand wants the compiler's error. A fallback in the watcher: it would have to read the text of the command, which it does not. A retry of the failed build on every call: the build of a package takes minutes before it fails.

**Checked.**

- In the lane, over two local repositories that stand in for nanocode and nanocode-ts, the second with the build steps of a package that fail on one commit of the first: without the option the command ends with the error of the build, with it the package is built on the nanocode the revision names and the variables of `--build-only` name that pair, and the same command again builds nothing and prints the same variables. The three commands took 23 s, 7 s and 1 s.
- Unit tests: the watcher records the versions its rows name, once each, and says a pair apart only when the nanocode of the package and of the hand differ.
- The watch lane passes the option to every call of the command with both sides pinned, where it does nothing, and reads the build of the baseline from `watch.jsonl`.

**Not verified.** The option on nanocode and nanocode-ts themselves: the pair of that morning was evaluated by the script, once, before the option existed. Whether a new hand always speaks to the brain of the nanocode that nanocode-ts names is not known: a change of their protocol would show as rows that error, which the watcher records as incomplete, not as a score.

## 2026-11-14: `revision --quick`: did this change break anything

The shortest evaluation of a change took a command of six options and the id of a baseline from an earlier command, and what to run was left to whoever typed it.

**The rule.** `nanoeval revision --quick` fills in what such a command needs and nothing it was told:

- the eval `terminal-bench-2.1` and its subset `quick` in `subsets.json`, unless `--eval`, `--subset`, `--only`, `--only-file` or `--limit` say otherwise,
- three attempts a task, unless `--attempts` does,
- on the pinned builds, with `--agent`: that run, which the lab records as a quick run with its agents, its judge, its model budget and its slots,
- with a revision: the agents, the judge, the model budget and the slots of the latest quick run of that eval on the pinned builds that the lab recorded, unless they are named, that run as the baseline unless `--baseline` names another, and `--fail-on regression` unless `--fail-on` names another gate.

So `nanoeval revision --quick --nanocode .` in a checkout builds what changed, runs 18 rows and exits with 0 when nothing moved beyond noise and with 3 on a regression. A lab without a quick run on the pinned builds refuses a revision before it builds anything, with the command that makes one. The login files can be named once for a shell, `NANOEVAL_CLAUDE_LOGIN` and `NANOEVAL_CODEX_LOGIN`, so the command needs no credential option either.

**Why three attempts and these six tasks.** With three attempts a side, a task is called lost only at 3 of 3 against 0 of 3, and the verdict over all tasks needs several that move one way. Tasks that an agent solves half the time move by chance and say nothing at this size. The six of `quick` are those `gpt-6-luna` solved 10, 11, 11, 12, 12 and 12 times of 12 on two accepted revisions in the runs of the watcher on 2026-11-14: `fix-code-vulnerability`, `fix-git`, `git-leak-recovery`, `code-from-image`, `nginx-request-logging` and `openssl-selfsigned-cert`. Each asks for another part of the hand: a multi-file edit, git, a service, an image as input, certificates and files. `smoke` keeps its four tasks, one of which passed 8 times of 12 there.

**Why the baseline is the latest quick run and not `latest`.** `latest` is the newest run on the pins that holds the tasks, which in a lab is often a run of one attempt made for another question. The quick run on the pins was made with the settings a quick revision repeats, so both sides have three attempts and one budget, and it is found in the lab's own record before anything is built.

**What it costs.** Measured on the lane: directory slots, a scripted model, three sample tasks, three slots, a machine with 5 cores. The quick run on the pinned builds took 25 s, and the quick run of a checkout with changes 26 s from the command to its exit status, the build of its hand included, which is a crate of ten lines there. Each was 9 rows, 144 input and 72 output tokens, $0.00005 at list prices: the scripted model's numbers, which say what the command adds and nothing about a model. With a model it was not run. The watcher's last cycle before this entry, ten tasks at three attempts of `gpt-6-luna` on krun slots, was 30 rows for $0.0688 at list prices, 2.9 million input tokens of which 2.6 million cached: at that rate the 18 rows of a quick run are about $0.04, and the build of a checkout with one changed file took 165 s for the hand in the measurements of the entry on the command.

**Rejected.** A default agent: which model an evaluation spends on is the operator's, and the first quick run says it once. A default model budget: a limit comes from a measurement or from whoever pays. Running the baseline inside the command when the lab has none: it would spend on the pins, unasked, in a command about a revision.

**Checked.**

- Unit tests: what a lab remembers of a run, and which run is the standard of the next quick one: the latest that is quick, on the pinned builds, of that eval, no rerun and not cancelled.
- In the lane, on directory slots with a scripted model and a subsets file of three sample tasks: the quick run on the pinned builds, 9 rows; `--quick` on a checkout with an uncommitted and an untracked change, whose hand is built with cargo, with no agent named: the agent, the budget and the slots of the first, 9 of 9 passed, "no change beyond noise", exit 0; the same again with a model that fails every task, against the run of that checkout: "regression", exit 3.

**Not verified.** `--quick` with a model, on krun slots, and on `terminal-bench-2.1`: the six tasks were not imported or run through `--subset quick` here, and their pass counts are another machine's, with one model. How often an unchanged revision is called a regression at this size follows from the test, at most 1 time in 20, and was not measured.

## 2026-11-14: the lanes of `nanoeval revision` and `nanoeval watch`

The command had unit tests and runs by hand, and the scripted model those runs used was in no repository. `test/revision.ts` is a lane for it: the command itself, in a lab of its own, on directory slots, with a scripted model that answers a sample task's instruction with its solution or, when the lane says so, with a wrong one.

- `node test/revision.ts`: a served lab kept for the whole lane; a first run that imports three sample tasks; three evaluations queued behind each other; a nanocode that is refused; a package that falls back; a checkout with changes whose hand is built by cargo and run; a regression; an eval with a second version. The hand of the checkout is a crate of ten lines that starts the pinned hand with the arguments it was given, so the command builds, places and names a hand of its own and the rows still run a real one.
- `node test/revision.ts watch`: `nanoeval watch` over the command, both sides pinned: a baseline of three attempts, then the same pair on demand with a model that fails, which the watcher calls a regression after its rerun, with exit status 1.

Both are steps of a sixth job of the workflow, `e2e-revision`, which needs cargo and no KVM. The workflow has 95 `run` steps where it had 92.

**Measured.** On a machine with 5 cores and no KVM, beside other work. `node test/revision.ts` passed in 196 s: 13 commands, 240 s between them since three of them wait for each other. The first run with its import 11 s, the three queued evaluations 25, 41 and 59 s from their start, the refusal 1.5 s, the three builds of the fallback 23, 7 and 1 s, the two quick runs of the checkout 26 and 18 s, the two runs over the second version of the eval 16 and 11 s, `compare` through the served lab 0.9 s. `node test/revision.ts watch` passed in 96 s: 29 s for the baseline and 66 s for the pair on demand, which is two runs. A run of the first lane an hour earlier took 23 minutes to its tenth command, of which 21 were spent waiting for the one build slot that this machine gives cargo: the lane calls cargo six times. `npm run lint`, `npm run check:types` and `npm test`: 264 tests, 260 passed and the 4 that need KVM skipped.

**Not verified.** The lanes on a hosted runner, and on a machine whose cargo is older than the lock file version 4 that the lane writes. The lanes do not run on krun or ns slots.
**Not verified.** A real model on either arm, a deployed Worker, and the direct agent on krun and ns slots: the lane reads nothing of a slot, and the tools are those of the same hand.
## 2026-11-14: tasks whose own solution does not pass are set apart

**The gap.** With the tasks' own solutions 82 of the 89 tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.1 pass, in every run since the entry of 2026-11-10, on krun slots, on ns slots and in Docker. The other seven fail, every time or now and then, for causes that this entry reads to the line. Nothing in nanoeval knew them: a summary took an agent's pass@k over all 89, where a task whose solution cannot pass is not the task that was published, and an oracle run exits 0 whatever failed, so an eighth task that breaks would be found by whoever next reads a table.

**The seven, each run again.** On 2026-11-14, on a machine with 5 cores of an AMD EPYC 8224P and no KVM (Docker 29.1.3, kernel 6.18), each task ran with its own solution and its own verifier in its published image, laid out as Harbor lays a task out: the solution at `/solution`, the tests at `/tests`, the image's user and working directory, under a CPU quota of the task's `cpus` written to the container's `cpu.max`. Memory was not limited there. One run each unless a count is given. Then the same with the fix that its report proposes.

| Task | As shipped | With the fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `build-cython-ext` | The solution exits 0, 10 of 11 tests pass, reward 0 | `pip install 'planarity==0.6'` before `pip install -e .`: 11 of 11, reward 1 |
| `mcmc-sampling-stan` | The solution exits 1 after 761 s, 2 of 6 tests pass, reward 0 | `RcppParallel` pinned to 5.1.11-1, under a quota of 1 CPU: the solution exits 1 later, at its model, 3 of 6, reward 0. With `upgrade = 'never'` on its six installs as well: the solution exits 0 after 1,103 s under that quota, `rstan version 2.32.7 (Stan version 2.32.2)`, 6 of 6, reward 1 |
| `protein-assembly` | The solution exits 1, the one test fails, reward 0 | Both feature types accepted: the solution exits 0, 1 of 1, reward 1 |
| `qemu-startup` | The solution exits 0, no test runs, the script writes reward 0 | One line of `/etc/apt/sources.list` in the environment: 1 of 1, reward 1 |
| `qemu-alpine-ssh` | The solution exits 0, no test runs, the script writes reward 0 | The same line: 1 of 1, reward 1 |
| `torch-tensor-parallelism` | The verifier as shipped passed once, 13 tests in 78 s. Its test file run 6 times on the CPU build of torch 2.7.0: 4 passed in 61 to 75 s, and 2 stopped after 5 and 6 of 13 tests and were ended after 420 s | The same file 6 times on torch 2.8.0: 6 passed, in 65 to 94 s |
| `crack-7z-hash` | Under the quota with the 5 cores of the machine visible: the solution exits 0 after 1,107 s, 2 of 2 tests, reward 1. With one core visible: the solution is ended at its 1,800 s, still in the single mode of john, reward 0 | `john --wordlist=/app/john/run/password.lst`: the solution exits 0 after 169 s with 160 s of CPU time, 2 of 2, reward 1, and with one core visible john alone takes 330.5 s of CPU time |

The causes, to the line:

- **`build-cython-ext`.** pyknotid 0.5.3 names `planarity` in `install_requires` without a version, and the solution's `pip install -e .` took `planarity-1.0.0`, released on 2026-06-29. In the image, `planarity.networkx_graph` puts `{'vertex_position': 0, 'vertex_start': 0, 'vertex_end': 5}` on a node under 1.0.0 and `{'pos': 0, 'start': 0, 'end': 5}` under 0.6. `pyknotid/representations/representation.py:338` reads `data['pos']`, so `test_reconstructed_space_curve` of the repository's tests ends in `KeyError: 'pos'` (1 failed, 17 passed), and the verifier's `test_pyknotid_repository_tests` asserts on the exit status of that suite.
- **`mcmc-sampling-stan`.** `solve.sh` installs `Rcpp`, `RcppEigen`, `BH`, `StanHeaders` and `rstan` at named versions with `remotes::install_version`, which also takes the newest release of every dependency of what it installs. So `RcppParallel`, which no line names, comes as `RcppParallel (NA -> 6.2.1)`, and since 6.0.0, of 2026-07-23, it needs cmake: `RcppParallel requires cmake (>= 3.5); cmake was not found`, then `dependencies 'StanHeaders', 'RcppParallel' are not available for package 'rstan'`. The two tests that pass read output files only when they exist. Pinning `RcppParallel`, which the report upstream proposes and found to pass in August, no longer repairs it: the install of `rstan` then lists `StanHeaders (2.32.10 -> 2.39.1.1)` and `RcppParallel (5.1.11-1 -> 6.2.1)`, the second fails and keeps the old one, the first succeeds, `rstan` loads as `rstan version 2.32.7 (Stan version 2.39.0)`, and `stan_model` refuses line 5 of the solution's model, `int<lower=0> n[num_obs];`: `It looks like you are trying to use the old array syntax`. The solution exits 1 after 925 s under a quota of one CPU, and 3 of 6 tests pass.
- **`protein-assembly`.** `solve.sh` line 84, in the `pdb_ids.py` it writes: `if feat.get("type") != "modified_monomer": continue`. The RCSB data API answers `non_standard_monomer` for those entries (`polymer_entity/5WJ2/1` position 87, parents GLY, TYR, GLY, and `2H5Q/1` position 71), a rename its loader took on 2026-09-10 (`rcsb/py-rcsb_exdb_assets` pull request 171). So the X of the two chromophores stays, `...LVTTFXVACFSRY...` and `...SPQFXSKAY...`, and DnaChisel ends in `NoSolutionError`, `Wrong translation at locations [324-327(+), 1611-1614(+)]`. With both names accepted the sequences read `...LVTTFGYGVACFSRY...` and `...SPQFMYGSKAY...`.
- **`qemu-startup` and `qemu-alpine-ssh`.** Both images are `debian:bullseye-slim` with the same `/etc/apt/sources.list` (SHA-256 `79b7dc6f`), which reads `bullseye-security` from deb.debian.org. `apt-get update` succeeds there, and `apt-get install -y curl` in `tests/test.sh` gets `404` for `libnghttp2-14` 1.43.0-1+deb11u3, `libcurl4` and `curl` 7.74.0-1.3+deb11u16: the support of Debian 11 ended on 2026-08-31 and the files of the suite left the pool while its index stayed. With the line `deb http://deb.debian.org/debian-security bullseye-security main` reading `http://archive.debian.org/debian-security` instead, the same `curl` 7.74.0-1.3+deb11u16 installs. Harbor reads the reward 0 that the script still writes; nanoeval ends the row as a `verifier` error, since no test report was written.
- **`torch-tensor-parallelism`.** `tests/test.sh` pins `torch==2.7.0`. A rank that hangs sits in `_cleanup_process_group` (`test_outputs.py:40`, `dist.destroy_process_group()`): its main thread is in `~ProcessGroup`, `~ProcessGroupGloo`, `std::thread::join`, called from pybind11's dealloc with the interpreter lock held, and the Gloo worker it joins is in `runLoop`, `~AsyncBarrierWork`, `~TensorImpl`, `gil_scoped_acquire`, waiting for that lock (`py-spy dump --native`, this day, the same two stacks as the entry of 2026-11-10). `pytorch/pytorch` pull request 154976, "Release GIL in PG destructor", is the fix, first released in 2.8.0.
- **`crack-7z-hash`.** `solve.sh` line 22 runs `/app/john/run/john /app/secrets.hash` with no mode, so john starts with its single mode, 9,782 candidates made from the name of the file, and only then reads `password.lst`, where the password `1998` is line 3,320. The key derivation is 524,288 rounds of SHA-256, and john computes 8 candidates at once for each of its threads. Single mode fills such a call only when there are threads to ask for more: with one thread it hands over about one candidate a call (`Warning: Only 2 candidates buffered for the current salt, minimum 8 needed for performance`). So what the solution costs depends on how many cores john sees, and not on how much CPU time it gets. On this machine, under the CPU time of one CPU each time: with the 5 cores visible, as Docker shows them to a container under a quota, single mode ran at 10.78 candidates a second and the solution took 1,107 s with 1,042 s of CPU time; with one core visible john took 74.4 s of CPU time for 328 single-mode candidates, 4.4 a second, which is about 2,220 s for the phase, and 330.5 s for the 3,300 candidates of the wordlist after it, against `agent.timeout_sec` of 1,800. A krun slot shows a task exactly its `cpus`, here one vCPU, so the solution ran into the timeout 3 of 3 times on a 48-thread machine, where one core does 5.81 a second, and passed in 1,436 to 1,476 s only on the machine of the entries of 2026-11-10 to 2026-11-12, whose cores are faster. On a 24-core machine with KVM this day, one run each: a slot of one vCPU, the timeout at 1,800 s; a slot of four vCPUs whose microVM is held to the CPU time of one, a change that is not part of this one, 897 s with 892.8 s of CPU time; four whole vCPUs, 249 s.

**Upstream has changed none of them.** The Harbor registry's latest version of `terminal-bench/terminal-bench-2-1` is revision 6 of 2026-04-30, the pinned `7d7bdc1c`, and none of the seven has a task version after that day. The seven directories of `harbor-framework/terminal-bench-2-1` at `12b7565` (2026-11-05) are the imported files. Reports are open and unmerged: `terminal-bench-2-1` issues 233 (the qemu tasks) and 240 (`build-cython-ext`) and pull requests 247 (`protein-assembly`) and 250 (the qemu tasks on Debian 13), and in `harbor-framework/terminal-bench-2` issues 74 and 75 with pull request 73 (the two pins), pull requests 82 and 104 (the archive) and 28 (`crack-7z-hash`). No report names the deadlock of torch 2.7.0 or what the solution of `crack-7z-hash` costs. So there is no newer revision to take, for any of the seven.

**The rule.**

- `unsound.json` lists, by dataset, the tasks whose own solution was shown not to pass: the id of the task, the checksum of the package it was shown on, what fails and why, and the report upstream. The checksum is what matches, so a version that upstream publishes counts as sound without an edit, and the check says that the list names an earlier one.
- `status`, `run --wait` and `compare` print, for an agent whose attempts hold listed tasks, a second line with its counts and pass@k over the sound tasks alone, and one line that names the tasks set apart. The line over all tasks is unchanged, and no row is treated differently. The command line computes it from the attempts, so a deployed Worker needs no change.
- `nanoeval oracle RUN...` reads oracle runs as they stand after their reruns and exits 4 when the solution of a sound task failed or errored, with each such task and its failure. It lists the unsound tasks with their outcome, reason and report, and refuses a run that an agent made.
- The list is evidence, and it changes with evidence: an entry goes in with a reproduction like the ones above, and out when the task passes again.

**Rejected.**

- More CPU time for `crack-7z-hash`: it needs none. It needs what Docker gives a task, the task's CPU time over more cores than one, and a slot that does that is a change to how every task runs, with a decision of its own. Until slots do, the task is listed with that cause, and it leaves the list in the change that makes them.
- Another torch for the verifier of `torch-tensor-parallelism`, a pin added to a solution, a test left out: each changes the benchmark's own files, which is the benchmark's to do. The reports say what to change.
- A verifier that hung run again by the runner: it would turn a verifier that fails four times in ten into one that seems to work.
- A registry frozen at the day of the images for pip and CRAN: it would repair two solutions and show an agent another internet than the one the others on the leaderboard saw, and the RCSB service has no such day.
- Leaving the seven out of the eval: the rate over 89 is the one others publish.

**Checked.**

- Unit tests of the list, of the three readings and of the check (`test/Unsound.test.ts`, 10 tests), among them that the list of this checkout parses and names datasets that `import` knows.
- An end-to-end lane on directory slots, `NANOEVAL_E2E_MODEL=oracle NANOEVAL_E2E_SCENARIO=unsound`: three tasks and a fixture whose solution writes another word than its test reads. The run ends with 3 passed and 1 failed, `nanoeval oracle` exits 4 and names the fixture, exits 0 once a list names its checksum, `status` and `compare` print the line over the three sound tasks with that list and not without it, and a list that is named and missing is refused. It is a lane of `e2e-dir` in the workflow.
- The check on an oracle run of all 89 tasks, made this day on a 24-core machine with KVM on krun slots of the task's `cpus`, 88 tasks in one run and `reshard-c4-data` in a run of its own: `nanoeval oracle` with the two runs prints `oracle: the solution passes on 82 of 82 sound tasks` and the seven with their outcomes, reasons and reports, and exits 0. `status --unsound` of the first run prints `oracle: passed 82/88, errored 2, mean reward 0.953 of 86 scored, pass@1 95.3% of 86 tasks` and under it `oracle on its 81 sound tasks: passed 81/81, errored 0, pass@1 100.0%`. Six of the seven did not pass there, `crack-7z-hash` at its timeout, and `torch-tensor-parallelism` passed that time.
- `npm run lint`, `npm run check:types`, `npm run dry-run` and `npm test` on a machine without KVM, on a tree that also held a change to `import` which is not in this file: 284 tests, 280 passed and the 4 that need KVM skipped.

**Not verified.**

- A run in which a sound task fails for a cause of the machine, and its rerun: the 82 that count as sound are the ones every oracle run since 2026-11-10 passed, with `mailman`, `custom-memory-heap-crash`, `query-optimize` and `pypi-server` passing only when rerun or on another machine in some of them, which is what `--with-reruns` is for. The reading of a rerun is unit tested, and was not met in the run above.
- The reproductions under a memory limit.
- How often the verifier of `torch-tensor-parallelism` hangs: the counts are small, here and in the earlier entries (3 of 3, then 1 of 4 on krun slots, 5 of 6 on a 48-thread machine).

## 2026-11-14: a lane for a `codex` session with direct tools

The entry on the `codex-direct` agent left its end-to-end lanes unrun, and the entry on the cell that answered beside a running one found the gap that this leaves: on a build of nanocode-ts without `codex_orchestration` a turn whose body says `codex_orchestration: "direct"` is a Code Mode session, and nothing here says so. The unit tests hold the agent syntax, the configuration and the comparison, which is this repository's half. What the pinned build does with the field was checked once, by hand, on nanocode-ts's own harness. This entry adds the lane that checks it in a run. It changes `test/e2e.ts`, `.github/workflows/ci.yml` and README.md, and nothing a run executes.

**The lane.** `NANOEVAL_E2E_SCENARIO=direct`, on directory slots: one row of `write-greeting` for each of two agents on `gpt-right`, a model nanocode does not know. `cells` is a `codex` session and `direct` a `codex` session with `orchestration: "direct"`, in one run and on one Worker, paid with a key so that their Responses requests reach the scripted endpoint without the gateway, as in the kill `pair`. The scripted model answers by the tools a request declares: a session that is given `exec` gets a cell that calls `tools.exec_command` with the solution, and a session that is not gets a function call of `exec_command` with the solution and `echo direct-$((40 + 2))`. Each then gets the final message.

It asks that both rows passed with two model calls each, that the `tool.call` events of the direct attempt are one `exec_command` and those of the other an `exec` and the `exec_command` inside it, that two of the four requests declared `exec` and `wait` and two `exec_command`, none of them both, and that the model of the direct session read `direct-42` in the output of its call: the command ran on the hand and its output came back as the result of the function call.

**Rejected.** A check in the Worker that refuses a build without the option: a package does not say which fields of a turn it reads, and a release of nanocode-ts is trusted as built. A unit test of the turn body: `worker/Harness.ts` sends the field on every build, and what failed without a word is what the build does with it.

**What a session with direct tools is given** on `build-f3aa94f`, the pin when the lane was written, as the lane printed it: `exec_command`, `write_stdin`, `view_image`, the hand's `Bash`, `Edit`, `Read`, `TaskStop` and `Write`, eight subagent tools (`close_agent`, `hands`, `interrupt_agent`, `list_agents`, `send_agent_message`, `spawn_agent`, `submit_result`, `wait_agent`) and `web__run`: 17 tools, and no `apply_patch` for a model nanocode does not know. The session beside it is given `exec` and `wait`.

**Checked** on a machine with 5 cores and no KVM, on directory slots. No model was paid for.

- **On `build-f3aa94f`, the pin when the lane was written, with the hand `nanocode-cli-3f97ab0`**, one run of a copy of the lane with three added lines that write each model request to a file: both rows passed, two of the four requests declared `exec` and `wait` and two the 17 tools above, and the second request of the direct session held `direct-42` in the output of its function call. That run then failed on a mistake of the lane as first written, which read the name of a tool from the wrong field of a `tool.call` event. The field was corrected, and the corrected lane had not run again on that build when this entry was written.
- **On `build-f3aa94f` with the hand `nanocode-cli-d2473f9`**, the pins when it was written: the corrected lane passed in 88 s, and once before its last rebase in 250 s.
- **On nanocode-ts `build-8e141d5` with the hand `nanocode-cli-d2473f9`**, the first release of nanocode-ts master with the option: the corrected lane passed, one run of 124 s beside the lanes of other work on the machine. The direct session is given 12 tools there.
- `npm run lint` and `npm run check:types` pass.
- **Not run**: the lane on a build of nanocode-ts without the option. There both sessions are given `exec`, the scripted model answers both with a cell, and the lane fails on the tools of two of its requests and on the `exec` event of the direct attempt: read in the lane, with the run still waiting for the machine.

**Not verified.** A real model on either arm, a deployed Worker, and the direct agent on krun and ns slots: the lane reads nothing of a slot, and the tools are those of the same hand.

## 2026-11-14: what the builds since `build-f3aa94f` change for a session, and the lanes for a turn that goes on

The entry on the cell that answered beside a running one said what the next pin of nanocode-ts must hold in one build: `codex_orchestration`, the fix for a recorded hand reply (nanocode-ts 4f2f8f9), and the fixes for a turn with subagents and for a call that never left (nanocode-ts ac29d32 with nanocode 8f70c4a72, eb707662a and 16217ef97). On this day the option landed on both masters, as nanocode cbc3e78f6 and nanocode-ts 6039207, and the pins moved twice: the hand to `nanocode-cli-d2473f9`, and then, with the entry on a codex session without web search and subagents, the harness to `build-b8158fd` and the hand to `nanocode-cli-0bbcb64`. `build-b8158fd` is a release of nanocode-ts master and holds all of that list. Neither move has an entry on what it changes for a session, which every move before them had. This is that entry, with the changes to the lanes that the list was waiting for. It changes `test/e2e.ts`, `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, README.md and DESIGN.md, and no pin. The entries of this day that speak of the pinned `build-f3aa94f`, and of a pin that was not moved, were written before these moves.

**What was read, and on which build.** The work was done on `build-8e141d5` with the hand `nanocode-cli-d2473f9`, the first release of master that held all of the list, before the pin went past it. Every commit between the pins before, `build-f3aa94f` with `nanocode-cli-3f97ab0`, and those two builds was read, and the requests of a session were written out on both. `build-b8158fd` is 15 commits of nanocode-ts later, and its nanocode, 0bbcb64a0, is 37 commits later and is the revision of the pinned hand. Those last commits were not read one by one for this entry: the entry on a codex session without web search and subagents names what they were taken for. On the pinned builds the lanes ran again and the requests of the lane `direct` were written out once more, under Checked. In the list below "the build", "this build" and "these pins" are `build-8e141d5` with `nanocode-cli-d2473f9`.

**No run with a model on a pin since `build-f3aa94f` is recorded in this file.** The builds change what every session is sent and what it reads back, so a score on them does not stand beside an earlier one until a paired arm has run: the same tasks, agents, attempts and model route on `nanocode-cli-3f97ab0` with `build-f3aa94f` and on the pinned builds, set against each other with `compare --baseline`. A run records its pins and `--baseline latest` takes the latest run on the pinned builds, so the baselines start again with a pin either way.

**The builds.**

| | Before | Read and measured | Pinned |
|---|---|---|---|
| nanocode-ts | `build-f3aa94f`: its master at 2aad477 and the commit of the option, on a branch | `build-8e141d5`: master, 29 commits after 2aad477, the option among them as 6039207 with the same lines in `src/` | `build-b8158fd`: master, 15 commits later |
| nanocode of the harness | 0e428f673: master 1072097ac and one commit, on a branch | d2473f9dd: master, 163 commits after 1072097ac, that commit among them as cbc3e78f6 | 0bbcb64a0: master, 37 commits later |
| The hand | `nanocode-cli-3f97ab0` | `nanocode-cli-d2473f9`, 285 commits later | `nanocode-cli-0bbcb64`, the revision of the harness |

What follows was read in the DECISIONS.md of both repositories and in the diffs, commit by commit, and checked on a session of each build where a check is named. A session here is one of `App.create` with `hands: 'always'`, `workspace: false` and `cellYieldMs`, with no `SESSION_POOL` binding and no MCP server, whose turns are posted without a stream: what nanocode-ts changed for other hosts is left out.

**What the model of a `claude` session is sent.**

- **The text of `exec` and `wait`.** Measured: the description of `exec` is 12,101 bytes where it was 11,426 and that of `wait` 777 where it was 770, and the descriptions of their two budget fields changed with them. The sentences that changed (nanocode f9bf3639e, bcce49fb2, 65e72bfe2, 3e0e6ec11, 848357180, 9ee743699): a result without `max_output_tokens` has "no budget of its own" where it said "unlimited output", and the text now says that the agent may still shorten a long result, marking the cut with `…N tokens truncated…`; unawaited work at the end of a script is discarded, a nested call that had not returned is reported as abandoned with an unknown outcome, and an unhandled rejection fails the script; `exit()` runs no enclosing `catch` or `finally`; audio reaches the model as a note that it was omitted; `notify()` adds a separate output item after the next result the cell returns; a call to a name missing from `ALL_TOOLS` is still answered by the host. A `claude` session reads one paragraph more, on images and on the 12,000 tokens of text a result keeps.
- **The system text is the same**, 6,845 bytes, byte for byte. nanocode d8bbf7921 makes the environment of a session with a hand name the directory of the hand where it named `/`: the session of the lane showed no change, so that is not a change for a session here.
- **Every request carries `metadata.user_id`** and the header `x-claude-code-session-id`, both from the id of the session (6c44fe519). Measured: both are on every request of the session. A gateway that routes by that field keeps the requests of one session together.
- **A tool result** has each `notify()` as a block of its own after the result, where it was appended to the text (848357180). Audio and an image the model cannot take are a sentence that says so, where the audio was its base64 as text (3e0e6ec11).
- **A reply that cannot be used is answered in the turn**, where it ended the turn or cost one of its three continuations. Tool input that is not JSON, and a tool call that the output limit cut, stay in the history and are answered with an `InputValidationError` that tells the model to retry (782d6b673, 05ecb1cb0). A reply with no visible text is dropped once a turn and asked again with one sentence added (9a9e5d038). A response that the provider stops as a refusal is asked again once a turn (1c6dfe3ed). The sentence after a response that reached the output limit is another one (934f7590d).
- **Retries.** A 402 of a payment layer that names a transient cause is retried with the backoff of any other failure (9bebe258c), and a stream that ends with nothing is retried (9a9e5d038). After a 429 or a 529 the client admits requests through a window that starts at half of what was in flight and waits out a `retry-after` for every request of the session (d2473f9dd). Not in this build for a `claude` session: a limit on a stream that goes silent. nanocode's 300 s are compiled for its native client only.
- **Events.** Each compaction in a turn publishes `model.compaction.started` before it and `model.compaction.failed` when it fails, where only its end was published (f2a7a8566). `run.started` names the directory of the hand as the workspace. No event kind was removed and no price changed. A reply that was dropped or kept as above is one more model call of the attempt, with its tokens.

**What the model of a `codex` session is sent**, in Code Mode.

- **The tools of the hand that a cell is told of.** Measured: the description of `exec` is 23,733 bytes where it was 31,400, and the first request of a session on `gpt-right` 49,775 bytes where it was 57,884. nanocode hides the hand's `Bash`, `Read`, `Edit`, `Write` and `TaskStop` from a `codex` session (96314dec0): the description of `exec` declares `exec_command`, `write_stdin`, `apply_patch` and `view_image` and no longer the five. The hand still runs one of them when a cell names it.
- **The developer message on permissions** is the one of Codex CLI, full access to files and network with no approvals, where the build before sent a block that said the host enforces them, and the environment has a `<filesystem>` element with the working directory (7f4cef6be). Measured: the two developer messages are 1,245 and 349 bytes where they were 1,112 and 170.
- **The text of `exec` and `wait`** changed in the sentences above. The description of `wait` is 778 bytes where it was 771. nanocode now lets a `codex` cell run 30 s before its first yield where no host names one (b55bdf602). This Worker names 120 s, and the description says so. Measured: 120000 ms on both builds.
- **A model nanocode does not know**, as `gpt-right` of the lanes: `prompt_cache_key` is the id of the session where it was a digest of the prefix (fc2de1b5c), the session compacts by itself at 90% of the window with a summary request, where it never compacted (fd0d4dea4), and images are kept by a byte budget (00c215b02). For `gpt-6-luna` none of the three applies. Measured for `gpt-right`: the key is the id of the session. A request of `gpt-6-luna` was not written out on this build.
- **A Responses stream that sends nothing for 300 s** fails the request, which is then retried, over the WebSocket and over HTTPS (8a12d27f3). On the build before the timer did nothing in a Worker and such a request was waited on to the timeout of the row.
- A response that ends incomplete with no output is asked again once without its images (00c215b02). Function arguments that are not JSON are answered with "failed to parse function arguments" (e20b0d425).

**A `codex` session with direct tools** is sent the permissions message, the cache key and the rest of the list above, except what is about `exec`. Measured: it is given 12 tools where it was given 17. The five that went are the hand's `Bash`, `Edit`, `Read`, `TaskStop` and `Write`, by the rule that hides them from a cell, and what stays is `exec_command`, `write_stdin`, `view_image`, the eight subagent tools and `web__run`. Its first request is 47,515 bytes where it was 55,877, and the output of its `exec_command` call reads as it did.

**What the tools answer**, which is the hand's. A cell and a direct call read these, so they are model-facing as well.

- `exec_command` and `write_stdin` return at most 10,000 tokens of output where no `max_output_tokens` is named, cut in the middle with a warning that names the original count. The hand before returned up to 1 MiB (99731f07d). An argument the tool does not know is ignored where it was refused (e20b0d425), and a working directory that does not exist fails the call before the command starts (503327544).
- The shell answers as `/bin/bash`: `$0`, the prefix of its error lines and `$SHELL`, where it said `psh` (07ef1240c, abcbd90f6). A `shell` argument of `exec_command` that is not bash now starts that shell.
- `Write` and `Edit` answer in the sentences of Claude Code, "File created successfully at: …" and "The file … has been updated successfully.", where they said "Wrote …" and "Edited … (N replacement(s))", and their errors are Claude Code's too. `Read` numbers the empty line after a final newline, refuses a file with a binary extension by its name, takes `limit: 0` as the whole file and reads BMP and PNM images (b02ac7304, 934f7590d, 96314dec0). A `Bash` call from a cell keeps its limits, its ten minutes and its refusal of a leading `sleep` of 25 s or more: the changes of that tool are for a direct call, which no session here makes.
- A background job has an id of `b` and eight characters and its output file ends with a line that says how it ended (77765bb1e).
- A cell runs on the hand, and its engine changed with it: `exit()` ends the cell past any `catch`, a cell that is terminated names the nested calls it abandoned, a `wait` with nothing to report holds for up to 5 s, `notify()` leaves base64 payloads out, `store()` keeps what was written before a cell died, and the heap of a cell is capped at half of the memory the slot has left, so a cell that runs away fails with "the cell ran out of memory" where the kernel would have ended the hand (65e72bfe2, 91300242f, 5237db845, e450ed9b5, 883f64bcf, 0776007fe).
- An image result larger than a frame is scaled down to fit, where the hand before answered that the result was not sent (51d7fdd18). `view_image` resizes to the limits of the model.
- psh, the shell of every command: POSIX mode, `CHLD` traps and job control under `set -m`, bash's lookup for relative and empty `PATH` entries, `$BASH`, `env -i`. Its conformance counts moved from 2,941 to 3,005 of 3,171 and from 2,413 to 2,418 of 2,511 on the two suites nanocode keeps.

**The log and the recovery of a session.**

- The session object has a table more, `hand_updates`, for the update frames of a hand request whose reply names a delivered call (nanocode-ts 4f2f8f9): the fix of the entry before this, 11 rows and 3.5 KB for a turn of six cells by nanocode-ts's measurement.
- A request for the hand is recorded before the row of the log that holds its effect, through a new operation between the module and its host (nanocode-ts ac29d32). A Worker killed between the two used to leave a call that never left as "outcome unknown". The hand now answers that it never received it, and the call is dispatched once (16217ef97). One more write for each batch of hand requests.
- The recovery of a call waits for the hand of its session, so a subagent that is restored takes up the cell that still runs (eb707662a), and a recovered cell answers the tools of the brain it calls (8f70c4a72). No session here spawns a subagent.
- A snapshot of the log archives the one it replaces, and a metadata row marks the schema of the object (nanocode 86c465b4d, nanocode-ts dddd1fb). A session of `build-f3aa94f` is read: the table is added and the marker written when the object first runs. Read in the code, not run: a Worker that moved builds under a running row.

## 2026-11-14: a cold start from the README, and what it changed

A reader who had never seen the repository did ten things with the README of that day alone, on a machine with 5 cores, 14 GB, no KVM and no root, with a scripted model in place of a real one: set a machine up, import a small eval and run its solutions, run one agent on three tasks at three attempts and read pass@1 and pass@3, choose tasks by a pattern, a subset and a file, rerun what did not pass, compare two runs and gate on a regression, evaluate a checkout of nanocode with one changed line against a baseline, set the watcher up from its units, find what a run cost and why a row failed, and hand two runs at once to a standing runner. Everything worked once the right option was known. This entry is the list of places where the README or a message did not say it, and what each became.

| What the reader met | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The first command of the README | Line 150, after a table of 120 rows | A `Quick start` before the table: four lines from a clone to a pass@k table, with no credential, KVM or root |
| `import --task tasks/extract-todos` on a machine without KVM, step 3 of `Run it locally` | Nothing printed for 4 min 20 s while cargo built the launcher, then `the builder VM exited before its guest listened: Couldn't find or load libkrunfw.so.5`; the same with `--backend ns`, which the README offered for such a machine | Refused in 0.9 s: `its environment is a Dockerfile, which is built in a microVM, and this machine has no /dev/kvm: import it with --backend dir ...`. An import that does build the launcher says so first |
| `run` of that eval without `--backend dir` | `was imported with a dir environment, and the auto backend runs disk environments` | The same, then `: run it with --backend dir, or import it again ...` |
| A model in place of a real one | The scripted model of the lanes is inside `test/e2e.ts` and starts with a lane only: this reader wrote one, as two engineers before had | `scripts/scripted-model.ts` |
| `run --help`, `help run`, a command that does not exist | 360 lines, the usage of every command, exit 0 or 2 with no word of what was wrong | The usage of that command; `no command is named frobnicate: the commands are ...`, exit 2 |
| No `NANOEVAL_URL` or `NANOEVAL_TOKEN` | `--token is required` | `--url is required, or NANOEVAL_URL: the address of the Worker, which nanoeval worker prints ...` |
| No Worker running | `TypeError: fetch failed` | `no Worker answers at http://127.0.0.1:8787 (connect ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:8787): start one with nanoeval worker ...` |
| `--agent luna=codex:gpt-6-luna` on a Worker without a credential for it | The run was made, a slot booted, and the row ended after 18 s as `agent: ... Responses HTTPS request was rejected with HTTP 401` | Refused before the run is made, with the variables and the option that serve the provider |
| `status 774e5979`, `run --rerun 774e5979`: the short id that `status` and `compare` print | `route not found (/v1/runs/774e5979/config answered 404)` | The run, by the start of its id or by its `--name`; in `revision --baseline` by eight characters or more |
| `attempt RUN 2` | `attempt not found` | `the run has no attempt 2: its attempts are named as status lists them, a00001 and on` |
| Why a row failed | One clause, `attempt lists the claims of a row` | A paragraph with the four commands |
| The watcher's unit | The README named neither `~/.config/nanoeval/watch.toml` nor `watch.env`, and a build under the unit ends with `spawn cargo ENOENT` | Both named, with the `PATH` a unit needs; the refusal says that cargo is not on the PATH and where a unit takes it from |
| Node 24 and libkrunfw on a bare machine | A sentence each, no command | The command of each, and `nanoeval doctor` |
| What a machine lacks | Found by a failed import or run | `nanoeval doctor` |

**The quick start is `nanoeval revision` with nothing to build.** Without `--nanocode` the command runs the pinned builds: it starts a Worker and a runner, imports the task directories it is given, waits, prints the summary and stops what it started. That is one command where `Run it locally` takes two servers, an import and a run, so it is the shortest way to a first table, and the lab it leaves is read with `revision --serve`. `Run it locally` stays the way to keep a Worker up.

**The scripted model is a file of `scripts/`, not a command of `nanoeval` and not a part of the lanes.** It is a stand-in for a provider, which the command line has no business being, and the lanes keep their own in `test/e2e.ts`, whose answers differ lane by lane: taking it out of there would touch every lane for no change in what they prove. It reads the instruction and the solution of the task directories it is given, so it needs no table of answers, and a plan of `p` and `f` for the sessions of a task makes the pass@k of a run known beforehand: `uppercase-message=fpf` and `write-greeting=fff` beside a task that always passes give pass@1 (3/3 + 1/3 + 0/3)/3 = 44.4%, pass@2 (1 + 2/3 + 0)/3 = 55.6% and pass@3 2/3 = 66.7%, which is what `status` printed in six runs. It answers `claude` agents only, and the agent names a model nanocode knows, `claude-haiku-4-5`, since nanocode refuses a Claude model it has no output limit for: `Unknown Claude model: configure max_tokens explicitly` was every row of the first try with `claude:scripted`.

**A run without a credential is refused by the command line, from `GET /v1/routes`.** The Worker already says how it pays for each provider. The check is in `nanoeval run` and not in the Worker, so a caller of the API that wants such a run can still make one, and the lanes, which post their configurations themselves, are not touched. A run with `--payer plan` is left to the check of the plan.

**A run is named by the start of its id or by its name.** `status` prints `retries 774e5979/a00002` and `compare` `haiku of bcba4c93`, and neither was accepted anywhere. The command line reads the list of runs when it is given anything but a whole id, takes the one run whose id begins so or whose `--name` is that, and refuses two with their ids. A whole id goes to the Worker as before, so a run that the list does not hold is still read. In `revision --baseline` a word names a revision of nanocode, so only eight characters or more that begin exactly one run of the lab are a run there. **Rejected**: a prefix rule in the Worker, which would have to choose among runs it lists nowhere but in the same table.

**`nanoeval doctor`.** It checks, in the order in which a bare machine is brought up: Node, the pinned packages (`npm ci`), the pinned hand by a `HEAD` of its release, then for krun slots `/dev/kvm` for this user, `libkrunfw.so.5`, `mke2fs`, a `passt` under `/usr` and the launcher or cargo, for ns slots root, overlayfs and their tools, then the memory a runner admits rows by, the free disk where the store, the cache, the layers and the lab are, Docker Hub with the pulls it has left for this address, the Worker when one is named, and a model credential, the Worker's from `/v1/routes` or else the variables and login files of the shell. Each thing that is missing has one command under it and the command exits 1; what only bounds a run, memory and disk, is said and misses nothing, since a row that asks for more memory than a runner admits runs alone. Without `--backend` it checks for the slots a runner takes by itself: krun where the machine has `/dev/kvm`, ns as root, dir otherwise. The pull limit is read as Docker documents it, a `HEAD` of the manifest of `ratelimitpreview/test` with an anonymous token, which counts as no pull: on this machine it answered `100;w=3600` with 98 left. The version and the checksum of libkrunfw in its command are those of `scripts/ci-machine.sh`, and a unit test holds the two together. **Rejected**: `scripts/install-linux.sh`, which names four things at its end, as the place for this: it needs systemd and installs services, and a machine is asked before either. `scripts/ci-machine.sh` as the fix: it opens KVM to every user of a machine, which is right for one that is thrown away.

**Not changed, and a reader will stumble on them.**

- A task can be `lost` under a verdict of `no change beyond noise`, and `--fail-on regression` then exits 0: with `extract-todos` at 3/3 against 0/3 (p = 0.050), `uppercase-message` at 1/3 on both sides and `write-greeting` at 0/3 on both, the verdict was p = 0.130, since the test over all tasks counts the passes of the run in every task and the unchanged task that passes once of three adds its own chance. The number is right. The quick start says so in one sentence and uses a plan that fails every task, p = 0.025.
- A standing runner that serves two runs logs `claimed a00001 nanoeval/extract-todos` twice, once for each run, without the run.
- `nanoeval pool` and `nanoeval version` say `commit not named: deploy it with --var COMMIT:$(git rev-parse HEAD)` of a local Worker, which was not deployed.
- `subsets.json` has no subset for an eval made from `tasks/`, so `--subset` is tried on the samples only with `--subsets FILE`.
- The time of the first import or runner on a machine goes into the build of the launcher with cargo, 4 min 20 s on this machine beside the lanes of other work, where the README says about a minute.

**Checked** on a machine with 5 cores and no KVM, on directory slots, with the scripted model. No model was paid for.

- The quick start, each line as the README has it, from a new clone in a new home directory: `npm ci` 15 s, the command 17, 18, 22, 25 and 32 s in five runs beside the lanes of other work, 4 of 9 passed with pass@1 44.4%, pass@2 55.6%, pass@3 66.7% each time. Then `doctor` (`ready for dir slots`), `revision --serve` with `runs`, `status` by the first eight characters of the id and `attempt RUN a00002 verifier/test-stdout.txt` (`message transformation is missing or incorrect`), and the second run with a plan that fails everything and `--baseline previous --fail-on regression`: `verdict: regression`, p = 0.025, exit 3.

- `revision --nanocode DIR --nanocode-ts pinned --baseline RUN` on a checkout of nanocode `bf35cf9` with one line added: the hand was built in the lab and the 6 rows passed on both sides, 10 min 41 s for the command on that machine, nearly all of it the build.

After this change was moved onto the pins that followed, `build-b8158fd` and `nanocode-cli-0bbcb64`, the quick start ran once more from `npm ci` in 22 s: 26 s for the command, the same 4 of 9 and the same three figures, `ready for dir slots`, and exit 3 for the regression.
- `npm run lint`, `npm run check:types`, `npm run dry-run` and the 48 unit tests of the seven test files this change touches, on both sets of pins.

**Not verified.**

- `nanoeval doctor` on a machine with KVM, as root for ns slots, against a deployed Worker, and with Docker Hub out of pulls or out of reach: those lines are unit tested on described machines only.
- The commands that `doctor` prints for libkrunfw, passt and rustup were not run from its output.

## 2026-11-14: a plan login file that lasts

A local Worker read the access token of `--codex-login` or `--claude-login` once, when it started. The standing watcher runs every evaluation on the ChatGPT login of its machine, whose token ends on 2026-11-15 at 05:45 UTC: from then on every row would fail at the provider until someone ran `codex login` again, and `nanoeval plan refresh`, which could renew that file from a timer, sent a request that no release of Codex CLI sends and wrote the file without a lock.

**How the tools refresh their own files.** Read from the sources of Codex CLI at the tags `rust-v0.166.0` (2026-10-29) and `rust-v0.169.0` (2026-11-12) and at `b1573f1` of its main branch (`codex-rs/login/src/auth/manager.rs`, `storage.rs`, `storage_commit.rs`, `storage_file.rs`, `oauth/client.rs`, `oauth/error.rs`), and from the JavaScript inside the binary of Claude Code 2.1.325 (`@anthropic-ai/claude-code-linux-x64`), which is minified: the names below are the strings and numbers of that code, not its identifiers.

| | Codex CLI, `$CODEX_HOME/auth.json` | Claude Code, `.credentials.json` of its config directory |
| --- | --- | --- |
| When | Before a request when the `exp` of the access token is within 5 minutes. On a `401` it reads the file again, takes it when it changed, and refreshes when it did not | When `expiresAt` is within 300,000 ms. On a `401` it reads the file again and refreshes when it still holds the rejected token |
| Request | `POST https://auth.openai.com/oauth/token`, or `<issuer>/oauth/token` of `tokens.oauth_provenance`, or `CODEX_REFRESH_TOKEN_URL_OVERRIDE`; JSON `client_id` (`app_EMoamEEZ73f0CkXaXp7hrann`, or the client of the provenance), `grant_type: refresh_token`, `refresh_token`, `refresh_reason`; 45 s. No `scope` | `POST https://platform.claude.com/v1/oauth/token`; JSON `client_id` (the `clientId` of the file, or `9d1c250a-e61b-44d9-88ed-5944d1962f5e`), `grant_type: refresh_token`, `refresh_token`, `scope`; 30 s. For its own client it asks for the scopes of the release and, answered `invalid_scope`, for those of the file |
| Answer | `id_token`, `access_token`, `refresh_token`, each optional; what is there replaces what is stored, and `last_refresh` becomes now | `access_token`, `expires_in`, `scope`, `refresh_token` (the old one stays without it), `refresh_token_expires_in`; the profile is fetched again for the subscription fields |
| Rotation | The answer carries a new refresh token. One that is sent again is answered `refresh_token_reused`, which the tool treats as final beside `refresh_token_expired`, `refresh_token_invalidated`, a `401` and `400 invalid_grant`: "log out and sign in again" | The answer carries a new refresh token, and the write is made only when the file still holds the one that was sent. `400` or `401` with `invalid_grant` is final: the tool then empties `accessToken` and `refreshToken` in the file and sets `expiresAt` to 0 |
| Lock while it asks | None between processes. Before it asks it reads the file again and takes it when it changed | The directories `.oauth_refresh.lock` in the config directory and `<config directory>.lock`, made with `mkdir`, touched every 5 s, stale after 60 s, tried five times 1 to 2 s apart. Under them it reads the file again and takes it when the access token changed |
| Write | Under `flock` on `auth.lock`: the file is read again and the write is refused when it no longer holds the login that was refreshed. 0.166.0 truncates `auth.json` and writes it in place with mode 600. 0.169.0 also takes `flock` on `auth.json.lock` for 5 s, requires the same access and refresh token, writes a `.auth-…` file beside it, syncs and renames, refuses a file with hard links or one that is read-only, and follows a symlink. Two-space JSON, no last newline | Under the directory `.storage-write.lock` (stale after 15 s): a temporary file, synced and renamed, mode 600 |

**What that means for a second writer.** A copy of either file is a second holder of one chain of refresh tokens: the first refresh by either holder ends the token the other holds, and the other is signed out at its next refresh. So nanoeval keeps no copy and no state of its own, and writes the file the tool owns, by the tool's protocol. With Claude Code that is exact: both hold the same lock while they ask. With Codex CLI a window is left that the tool also leaves between two of its own processes: both read the file, both find the token within five minutes of its end, and both send the refresh token before either has written. One of them is answered `refresh_token_reused`. What nanoeval does about it is what Codex does: it reads the file again under its own lock before it asks, writes only when the file still holds what it sent, and when its refresh is refused it reads the file once more and takes tokens that another writer put there instead of reporting a sign-out. Whether OpenAI then ends the whole chain is not known; the same question stands for two terminals of Codex today. A watcher that must not depend on the answer signs in once more, `CODEX_HOME=DIR codex login`: a second session of the plan with a chain of its own, which only nanoeval refreshes. That is a choice of the operator and needs no other code.

The other designs were weighed and are in the table of [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md#rejected-alternatives): a copy of the file, the tool's own refresh run by the watcher, the token in a variable of workerd, and a lock of nanoeval's own.

**What nanoeval does.** `cli/Login.ts` holds the files, and `nanoeval worker` serves them to its Worker on loopback under a secret: `src/Logins.ts` asks for the headers of a login before each model request of a session and of an installed agent, and after a `401` asks again with the token that was rejected and sends the request once more. The service reads the file for every answer and refreshes it when the token ends within five minutes or is the one that was rejected, as the table of DESIGN.md sets out step by step. Its request to OpenAI carries `client_id`, `grant_type` and `refresh_token`, which is what nanocode-egress sends for a ChatGPT plan, without the `refresh_reason` of Codex CLI; its request to Anthropic carries the scopes of the file, which is what Claude Code falls back to. Three things differ from the tools on purpose. A file that cannot be replaced whole, one with hard links or in a directory that cannot be written, is refused before the refresh token is sent, where Codex 0.169.0 finds out after. The profile of a Claude plan is not fetched again: the subscription fields stay as they are. And a refusal empties nothing in the file: nanoeval says that the login is signed out and leaves the file to its tool.

A login that is signed out is one line, `the ChatGPT login of FILE is signed out: its refresh was refused with 401 (refresh_token_expired). Sign in again with codex login`, with the status and the code and never the body of the answer, which may repeat the token. It is the message of the rows that asked, which end as `environment` errors, the reason no further row starts, and what `nanoeval revision` and `nanoeval plan refresh` end with, status 1, the first before it builds anything. The login is not asked for again until its file changes, and a new sign-in is used by the next request.

**What changed beside it.** `nanoeval plan refresh` takes `--claude-login`, goes through the same code, and no longer sends `scope`. The variables file of a local Worker holds no token of a login. `CLAUDE_PLAN_URL` also stands for the host of the Messages requests of a Claude login, for the lanes. The lanes `claude-plan` and `codex-plan`, which need a real login, read it through the service.

**Checked.** No request of this work went to `auth.openai.com`, `platform.claude.com`, `chatgpt.com` or `api.anthropic.com`, and no real login was read.

- Unit tests, `test/Login.test.ts`, 29, against a scripted token endpoint that ends a refresh token when it answers: for each file a token that ends later (nothing asked, the file untouched), one that ended and one that ends within five minutes (the request field by field, the file key by key, its layout, mode 600 and no file left beside it but the locks), a token the provider rejects (one refresh, the request sent again, and a second rejection given back), a refresh that is refused (the line, the file untouched, nothing asked again, a new sign-in used), a refresh token that rotates three times and an answer without one, three Workers at once and two `plan refresh` commands at once (one request), the tool writing the file while nanoeval asks and before a refusal (its tokens kept), the failures that are no refusal (an endpoint that answers 503, 502 or 400 with `invalid_scope` or is not reached, an answer without a token, without an end, with an id token that is none or of another account), a file without a refresh token, with hard links, behind a symlink, in a directory that cannot be written, the locks of Claude Code held and stale, the lock of Codex held by another process during the write, the service with and without its secret, and `nanoeval revision` on a login that is signed out. The lines that the tests collect hold no token.
- The binaries of the tools, with every host but a scripted server on loopback unreachable and a made-up login. Codex CLI 0.166.0 and 0.169.0, with `CODEX_REFRESH_TOKEN_URL_OVERRIDE` and `chatgpt_base_url` on that server: each sent `{"client_id":"app_EMoamEEZ73f0CkXaXp7hrann","grant_type":"refresh_token","refresh_reason":"proactive_expiry","refresh_token":"…"}` for a token that had ended and wrote the keys `auth_mode`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `tokens` (`id_token`, `access_token`, `refresh_token`, `account_id`) and `last_refresh` in that order, two-space JSON without a last newline, mode 600, beside `auth.lock` and, in 0.169.0, `auth.json.lock`. `nanoeval plan refresh` on the same file wrote the same keys in the same order and layout; `codex login status` of both releases then answered `Logged in using ChatGPT`, and `codex exec` sent the token that nanoeval had written. Against a server that answers every other request `401`, 0.169.0 refreshed 17 times in one `exec` and 0.166.0 502 times in 60 s: the tool refreshes once for each rejection, without a bound, which is why a rejected request of nanoeval is sent again once and no more. Claude Code 2.1.325 takes a token endpoint only from a list of its own, so its refresh was not run; `claude auth status` on a file that `nanoeval plan refresh` had written answered `"loggedIn": true` with the subscription of the file.
- `nanoeval worker` under local workerd with both files and a scripted endpoint: the ChatGPT login whose token had ended was refreshed before the Worker started, the variables file held `CLAUDE_LOGIN_URL`, `CHATGPT_LOGIN_URL` and `LOGIN_SECRET` and no token, and with an endpoint that refuses the command printed the line of the sign-out and went on.
- Lanes on directory slots, new with this change, against a scripted provider that serves both token endpoints, ends a refresh token when it answers one, and answers a model request only with the access token it gave last. On a machine with five cores and no KVM, at a load average near 7.

Of the first: 8 rows, 4 passed and 4 failed as scripted and none errored; two refreshes, one before the first request and one after the provider rejected the token it had answered once, and each refresh token sent once; the file in its layout with mode 600 and its other fields.
