## 2026-11-14: a failure miner classes the failed attempts of runs

`node scripts/mine-failures.ts --runs ID[,ID...]` reads `/v1/runs/<id>/results` of each run (a unique prefix resolves through `/v1/runs`), takes every attempt of the agents `--agents` matches (`^nano` by default) that did not pass, and pairs it with a passing attempt on the same task: another agent in the same run first, then another agent in the other runs, then a passing attempt of a matched agent. For both it reads `agent/trajectory.json` and `verifier/test-stdout.txt` and summarizes the trajectory with its subagents: tool calls and summed tool seconds by tool, failed calls, model calls, the final message, and excerpts of what matched for timeouts, environment failures, unknown tools or refused arguments, and Code Mode script errors. `src/Mine.ts` scores eight classes from that and the attempt's failure: `timeout`, `environment`, `harness_error`, `prompt_tool_mismatch`, `code_mode_overhead`, `give_up`, `tool_selection` and `wrong_solution`, the last for an attempt that ended normally with nothing else against it. The weights are one exported table (`Mine.weights`): an attempt's failure kind outweighs any count in its trajectory, and Code Mode counts as overhead when its scripts failed or it made at least twice the model calls of the passing competitor. `--classify codex` asks `codex exec` of the signed-in user for the class of each pair and keeps the heuristic scores beside the answer; a pair codex could not answer keeps the heuristic class, and `report.json` lists it under `llmErrors` and `report.md` counts the classes by source. Everything fetched is kept under `--out`/cache (in ignored `output/`), so `--offline` replays a report without the Worker. It writes `report.md` (classes ranked by count with agents, tasks and example attempts, and a table by task), `report.json` and `cases.json`.

Check, hosted Hand, Linux x86_64, Node 24: `node --test test/Mine.test.ts` 6 pass (each class from a constructed trajectory, Code Mode overhead from the call ratio, subagent steps counted with the parent, the pairing order, the ranking and the refusal of a model answer without a known class); a fabricated cache of one run with four attempts replayed with `--offline` ranked give_up, harness_error and timeout one each and paired the timeout with the passing `cx` attempt. Not yet run on the losing-set runs: the machine that holds the Worker's token was not reachable from this change's session.

## 2026-11-14: an agent can take a preflight, a probe of the slot whose facts go before the instruction

Bet B2 of the Terminal-Bench 2.1 losing set (wave 5): models spend turns finding out what the sandbox has (`which python`, `nproc`, `python: command not found`, a missing compiler) before they work on the task. A session agent named with `+preflight` after its harness (`nanoxp=codex+preflight:gpt-6-luna:high`, `codex-direct+preflight`, `claude+preflight`) now has the runner run `src/Preflight.ts`'s probe once in the slot, after it is up and before the first turn, with `slot.sh preflight SLOT SECONDS` (the script on stdin, in the task's working directory and as the task's user, bounded by the run's `--attach-sec`). The runner sends what it printed as `facts` with the instruction; the run checks the instruction against its digest as before, keeps the facts as the artifact `agent/preflight.txt`, and sends the first turn `<environment_facts>` with them, a blank line, then the instruction unchanged. Installed agents (codex-cli, claude-code) refuse the flag, and an agent without it is unchanged: no probe, the same prompt, so parity arms are untouched. A run that names a preflight agent on a runner that predates this change gets a 400 refusal at the first turn ("the runner sent no facts from its probe") instead of a silent prompt without them.

The probe is one POSIX `sh` script (alpine's busybox runs it): OS release, arch, user, cwd; `nproc` and a cgroup CPU quota when `cpu.max` sets one (the hosted Hand says 5 CPUs to `nproc` and has a 4.0 CPU quota); memory total and available; free disk at the working directory and `/tmp`; the path and first `--version` line of python, python3, pip, pip3, uv, node, npm, gcc, g++, make, cmake, cargo, rustc, go, java, R, Rscript, git, curl and wget, and the names of the missing ones; whether `https://pypi.org/simple/pip/` answers (curl, else wget, else a TCP connect from python3, each under `timeout` when the image has it). `reachSec` is 3 s because an unresolvable name made the python3 connect in a `python:3.13-slim-bookworm` container without egress take 13.8 s, and with the bound the whole probe there took 6.5 s including 1.3 s of container start. The probe always exits 0; a slot command that fails is an infrastructure error, as for the other slot commands.

Measured on the hosted Hand (Linux x86_64, Node 24.22.3), one run each: the probe printed 1,396 bytes on the hosted Hand itself (25 lines), 590 bytes in `python:3.13-slim-bookworm` (python 3.13.18, pip, `missing: uv node npm gcc g++ make cmake cargo rustc go java R Rscript git curl wget`, pypi unreachable without egress), and ran through `slot.sh preflight` on a dir-backend slot in 9.2 s wall (the hosted Hand's `cargo` and `rustc` shims are slow to answer `--version`). `npm run lint`, `npm run check:types` and `npm test` (404 tests, 399 passed, 5 skipped, `test/Preflight.test.ts` among them; 405 passed on `0269937` with the failure miner's tests) pass. Not measured here: the krun and ns paths of `slot.sh preflight` (no KVM on the hosted Hand) and the count of discovery calls in the losing-set trajectories (the eval API was out of reach from this turn); the arm to measure it is `nanoxp=codex+preflight:gpt-6-luna:high` against `nanox=codex:gpt-6-luna:high` on the losing tasks, after the Worker is deployed and the runners run this commit.

## 2026-11-14: speculative branches forked from one slot

An agent may now branch: `--agent nanoxb3=codex:gpt-6-luna:high:branches=3` (`branches: 3` in a run configuration, on a `claude` or `codex` session only). It is off unless an agent asks for it. The bet: a run's attempts on hard tasks fail on one bad trajectory, and best-of-N chosen by the agent's own tests, never by the hidden verifier, turns some of those into passes at N times the tokens.

### What happens

- The checkpoint is the start of the attempt. The runner brings the slot up as before, then runs `slot.sh fork SLOT SLOT-bK` for K = 1..N-1 before any hand starts (a fork of a slot whose hand started is refused). `_fork` copies the slot's task archives and inputs, and for krun and ns slots runs `sync` in the guest and copies `upper.ext4` with `cp --reflink=auto --sparse=always`, then runs `_up` on the copy with the arguments the slot was brought up with (`up.args`), which skips formatting a new upper disk when it finds `forked`. The shared base disk stays read-only under every branch. A directory slot copies its workspace. Branch slots are named `SLOT-bK` and their sessions `SESSION-branch-K`; branch 0 keeps the attempt's names.
- Each branch gets its own hand and session and the task's instruction unchanged. When a branch's turn completes, the Worker submits a second turn to it, request `self-check`, with `Branch.prompt`: run the tests and checks it can, fix what fails, end with `SELF-CHECK: PASS` or `FAIL`. This is the one prompt nanoeval adds to a session; it exists only on a branched agent.
- When every branch has ended (or the deadline passed, which cancels what still runs), `Branch.choose` keeps a completed branch whose check passed, else one with no verdict, else one whose check failed, the lowest index of equals; with no completed branch the attempt times out as before. The choice is written to `agent/branches.json` once and every later read returns it. The runner downs the other slots and swaps the row onto the kept slot, so the verifier runs there and nowhere else.
- Usage is the sum of `Atif.usage` over every branch session, both turns. `Proxy.session` reads `-branch-K`, so each branch's model requests are metered to the attempt and claim and the priced cost is theirs together. The kept branch's events and trajectory are `agent/events.jsonl` and `agent/trajectory.json`; the others are under `agent/branch-K/`. A lost claim halts, meters and removes every branch session.
- A runner counts a branched row as N rows of memory and of running slots in its load, so it offers less after claiming one; the Worker still fits a claim by the task's own resources. The Worker refuses a runner whose `slot.sh probe` does not say `fork: true` when the run has a branched agent. `Protocol.version` is unchanged: every new field is optional, and an unbranched run behaves as before.

### Checked

Hosted Hand (5 cores, Linux x86_64, no `/dev/kvm`), Node 24, nanocode-ts `build-39696b0`, hand `nanocode-cli-0bbcb64`, one run each:

- `NANOEVAL_E2E_BACKEND=dir NANOEVAL_E2E_SCENARIO=branches npm run e2e`: one `codex` agent with `branches: 3` on write-greeting. The scripted model writes the right greeting only where the hand's directory is the slot `-b2` (and only if the forked workspace holds the environment's README.md), and its check turn runs a command that compares the file. Result: passed, `branches.json` verdicts fail, fail, pass, branch 2 kept, the verifier saw the right greeting; 12 model requests reached the endpoint (3 branches × 2 for the task and 2 for the check), and the attempt's usage is 12 calls, 1,200 input and 84 output tokens, equal to the sum of the metered responses and to the agent steps of the three trajectories. Run time 24 s from start to verdict. After the rebase onto `488e5fd` (nanocode-ts `build-d5b21f1`) the lane passed again with the same numbers.
- `test/Sandbox.test.ts`: a directory slot forks into two branches that hold a file written to the slot's workspace before the fork; solving in one branch gives rewards 0, 0, 1 for slot and branches.
- `test/Branch.test.ts`: names, metering, verdicts, the choice and the configuration.
- `npm run lint`, `npm run check:types`, `npm test` (417 tests on the head rebased onto `2ede7fa`, 412 passed, 5 skipped), `npm run dry-run`, and the lanes `tasks` (3 tasks), `direct` and `restart` on directory slots passed.

### Not verified

- A krun or ns fork: the copy of `upper.ext4` after a guest `sync` was not run on a KVM machine. A slot's processes are not forked, only its disk, which at the start checkpoint holds nothing running.
- A checkpoint after the plan. It needs a session forked with its history in nanocode-ts and a disk snapshot of a slot whose hand runs, and was not built.
- Any real model: whether best-of-3 by self-check beats one session per token is what a run on the losing tasks must measure.


## 2026-11-14: a Codex arm with background jobs

`codex-jobs` is a harness beside `codex` and `codex-direct`: `nanoxj=codex-jobs:gpt-6-luna:high` (or `{ "provider": "codex", "orchestration": "jobs" }`) runs a nanocode `codex` session in Code Mode whose turns send `codex_orchestration: "jobs"`. nanocode-ts 1bb9797 maps that to `Tools::with_background_jobs(true)`, so the session's cells on a hand built from nanocode 16f93adbc or later get `job_start`, `job_wait` and `job_kill` beside codex-cli's tools; `codex` and `codex-direct` arms are unchanged. Why: bet B3 (async long-running commands) on the Terminal-Bench 2.1 losing set. nanox follows a long build with exec_command and write_stdin polls that each return the output printed since the last one (fix-ocaml-gc: 18 to 83 polls per attempt in runs 650d0782 and bec3e408, see nanocode's DECISIONS of 2026-11-14), and nanocode 16f93adbc's harness measured a 360 s build at 72 tool calls and 56,630 returned bytes that way against 3 calls and 1,041 bytes with the job tools. `parseAgent` maps `codex-direct` and `codex-jobs` through one table and `agentText` writes any orchestration back as `codex-<orchestration>`, so `compare` names the arm `codex-jobs:MODEL`.

### Verified

- `test/Installed.test.ts`: `nanoxj=codex-jobs:gpt-6-luna:high` parses to orchestration `jobs` and prints back unchanged; a configuration naming another orchestration is refused with "orchestration must be one of direct, jobs".
- `npm run check:types`, `node --test test/Installed.test.ts test/Compare.test.ts` (36 passed), `vp check` on the changed files, on the hosted Hand.

### Not verified

- An end-to-end lane and any real model: the arm needs the Worker on nanocode-ts 1bb9797 or later and a hand from nanocode 16f93adbc or later; an older nanocode-ts answers 400 to `codex_orchestration: "jobs"`.

## 2026-11-14: a turn that failed or was cancelled has a cost on nanocode-ts `build-39696b0`, and the lane of web searches counts it

**What failed.** Since the pin of nanocode-ts `build-39696b0` the lane of web searches at the list price of their provider, on directory slots, failed every time: 5 of 5 on a machine with KVM and 3 of 3 on one without, where the commit before the pin passed it 4 of 4 beside it. The message was `the spend is what the responses cost`, with a spend of $0.060364 where the lane expected $0.060336.

**The cause is the lane, which was out of date with a change of the harness that is right.** The build carries nanocode `2c3767224`, "a turn that fails or is cancelled reports the cost of the model calls it completed": the change that the entry "an attempt that hit its agent timeout has no cost" asked nanocode for. `run.failed` now carries `cost_usd`, and `Atif.usage` read it there already. In the lane the third row gets one response, with its searches, and is refused its second request for the budget, so its turn fails. On the build before, its result had tokens and no cost. On this one it has a cost of $0.020028, of which $0.02 are the searches the run priced, and the spend of the run holds the other $0.000028, the estimate for the tokens of that response. The lane added the estimates of the rows that passed only. Nothing in `worker/` or `src/` prices a response differently: the 13 responses carry no cost on either build, as the lane scripts them, and the 13 in `unpricedResponses` of the message is the same on both.

**What changed.** The lane adds the estimate of every row whose session got a response, asks that there are three of them, that each holds its searches at the list price and a cost above it, and that the run counts no attempt whose model calls have no cost. A row that got a response and reports no cost now fails the lane. The README rows on the cost of an attempt at its agent timeout and on the spend estimated from tokens said that nanocode does not price such a turn: they now say what the pinned build does.

**Checked,** on a machine with 5 cores and no KVM, at this commit from a fresh clone: `npm run lint`, `npm run check:types`, `npm test` and `npm run dry-run` pass, and the lane passed 5 of 5. With `Proxy.tools` changed to list no price for a provider tool, the lane fails, 1 of 1 (`the rows ask for more than the budget`: 36 responses, no row ended). With the lane as it is now on the commit before the pin, it fails, 1 of 1, with one attempt without a cost. The lane of failure kinds on directory slots, once on each build with its status printed: the attempt at its agent timeout, one model call of 8 input and 4 output tokens, has a cost of $0.000028 on this build and `status` counts no attempt without a cost, where the build before gave it none and `status` said `without 1 attempt whose model calls have no cost`.

**Not verified.** The cost of a cancelled turn against a real model, where a call may be cut while its response streams. A turn that failed and is resumed from its cursor: nanocode says its last event then reports the whole turn and the earlier `run.failed` the part before it, and `Atif.usage` keeps one cost for each request, so it should count the turn once; read, not run. No lane asserts the cost of the attempt at its agent timeout.

## 2026-11-14: a finished attempt says which artifacts it has

**What was wrong.** `nanoeval attempt RUN ID FILE` for a file that a finished attempt does not hold answered `artifact not found` and the path of the route. An attempt that still runs already names what it has so far. A finished one did not, and its names are otherwise only in the JSON that `nanoeval attempt RUN ID` prints. Seen while reading rows that a real model ran on ns slots: a name that was typed wrong got no hint of the right one.

**What changed.** `Run.absent` names the artifacts of a finished attempt as it names those of one that runs: `the attempt has no verifier/stdout.txt: it has agent/events.jsonl, agent/model-requests.jsonl, agent/trajectory.json, verifier/ctrf.json, verifier/reward.txt, verifier/test-stdout.txt`. An attempt that ended with no artifact, as a row that a budget ended before it was claimed, is answered `the attempt has no verifier/stdout.txt`.

**Tested** in the lane of web searches at list price on directory slots, the shortest lane that reads artifacts of finished attempts: it asks a row that passed and a row that was never claimed for a file neither holds, and compares the whole line of the command and its exit status of 1. `Run` is a Durable Object and has no unit tests of its own.

**Checked,** on a machine with 5 cores and no KVM, at this commit from a fresh clone: `npm run lint`, `npm run check:types`, `npm test` and `npm run dry-run` pass; the lane passed 3 of 3, and fails, 1 of 1, with `worker/Run.ts` as it was. With this change on main as it stood at `488e5fd`, beside the change of the entry above: the 51 lanes of the job `e2e-dir` passed once, two at a time. With the same change on an earlier base still, before the pin of nanocode-ts `build-39696b0`: a local Worker started on a copy of the state of a Worker that held 16 finished attempts of a real model printed the line above with the six names of the attempt and exited 1, and a file that the attempt holds was printed as before.

**Not verified.** The krun and ns lanes, which skip themselves on that machine: the change is in the Worker, which they share with the directory lanes.

## 2026-11-15: the model endpoint of a run forwards chat completions

The endpoint that a run gives its installed agents forwarded the Responses routes for an OpenAI credential and the Messages routes for a Claude one. A command line that speaks to an OpenAI-compatible endpoint mostly speaks chat completions, and so do the endpoints that serve open models, so `Proxy.route` now also forwards `chat/completions` with the OpenAI credential, to `<OPENAI_BASE_URL>/v1/chat/completions` as the Responses routes go to `<OPENAI_BASE_URL>/v1/responses`. `Proxy.meter` reads the usage of such a response where it reads that of a Responses one: `prompt_tokens`, `completion_tokens`, `prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens`, `completion_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens` and a `cost` the endpoint reports, from the last chunk of a stream or from a whole answer. A request counts as a model call, is checked against the model of its agent and is admitted against the budget like the other generation routes.

This is groundwork: no agent of this commit sends such a request, and a `codex-cli` agent, which could, does not. A ChatGPT plan login does not serve the route, the request is forwarded to the plan's Responses address and answered there with an error.

Ran, hosted Linux x86_64, Node 24: `node --test test/Installed.test.ts` with two new cases (a stream whose last chunk carries the usage, a whole answer with a cost), 21 of 21. Not run: a provider's chat completions endpoint.

## 2026-11-15: fx as an installed agent, and agents that name their API

A run compared nanocode with Codex CLI and Claude Code. fx 0.0.17, the coding agent of `vercel-labs/fx`, is a third stock harness: one static binary for Linux x86_64 and aarch64 in the GitHub release `v0.0.17`, pinned by the SHA-256 of both archives. [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md#installed-agents) has the table.

### What was established

- **fx speaks three model APIs through one setting.** `fx ask --help` and the project's page on custom model connections: a connection in `settings.json` has a `protocol` of `openai-chat-completions`, `openai-responses` or `anthropic-messages`, a `base_url` to which fx appends `/chat/completions`, `/responses` or `/messages`, and a bearer key read from a variable it names. So the token of the attempt reaches fx in the one variable every installed agent gets, and no file holds it. Against a scripted endpoint the binary sent `POST <base_url>/...` with `Authorization: Bearer <token>` for each of the three and ran the tool call it was answered.
- **So the agent names the API.** Codex CLI has one API and Claude Code one, and the kind of an agent said which credential the run adds. fx has three, and nothing in a model's name says which serves it: `claude-opus-5-5` is asked over Messages at Anthropic and over chat completions at a gateway that names it `anthropic/claude-opus-5-5`. The harness of such an agent is therefore `fx-chat`, `fx-messages` or `fx-responses`, parsed as `codex-direct` is, into the kind and an `api` that the configuration, the result and the comparison keep. `fx` alone is refused, and so is an API on a kind that has one.
- **fx skips settings it does not own.** Its home is made private at startup, and settings in a directory another user owns are skipped. The agent's state directory is made by root with the sticky bit, so `FX_HOME` is a directory the command makes under it.
- **fx takes http only at loopback.** `http://127.0.0.2:PORT` is refused before a request (`InsecureBaseUrl`, exit 1): a local Worker is reached at `127.0.0.1`, which is where a slot relays it, and a deployed one over https.
- **fx waits for an endpoint without end.** With nothing listening it printed "Offline, retrying" 26 times in 100 s and went on. The agent's timeout ends it, as an `agent_timeout`.
- **Its shell tool needs Bash or zsh.** In the Alpine fixtures, which have neither, the tool call failed (`termination_indeterminate`, "the login shell exited before reporting its state") and the row failed its verifier: fx ran, reached its model and could not run a command. With `bash` added to the image the same row passed.
- **What its output gives.** `fx ask --json` prints one object when it ends. The final message, the number of tool calls and their status are read from it, and the trajectory is one step with those calls and one with the message. Tokens come from the endpoint, as for every installed agent, and there is no cost unless the endpoint reports one.

### What ran

Before this commit, on its tree. Hosted Linux x86_64 without KVM, Node 24: `npm run lint`, `npm run check:types`, `node --test test/Installed.test.ts` (23 of 23), and the new lane on directory slots, 1 of 1. On a 48-thread Linux machine with KVM, four of its threads: the new lane on krun, directory and ns slots, 1 of 1 each, and the lane of the two older commands on krun slots with its failure kinds, 1 of 1 each.

The pinned binary, fetched by the runner, in krun slots against a scripted endpoint behind a local Worker with `OPENAI_BASE_URL`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` and `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` set, the endpoint refusing any request without that key: three agents (`fx-chat`, `fx-messages`, `fx-responses`) on a Debian 12 image and on Alpine 3.21 with `bash`, 6 of 6 rows passed, two model requests each, 2,400 input tokens (400 cached) and 68 output tokens a row as the endpoint scripted them, and 6 reasoning tokens a row on the two OpenAI APIs. On the repository's two Alpine fixtures, 0 of 6: the shell tool, above.

### Not verified

- A real model on any API (the entry that closes this series has the first rows), a ChatGPT plan, an OpenAI key, Cloudflare AI Gateway or another OpenAI-compatible provider.
- A thinking level against a provider. The fields are what the three APIs document, and on Messages what opencode 1.19.5 sends for `claude-opus-5-5`.
- linux/arm64: the archive is pinned by the digest its release lists and was not run.

## 2026-11-15: opencode as an installed agent

opencode 1.19.5 (`sst/opencode`, the release the project marks latest and its npm tag `latest`) is the second command line that names its API, after fx. Its GitHub release has a glibc and a musl build for x86_64 and aarch64, one binary each, pinned by SHA-256 and chosen by the loader of the image as Claude Code's are.

### What was established

- **One variable configures it.** `OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT` takes the configuration as JSON: a provider with the AI SDK package that speaks the API, a `baseURL` and `apiKey: {env:NAME}`, which opencode reads from the environment when it starts. `@ai-sdk/openai-compatible` sent `POST <baseURL>/chat/completions`, `@ai-sdk/openai` `POST <baseURL>/responses`, both with a bearer token, and `@ai-sdk/anthropic` `POST <baseURL>/messages` with `x-api-key`, which the endpoint of a run reads as well. The three packages are in the binary: nothing was fetched with the model catalog and the language server downloads turned off.
- **`opencode run` asks nothing.** With `permission: allow` in the configuration it ran its `bash` tool without a prompt, read the instruction from its input, and exited 1 with an `error` event when its endpoint did not answer for a minute.
- **It asks for a title first.** Each run sends one request without tools before its first step, to the same model since the provider has one. It is a model call of the attempt: three requests where fx and pi send two.
- **A thinking level needs the model marked.** `--variant high` changed nothing for a model the configuration only names. With `reasoning: true` it sent `reasoning_effort` (chat), `reasoning.effort` (Responses) and `thinking.type: adaptive` with `output_config.effort` (Messages, for a model named `claude-opus-5-5`). The command marks the model only when the agent has a level.
- **It is the largest of the three.** One small exchange peaked at 544 MB of resident memory, where pi took 92 MB and fx 10 MB. In a Debian fixture of 256 MB the kernel killed it before its first request, three times of three, and the rows ended as `environment` errors that name the OOM kill. With 2 GB the same rows passed.
- **Its musl build is not self-contained.** In plain Alpine it stopped at `_ZSt25__throw_bad_function_callv: symbol not found`: it links `libstdc++` and `libgcc`, which Claude Code's musl build does not. With the two packages in the image it ran. Nothing is installed into an image for it, so such a row is an `agent` error that says so.

### What ran

Before this commit, on its tree. Hosted Linux x86_64 without KVM: lint, both type checks, `node --test test/Installed.test.ts` (25 of 25). On a 48-thread Linux machine with KVM, four of its threads: the new lane on krun, directory and ns slots, 1 of 1 each. The pinned builds in krun slots against the scripted endpoint of the fx entry, three agents on two images of 2 GB (Debian 12, and Alpine 3.21 with `bash`, `libgcc` and `libstdc++`): 6 of 6 passed, three model requests a row, 3,600 input tokens (600 cached) and 102 output tokens a row as scripted.

### Not verified

- A real model (the closing entry has the first rows), a plan, an OpenAI-compatible provider, linux/arm64, and an x86_64 machine without AVX2, where the pinned builds are expected to stop: the release has baseline builds that are not pinned.
- Its cost. opencode prints one for each step from the prices of its catalog, which has none for a model of a provider it was given, so the stream said 0 and it is not read.

## 2026-11-15: pi as an installed agent, and a command that exits 0 on an error

pi 1.5.2 is the coding agent of `badlogic/pi-mono`. Its npm package moved: `@mariozechner/pi-coding-agent` stops at 0.73.1 of May, the repository publishes `@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent` and needs Node 22.19. The GitHub release `v1.5.2` has a compiled binary for Linux x86_64 and aarch64 with its files beside it, so that is what is pinned, by the SHA-256 of both archives, and no Node is fetched.

### What was established

- **A models file configures it.** `models.json` in the directory `PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR` names adds a provider with an `api` of `openai-completions`, `openai-responses` or `anthropic-messages`, a `baseUrl`, and an `apiKey` that pi takes from the environment when it is written `$NAME`. Against a scripted endpoint it sent `<baseUrl>/chat/completions`, `<baseUrl>/responses` and `<baseUrl>/v1/messages?beta=true`, each with the token as a bearer, and ran its `bash` tool in print mode without a prompt.
- **pi exits 0 when it never reached its model.** With nothing listening it tried four times in 16 s and exited 0. The failure is in its stream: an assistant message with `stopReason: error` and the text, then `auto_retry_end`. A runner that read only the exit code would have sent such a row to the verifier as a model's failure. So an installed agent that exits 0 with an error as the last word of its stream is an `agent` error (`sandbox/Runner.ts`). For Codex CLI and Claude Code the summary already took the error from the stream, and both exit non-zero with it, so no row of theirs is known to change.
- **No musl build.** The binary asks for the glibc loader and four glibc libraries. The command looks for the builds its release has, so in an Alpine image it prints that the image has no loader a build of pi runs with and exits 127: an `agent` error, 6 of 6 times on the Alpine fixtures.
- **A thinking level on Messages.** For a model its file adds, pi sent `thinking: {type: enabled, budget_tokens: 15360}` at `--thinking high`. The file sets `forceAdaptiveThinking` for such an agent, which is pi's switch for the form fx and opencode send.
- **What a subscription would take.** With a key that starts with `sk-ant-oat`, pi sent what Claude Code sends: a bearer token, the betas `claude-code-20250219` and `oauth-2025-04-20`, the user agent of `claude-cli`, Claude Code's first system block and tools renamed `Read`, `Bash`, `Edit`, `Write`. With any other key it sent its own prompt. The token of an attempt is not shaped like a plan token, so pi here sends its own prompt, which Anthropic does not serve for a plan token. An arm that hands pi a token of that shape would make it a different harness on a plan than on a key, and is not built. Its ChatGPT API (`openai-codex-responses`) stopped at "Failed to extract accountId from token": it reads the account from a ChatGPT token.

### What ran

Before this commit, on its tree. Hosted Linux x86_64 without KVM: lint, both type checks, `node --test test/Installed.test.ts` (27 of 27). On a 48-thread Linux machine with KVM, four of its threads: the new lane on krun, directory and ns slots, 1 of 1 each, and the lanes of the two older commands on krun slots, 1 of 1 each, with the new rule in the runner. The pinned build in krun slots against the scripted endpoint of the fx entry: three agents on a Debian 12 image, 3 of 3 passed at 256 MB and 3 of 3 at 2 GB, two model requests a row.

### Not verified

- A real model (the closing entry), a plan, an OpenAI-compatible provider, linux/arm64.
- A row of Codex CLI or Claude Code that ends with exit 0 and an error in its stream: none was produced.

**What was wrong.** Main pinned nanocode-ts `build-d5b21f1` (nanocode 3bab4efb3) and the hand `nanocode-cli-0bf3b0c`, while 1bdab26 added the `codex-jobs` harness, whose `codex_orchestration: "jobs"` only nanocode-ts 1bb9797 and later accept, with job tools only a hand from nanocode 16f93adbc or later has. **What changed.** `package` pins nanocode-ts `build-8a77345` (nanocode-ts 8a77345, SDK 13e49f790, which holds d5b21f1, 1bb9797, 7086541, a7fdac2, 67dea25 and 93d19da) and `Slot.runtime` the hand `nanocode-cli-92f4e0d` (nanocode 92f4e0d9c, Linux x86_64, gz SHA-256 9a7946e616d9b9a893e649bedd3f7b2e274aaec1933ecf890444d247b0135dc0, built like 0bf3b0c with `cargo fetch --locked` then `cargo zigbuild --locked --offline --profile dist --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.2.31`, zig 0.13.0, Rust 1.97.0: 51,123,856 bytes, GNU_STACK present, newest symbol GLIBC_2.30). ## 2026-11-15: fx, opencode and pi on real models, and how their commits landed

The three entries above were written before any of the three command lines had asked a real model. This entry has the first rows, what was checked of the commits as they landed, and what is still not verified.

### How they landed

The four commits (the chat completions route, fx, opencode, pi) were written on a main that moved under them: it gained `+preflight`, `branches` and the `codex-jobs` harness in the agent syntax. They were rebased onto it by hand. The parser keeps main's form and takes its installed names from `Installed.harnesses`, the kinds with one API and `fx-chat` and its like for the others, and the comparison labels and the configuration check carry both main's fields and the `api`.

Checked on the landed tip from a fresh clone, hosted Linux x86_64 without KVM, in one hold of a lane slot, one run each: `npm ci`, `npm run lint`, `npm run check:types`, `npm run dry-run`, `npm test` (423 tests, 418 passed, 5 skipped, 0 failed), and the lanes of fx, opencode, pi and of the two older commands on directory slots, 4 of 4. Each of the four commits from the public repository on a 48-thread Linux machine with KVM, four of its threads: `npm ci`, lint, both type checks and `test/Installed.test.ts`, 21, 23, 25 and 27 tests, none failed. The SHA-256 of the four aarch64 archives was computed from a download and equals the pin. On the same machine, at the landed tip from the public repository: the job `check` of `ci.yml`, 5 of 5 steps (`npm test`: 423 tests, 422 passed, 1 skipped), the three new lanes three times each on directory and on krun slots and once on ns slots, 21 of 21, the lanes of the two older commands on krun slots (tasks, failure kinds, a restarted runner) and on ns slots, 4 of 4, and the whole job `e2e-dir`, 56 of 56 steps in 18.2 minutes on four threads beside other work. The job `e2e-krun` was still running when this was written.

The model calls left through a Worker on that machine to an endpoint on another machine that held the credential: no key was on the machine of the slots, and none in a slot. These rows ran on the tree of the commits before their rebase: the adapters, the route and the runner's rule are the same lines.

| `pi-chat` | pi 1.5.2 | 3 of 4 | 1 | 8 min 52 s | 681,312 (544,768) | 44,260 | $0.1243 | $0.0414 |

This endpoint reports no cost, so the run says "not known" for all three: the cost here is the tokens of the run at $0.15 a million input tokens and $0.50 a million output tokens. The one error is the provider's: it answered `429`, "inference request per min rate reached", to each of the four requests of pi's `openssl-selfsigned-cert` row while the other rows ran. pi gave up and exited 0, and the row is an `agent` error with that line, by the rule of pi's commit. 165 of the 350 requests the forwarder saw for this model in those minutes were refused that way, other work's among them: fx and opencode asked again until they were answered.

`@cf/deepseek-ai/deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017` over the same route, one run of 12 rows, $0.30 and $1.20 a million tokens:

| Arm | Harness | Passed | Errored | Agent time | Input tokens (cached) | Output tokens | Cost by tokens | Cost a pass |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `fx-chat` | fx 0.0.17 | 4 of 4 | 0 | 7 min 31 s | 421,240 (376,576) | 18,101 | $0.1481 | $0.0370 |
| `opencode-chat` | opencode 1.19.5 | 4 of 4 | 0 | 7 min 32 s | 501,147 (452,672) | 16,027 | $0.1696 | $0.0424 |
| `pi-chat` | pi 1.5.2 | 1 of 4 | 3 | 4 min 14 s | 310,315 (278,784) | 14,997 | $0.1111 | $0.1111 |

All three errors are pi's and are the same refusal for the rate: pi asks four times in about fifteen seconds and gives up, where fx and opencode kept asking. On a provider that limits requests a minute, pi's rows want fewer slots at once or a longer retry in pi's own settings, which the command does not set.

This is a smoke test, not a comparison: four easy tasks and one attempt say that each arm runs end to end on both routes and that its row is recorded like the others, and nothing about which harness is better.

### What was tried and did not measure anything

`claude-opus-5-5` over Messages, one tiny fixture for `fx-messages` and `pi-messages`. The meter had no list price for the model and booked it at an upper bound. fx was answered twice (6,809 and 7,214 input tokens, none cached, 121 and 250 output tokens), ran the tool call it was given, and the run's model budget, counted at that bound, then refused its third request and pi's first: two `budget` errors, no verdict. It shows that fx's Messages requests are served for that model through the endpoint of a run, and that a budget ends an installed agent of each kind as a `budget` error. It was a planning mistake: the size of fx's prompt had been read from a scripted endpoint's made-up usage.

### Not verified

- `claude-opus-5-5` for any of the three, and a thinking level against a provider.
- The Responses API of a provider for any of the three, an OpenAI key, a ChatGPT plan and a Claude plan. [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md#installed-agents) says which of them can be served by a plan and why not the others: that is read from the requests each sent to a scripted endpoint, not from a provider's answer.
- Cloudflare AI Gateway addressed directly: the rows above went through a forwarder that adds its token and, for a Workers AI model, the `cf-aig-gateway-id` header, which nothing here adds.
- A nanocode session on a chat completions route. A `codex` session speaks Responses and a `claude` session Messages, so the open-model rows above have no nanocode arm beside them.
- More than one attempt, the other 85 tasks, linux/arm64, and an x86_64 machine without AVX2.

## 2026-11-15: every attempt of a longer task is claimed before any attempt of a shorter one

**The defect.** Rows were granted by attempt number, then longest worst case. With three attempts a task, the third attempt of the longest row waited for two whole waves of every other task, and the last row to end ends the run. One oracle arm of Terminal-Bench 2.1, 89 tasks and three attempts each, 267 rows, 28 krun slots: the three waves began 0 s, 155 s and 466 s after the first claim, the third attempt of the longest row (1,806 s, a solution that runs to its agent timeout) was claimed after 594 s, and the run took 2,399 s.

**What changed.** `Ledger.queue` orders the unclaimed rows by longest worst case first, then by attempt number, then by id. Every attempt of the task with the longest timeouts is offered before any attempt of a task with shorter ones, and tasks with the same timeouts still get all their first attempts before a second one. The share of runners that begin with a whole-machine row is unchanged.

**Measured.** Before and after on the same arm: the oracle on all 89 tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.1, three attempts, one run each side, 267 rows a run, one bare-metal machine with KVM (24 cores, 48 hardware threads), one runner with 28 krun slots pinned to 28 hardware threads, a local Worker. Before is main at ac039b7, after is that commit with this change to the queue and nothing else.

| | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| First claim to last verdict | 2,399 s | 2,203 s |
| The three attempts of the longest row were claimed after | 33 s, 274 s, 594 s | 367 s, 389 s, 395 s |
| Rows passed, failed, errored | 247, 13, 7 | 247, 13, 7 |
| Slot-seconds of the 267 rows | 31,031 | 32,702 |

The run ended 197 s sooner, 8.2 % of the run before. The rows whose outcome differs between the two runs: caffe-cifar-10 #2 (failed before, passed after); portfolio-optimization #3 (passed before, failed after); torch-tensor-parallelism #1 (errored before, passed after); torch-tensor-parallelism #2 (passed before, errored after).

**Simulated.** A slot model with the durations each task had before (the mean of its three attempts), no contention between slots: at 28 slots the order before ends after 2,397 s and the order after at 2,204 s, and with the durations of two real arms of the same benchmark, one attempt a task taken three times, the run that needed 25 slots to end within an hour needs 20, and the other needs 16 either way and ends 4 to 12 % sooner from 20 slots up. The order follows the timeouts a task declares, not how long it ran: claiming the longest measured row first would end the same arms at the longest row itself.

**Losses.** A run that ends early, by its model budget or by a cancel, has no longer given every task one attempt before any task its second: the tasks with the longest timeouts have all their attempts and the shortest may have none. The three attempts of a task now run at the same time, on one machine when one runner has the slots: their disk is unpacked once as before, and what they build or download they build or download three times at once (the three attempts of the longest build took 1,497, 1,483, 1,451 s side by side, against 1,556, 1,447, 1,422 s when they ran apart). The first verdicts come later, since the rows with the longest timeouts go first in all three attempts: after one minute the run before had ended 19 rows and after five minutes 98, the run after 12 and 56.

**Checked.** The unit test of the queue order. On the machine of the measurement, from a fresh clone of the change: the directory lanes with one runner, two attached runners, the free disk floor, memory packing, a standing runner with the rows of two runs, and the two model budget lanes, and the krun lanes with a model, the oracle, the free disk floor, memory packing and two attached runners, 12 of 12 passed. `npm test`: 423 tests, 418 passed, 5 skipped. Not run: the other lanes of the workflow at this change, and a run with a model.

## 2026-11-15: the run asks a model provider again when it limits an installed agent, and an attempt that ends on its limit is an error of the provider

**Found** in the first rows of `pi` on real models, in the entry above on fx, opencode and pi. The provider of an open-model route answers `429`, "inference request per min rate reached", once all the users of the route together pass its rate. pi 1.5.2 asks four times in about 15 s and ends its turn, where fx and opencode keep asking. Of the 8 rows of pi on two models, 4 passed, and the other 4 were agent errors that this answer caused: 1 of 4 on one model and 3 of 4 on the other. A comparison of harnesses on such a route measures how patient the retry loop of each vendor is.

**What the run did before.** The model endpoint of an installed agent passed every answer of the provider on to the agent, with two exceptions. A `402` of a payment layer is asked again or ends the row, as the entries on refused payments say. An attempt with an answer of `502` or `530` is retried once, as an error of the way to the model. A `429` reached the agent, and what the agent made of it was scored as the agent's.

**What changed.**

- **The run waits and asks again.** An answer of `429`, `503` or `529` to a model request of an installed agent is not passed on (`Retry.limited`, the loop of `worker/Meter.ts` that already asks again after a refused payment). The run waits and sends the same request again. The pause is `--poll-ms` doubled with every answer, up to `--lease-sec`, and never shorter than a `Retry-After` of the answer, which is read in seconds or as a date (`Retry.pause`, `Retry.after`). It asks for as long as the attempt has agent time left: when the next pause would pass the deadline of the attempt, the answer of the provider goes to the agent as it was sent, with its headers and its body. No option and no constant is new. With the defaults the pauses are 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and then 60 s.
- **Every wait is on the row.** Each limited answer is a line of `agent/model-requests.jsonl` with its status and `wait`, the ms the run then waited (a column `wait` of `model_requests`). The result of the row has `modelWaits: { count, sec }` for its last claim, `status` prints `model_waits=N (S s)` on the row, and the summary of each agent has `modelWaits: { attempts, count, sec }`: the rows that waited, their waits and the seconds.
- **An attempt that still ends on the limit is an error of the provider.** An attempt that ends as an `agent` error, or at its agent timeout without a pass, and whose last model answers were all limited, is an `environment` error (`Retry.throttled`): `the model provider limited the agent: its last 3 model requests were answered 429, and the run waited 2 s before it asked again: …`. It is one of the causes of the one automatic retry (`Retry.infrastructure`: `the model provider limited its requests`). The answers of a judge are not counted. This reads the requests of the attempt, so it holds for a session too.
- **The budget.** A request that waits keeps its admission, so `--model-budget-usd` still counts it as a request in flight.

**Sessions are not waited for.** Their requests go through the same relay, and the run gives it no hook for them. The client of nanocode keeps a window after a `429` or a `529` and waits out a `Retry-After` for every request of the session, as the entry on that build says, and a run that held those answers back would hide what the window is built on. A session that ends on limited answers is the error above. Not measured: how long that client keeps asking.

**Checked**, on a machine with 5 cores and no KVM, by a user who is not root, the change on main at `ace6b12`.

- `npm run lint`, `npm run check:types` and `npm run dry-run` pass. `npm test`: 427 tests, 422 passed, 5 skipped for KVM or root, 0 failed. Four tests are new. Two in `test/Retry.test.ts`: the pauses, `Retry-After` in both forms, the deadline, and the error with its cause. Two in `test/Meter.test.ts`, the relay against a scripted provider on a socket: `429` with `Retry-After: 1`, `429` without, `503`, then a reply, which is asked four times and settled as three waits of 1,000, 20 and 40 ms and one response with its tokens; and an attempt with no time left, or a relay that is given no hook, which gets the `429` with its `Retry-After` and its body.
- A lane, "installed agents whose model provider answers 429 twice, once with Retry-After", a step of the job `e2e-dir`: 3 tasks, 2 installed agents, 6 rows. The scripted provider answers the one request of each row `429` with `Retry-After: 1`, then `429` without it, then the reply. The lane asks that no row errored, that no row was claimed again, that the provider was asked three times for each row, that each row has `modelWaits` of 2 waits and 1.5 s (the second named by the provider, then twice `--poll-ms`) in `status` and in its result, that its request log has `429` with a wait of 1,000, `429` with 500 and `200`, that the summary of each agent sums them, and that `status` prints them. 5 of 5 runs passed, in 24 to 32 s.

**What the lane catches**, one run each:

| Broken by hand | Result |
| --- | --- |
| the model endpoint gives the relay no hook, as before this change | failed after 23 s: `a model request that the provider limited is asked again by the run, not by the agent`. All 6 rows had ended `errored` after 2 claims with `environment: the model provider limited the agent: its last 1 model requests were answered 429, and the run waited 0 s before it asked again: codex-cli exited with 22`, which is the error and the retry above, end to end |
| the relay does not read `Retry-After` | failed after 20 s: `the row has the pause the provider named and the pause of the run`, 0.75 s where the lane asks 1.5 |

**Rejected.**

- A number of tries or of seconds of its own for the wait. It would be a constant that a busier route outruns, as the four tries of pi are. The agent time of the attempt is the bound a row already has.
- `--step-retries` as the bound. It counts the tries of a payment refusal that passes within milliseconds, 3 by default, and a rate window is a minute.
- `--setup-sec`, the wait of a refused payment. A payment that stays refused will not come back by itself, and a rate window always does.
- Passing the `429` on after a while. What the agent then does with it is the patience this change takes out of the comparison.
- The same wait for `502` and `530`. They say the provider was not reached, and the row is started again in a new slot.

**Not verified.**

- A real route: these counts are of scripted providers. The rows of `pi` on the limited route are not run again here.
- The lane does not itself end a row on the limit: only the broken run above did. A row that waits until its deadline needs a task with a short agent time, and whether its first request comes before that time depends on the machine.
- A limit that a provider sends as an error event inside a `200` stream. It reaches the agent as before.
- An agent whose client gives up on a request that waits long and asks again. The run then waits for both, and the admission of the first is held until the row ends.
- krun and ns slots: the lane is a step of the directory job only. A deployed Worker. The workflow on GitHub: Actions is disabled for the repository.

## 2026-11-15: every harness runs in all 89 task images of Terminal-Bench 2.1

The entries of fx, opencode and pi name three limits found on fixtures: fx's shell tool needs Bash or zsh, opencode needs about 550 MB and its musl build needs `libstdc++` and `libgcc`, and pi has no musl build. Whether a task image of Terminal-Bench 2.1 meets one of them was not known, so it was not known whether arms of different harnesses compare on the same tasks. They do: every harness ran in every image. Nothing was changed for it.

### What ran

One run of 534 rows at `ace6b12`: the 89 tasks, one attempt, six arms (`claude-code`, `codex-cli`, `fx-chat`, `opencode-chat`, `pi-chat`, and a `claude` session of nanocode as the reference), krun slots, ten at a time on four threads of a 48-thread Linux machine with KVM, x86_64. The model was a scripted endpoint outside the repository, behind the Worker's `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` and `OPENAI_BASE_URL`: it answers the first request of a conversation with one call of the harness's shell tool and the next with a final message. The command it asks for reads `/proc`: the high-water mark of the resident memory of each process from its own shell upward, `MemTotal`, and which shells and loaders the image has. A row counts as runnable when the run counted its model calls, the output of that command came back as the tool result, and the row has no agent, environment or infrastructure error.

| Harness | Runnable | Resident memory of the harness at its command, MB: least, median, most | Most of a slot's memory |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| nanocode session, whose hand is what runs in the slot | 89 of 89 | 22, 23, 23 | 1.1% |
| Codex CLI 0.166.0 | 89 of 89 | 141, 150, 219 | 10.8% |
| Claude Code 2.1.318 | 89 of 89 | 155, 164, 186 | 9.2% |
| fx 0.0.17 | 89 of 89 | 3, 5, 5 | 0.3% |
| opencode 1.19.5 | 89 of 89 | 472, 515, 614 | 30.3% |
| pi 1.5.2 | 89 of 89 | 83, 86, 92 | 4.5% |

Every image has the glibc loader and none the musl one. Every image has Bash, 87 at `/usr/bin/bash` and 2 at `/bin/bash`, and none has zsh. A slot has 2,027 MB in 68 tasks, 3,941 MB in 13 and 7,966 MB in 8. So fx's shell tool always finds Bash, opencode and pi always take their glibc builds, and opencode's memory always fits.

That run did not run the tasks' verifiers. Its checkout had one line of `sandbox/slot.sh` changed so that the verifier command writes a reward of 0: the verdict was not the question, the agent has exited before the verifier starts, and the verifiers are most of the time of such a row. Its rows therefore end as `verifier` errors, which were read as a clean exit of the agent. With the repository as it is and the tasks' own verifiers, 93 rows on 16 of the tasks ran in three smaller runs at the same commit, one of them cancelled after six of its tasks: 93 of 93 runnable, each `failed`, as an unsolved task is, and none errored.

### What it means for a comparison

No task has to be left out for a harness. What differs is how much of the task's memory the harness itself holds, since an installed agent runs inside the slot and a slot has the memory of its task: after one tool call opencode holds 23 to 30% of a 2 GB task, Codex CLI 7 to 11%, Claude Code 8 to 9%, pi 4.5%, fx 0.3%, and the hand of a nanocode session 1.1%. A task whose own work needs most of its memory has less of it under opencode than under the others. That is the task's limit, so the slot was not given more.

### Not verified

One attempt for each row. The memory is the high-water mark at the first tool call of an exchange of two requests, not that of a long session. ns and directory slots, arm64, and fx, opencode and pi over Messages and Responses did not run in these images. Nine nanocode rows of the smaller runs are not counted: the scripted endpoint sent them a script that Code Mode could not run, an error of the measurement.

## 2026-11-15: a codex agent calls its tools directly unless it asks for Code Mode

**What changed.** The agent spec `ID=codex:MODEL` now means a nanocode `codex` session with direct tools (`orchestration: "direct"`, which the turn sends as `codex_orchestration: "direct"`), as `codex-direct` did. Code Mode, which `codex` meant until now, is opt-in as `ID=codex-code-mode:MODEL`; `codex-direct` still parses, to the same agent as `codex`. `agentText` prints a direct agent as `codex` and a codex agent with no orchestration as `codex-code-mode`, so each spec reads back as the agent it names. A run configuration is unchanged: `{ "provider": "codex" }` without an orchestration is still Code Mode, so the stored agents of every earlier run, and `run --rerun` of them, keep the orchestration they ran with, and `compare` labels both as before (`codex:MODEL` for Code Mode, `codex-direct:MODEL` for direct). nanocode's own CLI makes the same switch the same day (`--codex-orchestration` defaults to direct, `code-mode` opts in).

**Why.** Two A/B runs on dev-georgios with gpt-6-luna at high effort on the ChatGPT plan, runs `16e15f9a` and `650d0782`, each carrying nanox (Code Mode) and nanoxd (direct) on the same Terminal-Bench 2.1 rows: on the 94 attempts matched across both arms over 22 hard tasks, direct passed 50.0 % against Code Mode's 43.6 % (+6.4 points), with 15 % fewer tokens and 11 % fewer agent-seconds per pass, and direct led in both runs (`report.py` over the runs, 16:59 PST Nov 14). The loss kept: circuit-fibsqrt went 0 of 3 for nanoxd against 2 of 3 for nanox in `650d0782`, which nanocode's DECISIONS.md traces to the model's trajectory, not the request. On the full Codex pair of that report, nanox in Code Mode passed 59.1 % against codex-cli 0.166's 59.9 %.

**Checked.** `npm test`, `npm run lint`, `npm run check:types` and `npm run dry-run` on the thread's hosted Hand (Node 24, 5 cores). New cases: `nanox=codex:gpt-6-luna:high` parses to orchestration `direct`, `nanoxc=codex-code-mode:gpt-6-luna:high` to none, `codex-direct` reads back as `codex`, `codex-code-mode` and `codex-code-mode+preflight` read back unchanged, and a configuration agent `{ "provider": "codex" }` keeps no orchestration.

**Not verified.** A run of the new default with a model: the confirmation arm (Terminal-Bench 2.1, 89 tasks, one attempt, nanox beside codex-cli) is to be started on dev-georgios once this lands.

## 2026-11-15: the scripted model waits until its solution has exited

**What was wrong.** `scripts/scripted-model.ts` answered a task with one cell, `await tools.exec_command({ cmd })`, and ended the turn at the first tool result. `exec_command` returns after 10 s with the process still running ("Process running with session ID 1"), so a solution that takes longer was verified while it still ran. It showed on the first arms of the scripted model over tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.1, on krun slots of a machine with 48 hardware threads, at `ac039b7`, 68 tasks whose solutions are short, where the oracle passes 203 of the same 204 rows at 28 slots:

| Run | Rows | Passed | Failed | Errored | Rows whose turn ended at the 10 s yield |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| one agent, 3 attempts, 28 slots | 204 | 153 | 39 | 12 | 43: 32 failed, 11 errored |
| one agent, 3 attempts, 56 slots | 204 | 151 | 38 | 15 | 44: 32 failed, 12 errored |
| four agents, 1 attempt, 56 slots | 272 | 192 | 53 | 27 | 66: 41 failed, 25 errored |

The errored rows are verifiers that found the package lock held by the `apt-get` of the solution, `E: Could not get lock /var/lib/dpkg/lock-frontend. It is held by process 771 (apt-get)`, and wrote reward 0 without their report. The other errored rows, 1, 3 and 2, were cancelled by hand. So an arm of the scripted model counted 5% to 9% of its rows as errors that no slot, runner or Worker had made, and it could not stand in for an arm of a model.

**What changed.** The cell keeps the result of `exec_command` and, while that result names a session, asks `write_stdin` for it with no characters, which waits for the process for the time the hand gives a poll. The cell ends when the process has exited. A cell that runs longer than the Worker lets one run (`CELL_YIELD_MS`) comes back as "Script running with cell ID N": the model answers that with `wait` on the cell, as often as it comes back, and ends the turn after "Script completed". The script names no time.

**Checked.** At `ace6b12` and with this change on it, on a machine with 5 cores that other work shared, by a user who is not root, on directory slots, `nanoeval revision --task ... --agent scripted=claude:claude-haiku-4-5 --attempts 2 --backend dir` against the script on a port of its own:

- A task whose solution writes its file after 14 s, beside `tasks/write-greeting`: before, 2 of 4 rows passed and both rows of the slow task failed, verified 10 s into their solution. After, 4 of 4.
- A task whose solution takes 135 s, past the 120 s of a cell: after, 2 of 2 passed, each session in 3 model calls: the cell, one `wait`, the end.
- The five tests of `test/Scripted.test.ts` pass, among them the cell run against a process that exits at its third poll, and the endpoint answering a cell that still runs with `wait`. Against the script as it was, three of the five fail.

**What did not run.** An arm of the scripted model on krun slots with this change. Two more limits of the script show in the same arms and stay: a solution longer than one argument of a process is refused by the hand, `Argument list too long (os error 7)` (`make-doom-for-mips`), and a solution that reads other files of its `solution/` directory does not find them, since the script sends `solve.sh` alone (`headless-terminal`). Those are 6, 6 and 8 of the rows above. One row of the first run and three of the third failed the timing test of `tune-mjcf`, which the oracle also fails once in three attempts at 28 and at 56 slots, and one row of `make-mips-interpreter` in the third failed its tests after its solution had exited.

## 2026-11-15: a model has a list price where its endpoint names no cost, and an arm is one line

**What was missing.** An endpoint that reports tokens and no cost, such as an open model behind a chat completions route, left an installed agent with nothing that prices it. The two runs of fx, opencode and pi on two open models printed `cost not known` for every arm and `spend: model $0.0000 of a budget of $1 estimated from tokens, without 11 attempts whose model calls have no cost`: the budget counted nothing, so it bounded nothing. Their cost a pass was worked by hand from the token counts, and so was every line of a report: passes over rows, the two pass rates, tokens, the time and the errors by class were read from `status` and `compare` and put together outside nanoeval, by a script of 60 lines beside the runs.

**The price.** `run --model-price MODEL=INPUT,CACHED,OUTPUT`, once for each model, gives the run a list price in USD for a million input tokens, cached input tokens and output tokens (`prices` of its configuration, `src/Price.ts`). A response costs its uncached input tokens at the first, its cached ones at the second and its output tokens at the third. The input tokens of a response hold its cached ones as `Proxy.meter` reads both APIs, so they are taken out before they are priced. Tokens written to a cache are priced as input: no endpoint that was seen without a cost reports them, and a fourth amount can follow the first that does.

The run prices a response where it records it, as it ends (`record` of `worker/Run.ts`): a response with usage and no cost, of an agent or a judge whose model has a price. The amount goes where a reported cost goes, the cost of the request, so everything that reads a cost reads it and nothing else changed: the spend, the largest response that an admission reserves for each request in flight, the refusal once the budget is spent, and the cost of the attempt at its end, for a session and for an installed agent. A web search at its provider's list price in the same response is added to it. What says that it is no charge: `costBy: "list"` in the usage of the request and of the attempt, a column `listed` of the request, `spend.listedResponses`, `N responses priced at the list prices of the run` and `cost $0.0520 at list prices` in `status`, and the same words in `arms`.

The price is looked up by the model of the agent, not by the name in the response. A run forwards an installed agent's request only for the model of its agent, and a response may name a dated alias of what was asked. A session whose subagent runs another model is priced as the model of its agent: read, not run.

**Why the prices are given and none is kept.** The entry on tool prices holds three prices in this repository as the exception to having none. A table of model prices would be a fourth thing to keep true, for models that change by the week, and the person who starts a run on an endpoint without a cost has its price sheet open. A model that is given no price is as before: a session's estimate, or `not known`.

**The line.** `nanoeval arms RUN` prints one line for each agent of a run (`src/Arms.ts`), a table with a row an arm for several runs, and the arms as JSON with `--json`. `--results FILE` reads a run from what the Worker answers for `/v1/runs/RUN/results`, so a run whose Worker is gone is read from the file kept of it, and `--model-price` prices its attempts that have tokens and no cost with the same function.

- Passes over the rows that ended.
- Micro: passes over scored attempts. Macro: the mean over the tasks of each task's pass rate, which is pass@1. An attempt that errored is a trial of neither, as everywhere in nanoeval, and both say how many attempts and tasks they rate.
- The cost of a pass: the whole cost of the arm over its passes, with the rows that did not pass, and the cost beside it with how much of it is by list and how many attempts have none.
- Input, cached and output tokens.
- Wall time: from the start of the arm's first attempt to the end of its last. For the one arm of a run that is the time of the run.
- Errors by class: infrastructure is `environment`, `internal`, `verifier` and `verifier_timeout`, with its share of the rows, the agent or its model is `agent`, `agent_timeout` and `budget`, and a row that was cancelled is neither. An attempt that errored without a recorded failure counts as infrastructure under `unrecorded`.

**Read from stored results**, with no arithmetic by hand. The two runs of the entry on fx, opencode and pi, 4 tasks and 1 attempt for each of three agents, with `--model-price` at 0.15, 0.15 and 0.50 for the first model and 0.30, 0.30 and 1.20 for the second, which is how that entry priced them, cached tokens at the input price:

| Agent | Model | Passed | USD a pass | Cost | Input tokens (cached) | Output tokens | Wall time | Agent or model errors |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| fx-chat 0.0.17 | glm-5.3-flash | 4/4 | $0.0217 | $0.0867 at list prices | 472,486 (364,288) | 31,753 | 7 min 13 s | 0 |
| opencode-chat 1.19.5 | glm-5.3-flash | 4/4 | $0.0328 | $0.1312 at list prices | 755,846 (619,520) | 35,671 | 8 min 25 s | 0 |
| pi-chat 1.5.2 | glm-5.3-flash | 3/4 | $0.0414 | $0.1243 at list prices | 681,312 (544,768) | 44,260 | 7 min 38 s | 1 (agent 1) |
| fx-chat 0.0.17 | deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017 | 4/4 | $0.0370 | $0.1481 at list prices | 421,240 (376,576) | 18,101 | 5 min 30 s | 0 |
| opencode-chat 1.19.5 | deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017 | 4/4 | $0.0424 | $0.1696 at list prices | 501,147 (452,672) | 16,027 | 6 min 7 s | 0 |
| pi-chat 1.5.2 | deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017 | 1/4 | $0.1111 | $0.1111 at list prices | 310,315 (278,784) | 14,997 | 4 min 59 s | 3 (agent 3) |

Without a price the same command prints `not known` in both cost columns. The six costs a pass are the ones worked by hand; the first total was written $0.0868 there and is $0.086749. The time here is the span of the arm, where that entry summed the agent time of its rows. Two arms of the solutions of all 89 tasks, 3 attempts each, on 28 microVM slots: both `passed 247/267 rows, pass micro 95.0% of 260 scored, pass macro 95.0% over 87 tasks, no model usage`, `wall time 39 min 59 s` and `36 min 43 s`, `errors: infrastructure 7 or 2.6% of its rows (verifier 6, verifier_timeout 1), agent or model 0`, which is what the script beside those runs had counted, 2,401 s and 2,204 s on its own clock.

**Checked.** On a machine with 5 cores and no KVM, by a user who is not root, on directory slots.

- A new lane, `NANOEVAL_E2E_SCENARIO=priced`: a scripted model that names no cost, 8 input and 4 output tokens a response, 6 responses a row, 6 rows one at a time, a price of 250, 25 and 500 and a budget of $0.05. 13 responses were answered, at $0.004 each $0.052, which the run recorded to the millionth of a dollar; 2 rows passed at $0.024, the third was refused its second request, and 3 never started, 4 `budget` errors. The run passed its budget by $0.002, under the $0.004 of one request. Every answered response is in `spend.listedResponses`, none is unpriced, every attempt says `costBy: "list"`, each request in the log of an attempt carries its price, and `arms` of the run, as JSON and as its line, has the cost, the passes over rows and `agent or model 4 (budget 4)`.
- The lanes of fx, opencode and pi with a scripted command now give the model of their chat completions agent a price and leave their Messages agent without one, in one run: the first has 100 input tokens of which 40 cached and 7 output tokens a response, $0.0195 by list, and a spend of $0.0585 for its 3 rows, and the second has tokens and no cost.
- On main at `ace6b12`: `npm run lint`, `npm run check:types` and `npm test` with 430 tests, 425 passed, 5 skipped, 0 failed; the lane of prices 5 of 5, in 15 to 30 s; the lane of fx 2 of 2, of opencode and of pi 1 of 1; and once each the lanes that read a cost: web searches at list price, both lanes of a model budget, the judge, the scripted tasks and the installed agents. No run failed.
- On main at `a35ddf7`, where the record of a request had gained the wait a provider's limit asks for, from a fresh clone: `npm ci`, `npm run lint`, `npm run check:types`, `npm run dry-run`, `npm test` with 436 tests, 431 passed, 5 skipped, 0 failed, and 1 of 1 each: the lane of prices and the lane of fx.

The unit tests are 4 of prices, with a rerun that keeps the prices of its run, and 4 of arms with their sums by hand.

**What each catches**, one run each on main at `ace6b12`, with the code broken by hand in a copy:

| Broken by hand | Result |
| --- | --- |
| the run finds no price for any response | the lane of prices failed after 20 s: `the rows ask for more than the budget`. All 6 rows passed with 36 responses, $0.144 by list against the budget of $0.05, and the run recorded $0.001008, the estimate of its sessions |
| the same, in the lane of fx | failed after 15 s: `the agent whose model has a list price is priced by it, and the other has no cost` |
| cached input tokens are priced as input | the lane of fx failed after 18 s on that line, and 4 of the 8 unit tests of prices and arms fail. A first run of the lane passed: it worked its expectation with `Price.usd`, and now has the sum in its own words |
| the price is written to the usage of the request and not to its cost | the lane of prices failed after 18 s: `the rows ask for more than the budget`, with the same 36 responses |
| micro is taken over the rows, not over the scored attempts | the lane of prices failed after 14 s on the line of `arms`, `pass micro 33.3% of 2 scored`, and 3 of the 8 unit tests fail |

**Rejected.**

- Pricing at the end of the attempt, from the usage of its session, as the estimate of nanocode is. The budget would see a row when it ends: 6 responses a row here, and many more on a real task.
- A price in the agent, `--agent ID=HARNESS:MODEL:...`. Two agents on one model would name it twice, and a judge has no agent.
- Two amounts, with cached tokens at the input price when no third is given. A default that is right for one endpoint is a wrong price on the next, and it would not say so.
- Reading the price from the endpoint's list of models. The one that was run reports none.
- A new column of `compare`. It compares runs against a baseline and gates on it. A report wants one line that can be pasted, and the two share `Compare.standing`, so a rerun counts once in both.

**Not verified.**

- A run on a real model with `--model-price`. The six rows above were made before it existed and are priced from their stored tokens. What the endpoint charged for them is not known to nanoeval.
- krun and ns slots. Nothing in the change is in a slot.
- A judge priced by list, a subagent on another model, and a response that has both a list price and a search at list price: read, in no lane.
- An installed agent that reports a cost of its own on an endpoint that names none, with a price given: the price of the run stands, read in `metered`, in no lane.
- The workflow on GitHub: Actions is disabled for the repository.

## 2026-11-15: an import converts several tasks at once

**What was slow.** A machine that lives for two hours spent ten minutes of them importing Terminal-Bench 2.1: 577 to 683 s for the 89 tasks on a 48-thread machine with KVM. The report of one such import, 576.6 s, gives the adapter 51.7 s, the conversions 434.0 s, the packing 64.4 s and the upload 14.0 s, each summed over the tasks. `Import.cases` took one task at a time: it read the task from the adapter, converted its image in a builder microVM, packed the disk and put it in the store, and only then read the next. Nothing under it needed that. The launcher keeps its scratch beside each disk it writes, and the layer cache has one lock and one download for each blob, so conversions side by side were safe and were never asked for.

**What changed.**

- `nanoeval import --jobs N` converts N tasks at once, and one without it, which is the import as it was. `Import.cases` starts up to `jobs` tasks and reads the next task from the adapter while they run. A row and its timing are kept at the place the adapter gave the task, so the rows of the version are in the adapter's order whatever ended first. The line of a task is written when it ends.
- Two tasks with one source, the same image and size, that are in flight together convert it once: the second waits for the first and then finds its record, as it did when it came later. Without that the two would have shared one scratch directory.
- A conversion starts only while the disk of the cache has room for its `storage_mb` beside the `storage_mb` of every disk that is being written, and asks again when one of them ends. A conversion with nothing beside it starts whatever the room, as before, so no import waits for ever and none is refused that ran before.
- A task that fails ends the import as before, once the tasks beside it have ended: no other task is started, what the others converted stays recorded for the next import, and no scratch is left. With `--keep-going` it is named and left out, and the rest go on.
- `Store.addBytes` writes each blob it puts from a scratch file of its own. Two tasks with the same bytes, an instruction or a test archive, used one file name, and the one that ended first removed it under the other.
- The report of `--report` says how many tasks were converted at once, as `jobs`.

**Why one is still the default.** How many builders a machine has room for can be read from it: each is a microVM of 2 threads and 2,048 MiB, the launcher's defaults. That default is written and not landed, because three things it would change for every import have not run on a machine with KVM, and the machine they were to run on did not come in time: conversions side by side with no layer on the machine, the tasks' own solutions on disks made side by side, and Dockerfile builds side by side, which is what every lane on krun and ns slots would then do with its fixtures. Until they have, the number is the operator's to give.

**What stays the same, and what never was.** A version is the digest over its rows, and a row names its packed disk by SHA-256. Two conversions of one image never gave the same packed disk: a kernel in the builder writes the file system, with its clock in the inodes and its own choice of blocks, which the entry of 2026-11-11 on task images found, and which is why a row records the digest of the image beside the digest of the disk. So two imports of the same tasks never had the same version, one at a time or not. What an import decides is everything else in a row, and the order. That was compared, below. With a converter whose disks follow from its input, the unit test asks that six tasks converted three at a time give the rows and the version digest of the same six converted in turn.

**Measured.** One machine, 48 hardware threads and 377 GB with KVM, on the code of this entry before its last rebase. Every import here was pinned to 6 of the threads, which other runs on the machine used as well: its load was 50 to 80 throughout. The layers were on the machine, a copy of the layer cache of the import above, and each import had a store, a cache and task sources of its own, so every task was read from the registry, converted, packed and stored.

| Tasks | `--jobs` | Wall | Summed over the tasks |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| the first 12 | 1 | 106.3 s | |
| the first 12 | 3 | 48.1 s | |
| the first 12 | 6 | 34.4 s | |
| the first 12 | 12 | 32.5 s | |
| all 89 | 6 | 205.1 s | adapter 46.8 s, conversions 949.3 s, packing 188.7 s, upload 32.2 s: 5.9 tasks at once |

All five ended with every task imported and none refused. These are not the conditions of the 576.6 s: that import had no layer on the machine, 28 threads to itself and a quiet machine, and the same first 12 tasks took it 64.3 s where they took 106.3 s here one at a time. So the table says what side by side gains on the same threads, 3.1 times at six for the 12 tasks, and that 89 tasks went through six at a time; it does not say how long a fresh machine takes. An import with the layers on the machine asked Docker Hub for no counted pull: the limit of the address read 100 of 100 before and after.

The rows of the 89 were compared with the rows of the import made one at a time on that machine an hour and a half earlier, read from the two Workers: the same 89 ids in the same order, 89 of 89 rows equal with the packed disk left out, 89 of 89 with the same image digest, and no packed disk in common.

**Where the rest goes.** Of the 576.6 s, conversion is 75 %, packing 11 %, the adapter 9 % and the upload 2 %. Conversion, packing and upload run side by side with this change. The adapter does not: it is one request for each task, in turn, and at six at once it was 46.8 s of requests that nothing waited for only because six conversions kept the threads busy meanwhile. It is the next entry. Layer downloads are inside the conversions and were not measured apart: the only import with no layer on the machine is the one above. Docker Hub counted 44 pulls for it, of the 100 an hour it gives an address without a login, so a machine can import the dataset twice in an hour from nothing and not three times, however many tasks convert at once.

**Checked.**

- `test/Import.test.ts`, with a converter that waits and counts: six tasks at three jobs convert three at once, a later task ends before an earlier one, and the rows, their order and the version digest are those of the six in turn, with nothing left in scratch and nothing converted when imported again; four tasks of two images at once convert each image once and three rows name one disk; a conversion that fails beside a slow one ends the import with its task named after the slow one ended, starts no third, leaves no scratch and keeps the slow one's record, and with a `refused` callback the other three become the rows in order; with room for two environments on the disk five tasks convert two at once, and with no room at all one at a time, all five.
- `test/Store.test.ts`: the same bytes added twice at once, to a store whose first put is slow, are both kept and no scratch file is left.
