## 2026-11-15: a registry dataset reads its task archives ahead of the import

**What was left.** With conversions side by side, the piece of an import of Terminal-Bench 2.1 that still ran in turn was its adapter: one request to the Harbor registry for the archive of each task, awaited before the next was asked, 51.7 s for the 89 in the import the entry above starts from and 46.8 s in the import that converted six at once. The archives are small, 51 MB in all, and the time is the round trip. Six conversions hid it. More would not: tasks would arrive one every half second, and an import of 89 would take the 50 s of its requests however many builders the machine had.

**What changed.** `Dataset.Context` has `ahead`, how many tasks the reader of the cases takes at once, and `nanoeval import` gives it its `--jobs`. The registry adapter keeps a request in flight for the task it is about to yield and for the next `ahead - 1` after it, so there is one for each task the import can start and never more. The cases still come in the order of their ids, each is still checked against its pinned digest when it is yielded, and an archive that the registry does not serve fails at its own task, after the ones before it were yielded. Without `ahead`, and with `--jobs` left at one, the adapter asks for one archive at a time, as it did. The other adapters read one file for the whole dataset and have nothing to read ahead.

**Measured.** The machine, the threads, the load and the layers of the entry above, fresh task sources, all 89 tasks at `--jobs 6`: 189.7 s where it was 205.1 s, every task imported, the adapter 2.2 s summed over the tasks where it was 46.8 s. One run each. The rows were again those of the import one at a time, 89 of 89 with the packed disk left out and in the same order.

**Checked.** A unit test with a registry of five tasks whose archive requests it counts: one in flight without `ahead`, three with `ahead` 3, the same five cases in the same order either way, and with the third archive refused the first two cases are yielded and the read fails with the registry's answer. It fails when `ahead` is ignored, when every archive is asked for at once, and when a refused archive that was read ahead is left unhandled until its turn. On the 5-core machine without KVM: `npm run lint`, `npm run check:types`, `npm run dry-run` and `npm test` with no failure.

**Not verified.** How many requests at once the registry accepts beyond the six that were in flight here. A dataset of thousands of registry tasks. `terminal-bench-2.0`, which the same adapter reads, was not imported.

## 2026-11-15: the pause before a limited model request is asked again stops doubling after the step retries of the run

**What was wrong.** The entry above made the pause `--poll-ms` doubled with every answer up to `--lease-sec`: 0.25 s to 60 s with the defaults. The limit of the route its rows are from was then measured by its own requests, 398 of them: a model answers 20 requests in any 60 s for all callers together, so once the window is full a place comes free every 3.0 s; its `429` names no `Retry-After`, comes back in 0.16 s and does not count against the limit. A caller that waits a minute between two asks, beside callers that ask every few seconds, finds a free place rarely: the callers beside it take each place within seconds.

**Simulated**, not measured: a provider that hands out 20 places and one more every 3 s, 4 rows of 20 requests each with 2.5 to 7.5 s between an answer and the next request, beside 0 to 16 other callers that ask again every 3 s, 20 seeds each.

| Other callers | Pause up to `--lease-sec`: a row ends after, mean and worst | Pause that stops doubling at 2 s: mean and worst |
| ---: | --- | --- |
| 0 | 157 s, 234 s | 160 s, 199 s |
| 4 | 411 s, 3,956 s | 213 s, 279 s |
| 8 | 470 s, 6,342 s | 226 s, 308 s |
| 16 | 554 s, not within 7,200 s | 246 s, 362 s |

**What changed.** The pause is `--poll-ms` doubled with each of the first `--step-retries` answers and then stays: 0.25, 0.5, 1 and 2 s with the defaults, then 2 s for as long as the attempt has agent time left (`Retry.pause`). A `Retry-After` that names more is still kept, and `--lease-sec` no longer bounds the pause. Both options existed and no constant is new. `--step-retries 0` asks every `--poll-ms`.

**Checked**, on a machine with 5 cores and no KVM, by a user who is not root: the unit test of the pauses asks the new ones, the two tests of the relay pass with them, and the lane of a provider that answers `429` twice passes unchanged, since its second pause is the first doubling. `npm run lint` and `npm run check:types` pass.

**Rejected.**

- Asking every `--poll-ms` without doubling. With 28 slots waiting that is 112 requests a second to a provider that is already refusing.
- A pause read from the route. The provider names none, and the run does not know the rule of a route it is given.
- A limit of the run on its own requests a minute. It would keep the run under a rate it is told, and is a change of its own: this entry is about what the run does once it is refused.

**Not verified.**

- A real route: the table is a simulation, and its other callers do not back off, which is what was seen of two installed agents on that route and not of every caller.
- A provider that counts refused requests against its limit. For such a one a pause of 2 s is too eager, and a `Retry-After` is what tells the run.

## 2026-11-15: two task lists for loops that compare arms, chosen from recorded attempts

A full arm of Terminal-Bench 2.1 cannot end sooner than its longest row, 26 to 37 minutes, and six arms of 89 tasks at three attempts are 1,602 rows. A loop that compares several harnesses every hour needs fewer tasks, and which ones was so far a choice by hand: `smoke` and `quick` hold a few cheap tasks that the recorded arms pass almost always. `subsets.json` now also holds `hourly`, 30 tasks, and `ten-minute`, 12 of those 30, chosen by a rule from the attempts recorded so far. No code changed.

**The records.** 914 scored attempts of the 89 tasks: 538 of nanocode sessions on claude-haiku-5-5 (a full arm with second and third attempts of the tasks that had not passed, two more full arms of one attempt, and smaller runs), 256 of nanocode sessions on gpt-6-luna (two full arms of one attempt on two builds, with retries), 88 of Claude Code on claude-haiku-5-5 (one arm and four rows), and 32 of fx, opencode and pi on four tasks with three models. An attempt that ended on its agent timeout or the output limit counts as failed; 87 that ended as errors of the environment, the verifier, a budget or a refused payment are left out. And 2,618 oracle attempts of 72 runs, 1,512 of them on one 48-thread Linux machine with KVM in one night, where two oracle arms of 89 tasks at three attempts ran on 28 slots.

**The rule.**

1. Leave out a task whose verdict is not the agent's: the 7 of `unsound.json`; 3 whose oracle failed on that machine while it was loaded (`tune-mjcf` 3 of 20 attempts, `portfolio-optimization` and `caffe-cifar-10` 1 of 6 each); and 7 whose solution or verifier fetches from a model hub, which answered the machine's address 429 after an hour of arms (`count-dataset-tokens`, `hf-model-inference`, `mteb-leaderboard`, `mteb-retrieve`, `reshard-c4-data`, `sam-cell-seg`, `torch-pipeline-parallelism`). 72 tasks are left.
2. Bound a row. 540 rows in an hour on 36 slots are 15 rows a slot, a mean of 240 s. A task is taken only if its agent timeout is 1,800 s or less (12 of the 72 allow more) and no recorded attempt of a model took more than 900 s from claim to verdict (8 more did). 52 tasks are left. For `ten-minute` the bounds are 900 s and 300 s, among the tasks of `hourly`.
3. Rate each task. Its difficulty is the mean of the two models' pass rates over every recorded attempt, each as (passes + 0.5) / (attempts + 1). Its information is p(1 - p) averaged over arms whose odds of passing are e^-2, e^-1, 1, e and e^2 times the recorded ones, so that a task the recorded models always pass still counts for a weaker arm. Its discrimination is the distance between the two models' rates, and its cost is the mean recorded row in minutes. Its value is information x (1 + discrimination) / cost.
4. Keep the shape of the benchmark. Each of its 16 categories gets a share of the list in proportion to its tasks among the 89, by largest remainder, as far as it has tasks left; each of three bands of difficulty (below 0.25, 0.25 to 0.75, above 0.75) gets a share in proportion to the 72. The bands are filled in the order of their shares, the smallest first, each with its tasks of highest value while the category has room; what is left is filled by value within the categories.

**The lists.** `hourly`: 9 tasks of software-engineering, 3 each of system-administration, scientific-computing and security, 2 each of debugging, file-operations, data-processing, mathematics and model-training, 1 each of machine-learning and personal-assistant; 9 easy, 16 middle, 5 hard, where the 72 have 19, 42 and 11. 29 of the 30 ask for one CPU and 27 for 2 GB; none asks for more than 2 CPUs and 8 GB. `ten-minute`: 3 easy, 7 middle, 2 hard.

**What the records say on them.** First scored attempt of each task, pass rate in percent:

| Arm | 89 tasks | 72 left by step 1 | `hourly` | `ten-minute` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| nanocode, claude-haiku-5-5, the arm with retries | 71.3 | 70.8 | 76.7 | 75.0 |
| nanocode, gpt-6-luna, the later build | 39.8 | 38.6 | 43.3 | 50.0 |
| nanocode, claude-haiku-5-5, an earlier arm | 71.8 | 73.2 | 83.3 | 75.0 |
| Claude Code, claude-haiku-5-5, the same night | 76.2 | 76.8 | 83.3 | 91.7 |
| nanocode, gpt-6-luna, the earlier build | 59.8 | 58.2 | 56.7 | 50.0 |
| two models, one harness: row 1 minus row 2 | +31.5 | +32.3 | +33.3 | +25.0 |
| two harnesses, one model: row 4 minus row 3 | +4.4 | +3.6 | 0.0 | +16.7 |
| two builds of one harness: row 5 minus row 2 | +20.0 | +19.6 | +13.3 | 0.0 |

The rank correlation of the two models' pass rates over tasks is 0.50 on the 87 tasks both have attempts of, 0.48 on the 72, 0.47 on `hourly` and 0.53 on `ten-minute`.

**The error of a difference.** Two arms with no true difference, three attempts a task, the tasks held fixed, 4,000 draws: on `hourly` the standard error of the difference of their pass rates is 3.1 to 4.9 points for arms like the haiku one and 4.2 to 5.9 for arms like the luna one. The lower figure draws each attempt from the recorded attempts of the task, which have no spread where there is one attempt; the higher draws from the smoothed rate. On the 72 tasks it is 2.5 to 3.8, on `ten-minute` 6.1 to 9.6. So at three attempts `hourly` shows a difference of 6 to 12 points and nothing smaller. A difference of 10 points is seen at twice the standard error with 2 to 4 attempts a task, and four times in five with 3 to 9; a difference of 5 points needs 5 to 16 and 9 to 33. On `ten-minute` 10 points need 5 to 11 attempts and 9 to 22, and 5 points 18 to 43 and 36 to 87. If the tasks are drawn again as well, the error of the difference of the two models is 8 points on 30 tasks and 5 on 72.

**The time.** By a slot model with no contention and the queue of the run, 6 arms x 3 attempts of `hourly`, 540 rows, on 36 slots: 26.9 minutes if every row takes the mean recorded row of its task, 58.1 if every row takes the longest recorded one, 40.1 and 85.3 on 24 slots. The longest recorded row is 693 s. If every agent runs out its timeout it is 267 minutes: no choice of tasks bounds that. `ten-minute`, 216 rows: 9.6 and 15.8 minutes on 36 slots, 7.5 and 12.5 on 48. The six arms make about 4,100 model requests at the median recorded count of a row, 1,800 for `ten-minute`.

**The oracle.** In the two oracle arms of that night the 30 tasks passed 90 of 90 attempts each time, in 2,427 and 2,622 slot-seconds with a longest row of 131 and 148 s, which the slot model packs into 2.7 minutes on 36 slots; the 12 passed 36 of 36 twice. Of 604 oracle attempts of the 30 on that machine 603 passed: one of `pytorch-model-recovery` ran out of disk in a run with `--verifier-cache`. Over every recorded oracle attempt of the 30, 971 of 973 passed; the other is an attempt of `custom-memory-heap-crash` on an earlier commit.

**Limits.**

- The rule was fitted to the arms it is then read on. Chosen from one half of the records and read on the other, the difference of the two models came out as +23.3 points where all 89 tasks say +31.5, and as +23.3 where they say +15.0: the lists keep the sign and the rough size of a difference of that size, not its value. The two lists so chosen share 22 and 21 of their 30 tasks with `hourly`.
- A pass rate on `hourly` is not a pass rate on the benchmark. The tasks that take long are the ones left out, so a strong arm stands 5 to 12 points higher on the list, and an arm that already passes 83 % of it has little room above.
- The two lists did not tell the two harnesses on one model apart, and neither did the 89 tasks at one attempt: 4.4 points is under the error above.
- Most tasks have one to four recorded attempts of an arm, by two models and, but for four tasks, two harnesses. No arm of an open model is in the records, and those arms take about twice the requests of a row.
- `data-science`, 8 of the 89 tasks, is in neither list: 5 of its tasks fetch from a model hub, 1 is in `unsound.json` and the other 2 take 16 to 22 minutes a row. `largest-eigenval`, in both lists, has a verifier that measures time; its oracle passed 18 of 18 attempts on the loaded machine.
- The bounds of step 2, the five arms of step 3 and the three bands of step 4 are choices. Three earlier forms of the rule are kept with their figures outside the repository: without the bound on recorded rows two tasks took 47 % of the slot-seconds, and with a fixed count for each band instead of a share the difference of the two models came out as +16.7.

**Not verified.** No run was made through `--subset hourly` or `--subset ten-minute`: the names were resolved with `src/Subset.ts` against the 89 task names of an import, and every figure above is computed from recorded rows, none from a run of the lists. The oracle arm of `hourly` by itself was not run. The times are a model, not a measurement, and leave out the rate at which a model route answers.

## 2026-11-15: a codex session of glm-5.3 asks its model over chat completions

A route that serves chat completions only ran fx, opencode and pi, and no nanocode session: a `codex` session speaks Responses and a `claude` session Messages. nanocode has a chat completions transport of its own for one model, `glm-5.3` on Workers AI: the pinned nanocode-ts opens such a session with the Cloudflare account of `WORKERS_AI_ACCOUNT_ID`, and the session then posts to `/client/v4/accounts/ID/ai/v1/chat/completions` with the model `@cf/zai-org/glm-5.3`, streamed, with nanocode's own prompts, tools and effort. The Worker already forwards that request like any other of a `codex` session, to `OPENAI_BASE_URL` when one is set, with `OPENAI_API_KEY` as the bearer token, and meters its usage. Only `nanoeval worker` stood in the way: it hands the Worker a fixed list of the variables of its environment, and the account was not in it, so every such row ended at once as an agent error, `the Workers AI gateway needs cloudflare_account_id`. It is in the list now. `nanoeval revision` starts that command, so it takes the variable the same way, and a deployed Worker takes it as it takes any other.

The list is now a function, `workerVariables`, so that a unit test holds it. The test gives it an environment with every variable of the list and two more, one of them a wallet key, and asks for exactly the list back, that every variable a provider's key is read from is in the list, and that an empty variable is left out. With the account taken out of the list the test fails.

### Why not a translator in the Worker

The other way to put a session on such a route is to translate a `claude` session's Messages requests into chat completions. That was built outside the repository and measured, and it stays outside. A translator decides what the model is sent where the two APIs differ: five system blocks become one message, an image in a tool result has to move into a user message, the session's `thinking: disabled` has no field to go to, a keep-alive of the prompt cache has nothing to keep warm. nanoeval sends models only nanocode's native prompts and tool text, and those choices would be nanoeval's. Such a row also carries a model name that is not the model: a `claude` session starts only for a model nanocode knows.

### What ran

The route in every run was Workers AI through a forwarder outside the repository that holds the credential and answers on the path above. It serves `@cf/zai-org/glm-5.3-flash` and not `@cf/zai-org/glm-5.3`, so it renamed the model: the rows are labelled `glm-5.3` and were answered by the flash model.

With this change and without it: one Linux machine with 5 cores and no KVM, x86_64, directory slots, four rows at a time, the three fixture tasks, one attempt, `nanoeval revision` with the three variables set, at `a35ddf7` and at `a35ddf7` with this change, nanocode-ts `build-8a77345`, hand `nanocode-cli-92f4e0d`. At that commit `codex` is a session with direct tools and `codex-code-mode` one in Code Mode.

No lane ran a preflight end to end, and the branches lane refused every backend but directory slots, since its scripted model told the branches apart by the `-b2` in `$PWD`, which a guest does not see.

On krun and ns slots it also asserts `Alpine Linux`, `cwd /app` and `python3` among the missing tools, which only the guest gives.
- The `branches` scenario runs on every backend without the gateway. On krun and ns slots the scripted model tells the branches apart by `prompt_cache_key`, one per session, and gives the right greeting to the third session that asks. The lane asserts one passing verdict, the kept branch equal to it, three sessions, and a failing self-check in each other branch. Directory slots keep the `-b2` rule and the exact verdicts fail, fail, pass.
- ci.yml gains the preflight lane on directory slots, and both lanes on krun and ns slots.

On the pinned runtime `nanocode-cli-92f4e0d`, a known Codex model rejects a window above `MAX_CONTEXT_WINDOW_TOKENS` (872,000): `nanocode exec --model gpt-6-luna --harness codex --context-window 1048576` printed `--context-window 1048576 is over gpt-6-luna's window of 872000 tokens` and exited 1, so every `nanocode-codex` row on a gpt-6 model ended before its first model call. The same command also named no hedge policy, and the CLI then hedges with `HedgePolicy::DEFAULT` (cap 10%), the duplicate requests that 4c6a9a5 turned off for Worker sessions only.

**What changed.** A `codex` harness in the slot gets no `--context-window`, so nanocode takes the window of its catalog, or of the endpoint's model list for a model it does not know. Both harnesses get `--hedge-cap-percent 0`. A `claude` harness keeps `--context-window 1048576` and `--max-output-tokens 65536`.

**Which arm is which.** The Terminal-Bench 2.1 `nanox`, `nanoxd` and `nanoxj` arms are `codex` sessions of nanocode-ts in the Worker, outside the slot. `Turn.body` sends no window, and `App.create` in `worker/Sessions.ts` takes none. The catalog of nanocode-ts build-8a77345 gives gpt-6-luna 272,000 tokens and an `auto_compact_token_limit` of 244,800, the same as codex-cli. Those arms never had the override, and this change does not move them. The window reached only the `nanocode-codex` and `nanocode-claude` installed agents. Every Worker session, the judge included, comes from the one `App.create` with `hedge: { cap_percent: 0 }`. The two installed nanocode agents were the only eval sessions that still hedged.

**Claude.** A nanocode Claude session compacts at its window less 33,000 reserved tokens: 1,015,576 with the override, 967,000 at the default window of claude-opus-5-5. The `claude-code` agent sets no window, and `stock-claude` sets `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS=1048576`, which matches the override. This change does not compare the threshold of Claude Code 2.1.318 itself, so the Claude flags stay.

**Checked.** `test/Installed.test.ts`: a new test asserts that `nanocode-codex` with gpt-6-luna gets no `--context-window` and `--hedge-cap-percent 0`. It and the updated command test fail before the change and pass after. The pinned runtime (sha256 `9a7946e6…`, x86_64) exits 1 with the old Codex flags. With the new flags, for both harnesses, it parses the command and requests `/v1/models` from a local stub. The model turn itself was not run here. From a fresh clone of the commit on 91c7f6f, on the hosted Linux x86_64 machine without KVM and not as root, the steps of the check, e2e-dir, e2e-revision and e2e-ns jobs passed, 78 of 78 (the ns lanes skip without root). After the rebase onto e5ccad0, the check job passed again from a fresh clone. The e2e-krun and krun jobs were not run here (no KVM).

## 2026-11-15: a sandbox paid over MPP takes a session where the service offers one, on one channel per payee for the run, closed when the run ends

**What was wrong.** `src/Payment.ts` registered `tempo.charge` alone, so every paid request of the `e2b` provider (each sandbox create at `https://mpp.e2b.dev/sandboxes`) was one onchain charge from the run's wallet. The service already offers sessions: an unpaid `POST /sandboxes` read on this day answers `402` with four challenges, `tempo` `charge` in two currencies and then `tempo` `session` in the same two, each session on the TIP-1034 escrow `0x4d50500000000000000000000000000000000000`, `sessionProtocol` `v2`, `unitType` `request` and `suggestedDeposit` `1000000` (1 USD). mppx picks the first offer it can pay at equal preference, which was a charge.

**What changed.**

- `Payment.payer` registers `tempo.session` before `tempo.charge` and orders the offers with `Payment.prefer`: every session offer first, then the rest, each in the order the server sent them. A server that offers only charges is paid as before.
- The channels live in a `Payment.Wallet`: mppx's JSON channel store over a key-value table, `payment_channels`, in the Durable Object's SQLite. `Run` and `Pool` each hold one wallet for their object, so every payer the object builds (one each tick) and every request of the run share one channel per payee, token, escrow and chain, which for one service is one channel per origin. mppx serializes opens and top-ups per channel, so concurrent creates do not open a second one. A Worker that restarts finds the channel in its table.
- The deposit is the server's suggestion, capped for a run by `--sandbox-budget-usd` (`maxDepositUsd`), so a run never escrows more than it may spend. Top-ups follow mppx's policy, the bounded suggestion before the exact shortfall.
- The payer keeps the last unpaid `POST` that was answered with a session offer, with its headers and body. `Payment.close` sends it again unpaid with `Payment-Session` set to the channel, takes the session challenge of the channel's payee, token, escrow and chain, signs a close for the cumulative amount the server reports it accepted in its snapshot (the locally signed cumulative when it reports none) and sends that request with the close credential. The body goes along because the service answers a `POST` without a body `400` before it reads any payment. A closed channel leaves the table. A close that is refused, or a channel with no recorded request to close on, stays in the table and is reported with its reason, never dropped.
- `Run` closes its channels when every row is done and no sandbox is open, before it writes `finishedAt`, and marks `payment.close` or `payment.unclosed` on its timeline. `Pool` closes them when it shuts a member and no member is assigned or idle. A failed close is logged and does not hold the run open.
- The charge written to `payments` and to the budget is the challenge's amount, as before: for a session that is the price of the request, not the deposit, which comes back at the close.

**Transactions saved.** From the wallet's side a charge is one transaction per paid request. A session is one open, one top-up for each further deposit the requests use up, and one close that the payee settles. At the live price of a 2 vCPU, 512 MiB, 300 s sandbox (8,721 base units, `test/E2b.test.ts`) 1,000 creates are $8.72: 1,000 transactions as charges, 1 open and 8 top-ups of the suggested 1 USD as a session, so about 991 fewer per 1,000 paid requests. A run that opens 8 sandboxes goes from 8 charges to 1 open. Counted from the challenge and mppx 0.16.0's top-up rule, not from a paid run: this change sent no transaction.

**Checked.** `test/Payment.test.ts` against a local server that offers a charge before a session: the order of the offers, the request kept for the close, a close credential of action `close` for the cumulative amount of a channel built with its real ID, sent with the recorded body and `Payment-Session`, a refused close that keeps the channel, and a channel with no recorded request. The tests of `test/E2b.test.ts` pass unchanged. On the hosted machine with 5 cores, no KVM and a user who is not root, every `run` step of `ci.yml` from a fresh clone of `e5ccad0` with these changes, one after another: 118 of 118 exited 0 (and every step on `ace6b12`, `c8bc92b`, `808a66d` and `fa3176f` as main moved). `npm run lint`, `npm run check:types` and `npm run dry-run` pass; `npm test` ran 448 tests, 443 passed, 5 skipped for KVM or root, 0 failed; `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings` and `cargo test --locked` in `krun/` pass; the two lanes of `e2e-revision` and the 58 lanes of `e2e-dir` passed at the first try. The krun and ns lanes skipped themselves on that machine. No lane pays a session: the scripted gateway and the E2B mock of the lanes are not paid through `Payment.payer` with a session offer.

**Not verified.** A session paid against the real service: that sends transactions from a funded key, and this change sent none. Whether the service closes a channel on a replayed create body with a close credential, as the mppx server does for any route (a close is a management request that runs no handler). Until that is seen, a run's channel that fails to close stays in `payment_channels` with the error on the timeline.

## 2026-11-15: a 401 that the refresh of a plan login does not end is an `environment` error, retried once

A session or an installed agent paid by a plan login (`CLAUDE_LOGIN_URL`, `CHATGPT_LOGIN_URL`, the fixed `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` or `CHATGPT_ACCESS_TOKEN`) or by the plan signed in on the Worker already sent a request once more after a `401`, with the credential the login service or the vault gave after it refreshed (`Logins.send`, `Plans.send`). When that second request was answered `401` too, or the login could not refresh (a fixed token, which `Logins.send` does not send again), the `401` went to the agent. The agent then ended its turn (`Messages HTTP 401`, `curl: (22) ... 401`) and the row ended as an `agent` error: a fault of the credential counted against the harness, and `run --rerun RUN --errored` was the only way back. One of the 28 errors of Nano in the last Claude parity run was such a `401`, and a ChatGPT access token held as a Worker secret ends every day near 05:45 UTC.

**What changes.**

- `Meter.rejecting` wraps the hooks of a request that a plan login or the vault pays for, and records each `401` of the provider with the refusal `login`. A key is never marked.
- `Run.finish` reads the requests of the claim, without the judge's. When the runner reports an `agent` failure and the last request is a `login` refusal, `Retry.rejected` makes it an `environment` failure whose message starts with `Retry.rejectedPrefix` ("the model provider rejected the plan login of the run") and keeps the message of the agent after it.
- `Retry.infrastructure` names that prefix ("the model provider rejected the plan login"), so the run retries the row once on a new claim, as it does for an unreached endpoint. A second rejection completes the row as an `environment` error, which `--rerun --errored` takes up.
- A `401` that the refresh ended is followed by a request that succeeds, so it is never the last request and leaves the verdict to the agent. The run is not stopped, unlike a login whose refresh is refused (the refusal `plan`): a rejection can be transient, and each row retries on its own.

**Checked**, on the hosted Hand (5 cores, no KVM, load average 7 to 14), from `ace6b12` with this change:

- `test/Rejected.test.ts`, 4 tests, against a scripted provider on loopback through `Logins.send` and `Meter.relay`: a token refreshed after a `401` records `[401 login, 200]` and no rejection; a fixed login and a login whose refreshed token is rejected again end as the `environment` failure with the prefix, and `infrastructure` names it; only an `agent` failure is changed; a key's `401` carries no refusal.
- The lane `NANOEVAL_E2E_SCENARIO=login` has a fourth run in which the scripted provider rejects every token, the refreshed ones too. With `claude` sessions: 8 of 8 rows `errored environment` with `claims=2` and the message `the model provider rejected the plan login of the run: Messages HTTP 401: ...`, `refused` null, in 51 s for the whole lane. With `NANOEVAL_E2E_MODEL=installed` (codex-cli and claude-code fixtures): 8 of 8 the same, with `codex-cli exited with 22: curl: (22) The requested URL returned error: 401` and the same for claude-code, 267 s. The first three runs of both lanes end as before, and no file of either holds a token.
- The lane `plan` passed as before.
- Every step of `ci.yml` from a fresh clone, one job after another on the hosted Hand, twice: on ace6b12 108 steps exited 0, and after the rebase onto fa3176f 113 steps exited 0 (`check` with `npm test`, every `e2e-dir` lane, both `e2e-revision` lanes and `krun` with `cargo fmt`, `clippy` and `test`). The 43 `e2e-krun` and `e2e-ns` lanes skipped themselves, as they do without KVM and without root. On d68d7d6, after commits that change the installed agents, add krun and ns lanes and pay sandboxes over an MPP session, `check` and the `login` and `plan` lanes ran again.

**Not verified.** A real provider's `401` after a refresh. A Codex session over a WebSocket upgrade through the relay of nanocode-egress: the upgrade is not metered, and a rejected upgrade is answered `502` by the relay, so it is not marked.

## 2026-11-15: a run sends the requests for a model at the pace its endpoint answers

**What was wrong.** The route of the entries above answers 20 requests of a model in any 60 s, for all callers together, and `429` for the rest. The run waits a refusal out for an installed agent, so an arm is refused more often than it is answered: the arm without a pace below was answered 166 times and refused 228 times. The entry on the pause left "a limit of the run on its own requests a minute" as a change of its own. This is that change.

**What changed.** `run --model-requests-per-min [MODEL=]REQUESTS` gives the run the requests a minute the endpoint answers for a model: `paces` in the config of the run, no default, a number alone for each model of the agents of the run, a model of no agent and no judge refused, and a rerun keeps the paces of its run unless it names its own.

- `src/Pace.ts`. `reserve` hands out send times one interval apart, 60 s over the pace, in the order requests come, and never a time before now, so a pace that sat idle sends no burst. `demand` is the requests a minute of the rows of a model over the time of their agent execution in which they were not held, and `room` the rows a pace still feeds: the pace over that demand, rounded up, less the rows asking, and one row while no row has asked.
- `worker/Meter.ts` asks a hook `pace` before every request it sends upstream, the first ask and each ask again, and holds the request for what the hook returns. The hold is the `wait` of that request in `agent/model-requests.jsonl` and counts in `modelWaits` of the row, as a wait after a refusal does.
- `worker/Run.ts` keeps the next free time of each model in a table, `model_pace`, so the requests of installed agents, of sessions and of the judge, the last two through `/metered` of `worker/Sessions.ts`, take their turn in one queue. A `429` without `Retry-After` on a paced model is asked again after one interval instead of the doubled pause. A second table, `model_paced`, counts the requests and the held time of each claim.
- Claims. `grant` gives a runner a row on a paced model only while a request that came now would be held at most two intervals and `room` is above zero. A claim it declines for the pace does not count the runner as one that fits no row.
- `nanoeval arms` prints `model waits N (S s)` for an arm and has a column for it.

**Checked**, on a machine with 5 cores and no KVM, by a user who is not root. Unit tests of the send times, of the room, of the option and of a rerun, and a simulation of 4, 8 and 16 rows that ask every 5 s for an hour against a provider that counts a sliding minute of 20: with the pace no request is refused and at least 1,195 are answered, without it more are refused than answered. An end-to-end scenario, `pace`, on directory slots: two models at 20 a minute each, a scripted provider that answers one request of a model in 2 s and refuses the rest. With sessions the provider answered 6 and 6 and refused none, and the run held 6 requests for 17.0 s. With installed agents it answered 3 and 3 and refused none, and no request was held: each row of that lane asks once. The lane of sessions was then run on three changed copies, and failed on each as it should: without `paces` in the config the provider refused 25, with the rule for claims off two rows of one model ran at once, and with the hook returning no hold the provider refused 12. Before this commit was pushed, `npm run lint`, `npm run check:types`, `npm run dry-run`, `npm test` and the lanes `pace` for sessions and for installed agents, `limited`, `priced` and `budget` on 2 slots passed on it from a fresh clone.

**What ran on a real route.** Two arms on the same machine, one after the other, each one run: `fx-chat` 0.0.17 on `@cf/zai-org/glm-5.3-flash` through a forwarder that adds the credential of the endpoint and keeps a ledger, the 12 tasks of `ten-minute`, 1 attempt, 4 ns slots, `--model-price '@cf/zai-org/glm-5.3-flash=0.15,0.15,0.50'` and `--model-budget-usd 1`. The first on main at `fa3176f`, the second on this change over that commit with `--model-requests-per-min 20`. Both ended on the budget, which one task, `gcode-to-text`, spends most of.

| | No pace | 20 a minute |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Requests answered | 166 | 207 |
| Requests refused with `429` | 228 | 25 |
| Refused for each answered | 1.37 | 0.12 |
| Answered a minute, first answer to last | 10.2 | 13.9 |
| Rows passed, of 12 | 7 | 8 |
| Rows ended by the budget | 5 | 4 |
| Rows ended by the route | 0 | 0 |
| `model waits` of the arm | 228 (228 s) | 200 (972 s) |
| Wall time | 16 min 23 s | 15 min 33 s |
| Agent time of the 7 rows that passed in both | 670 s | 765 s |

Waits of each row, without and with the pace: `configure-git-webserver` 11 (7 s) and 9 (30 s), `fix-code-vulnerability` 0 and 13 (77 s), `fix-git` 6 (8 s) and 9 (56 s), `gcode-to-text` 67 (58 s) and 49 (234 s), `git-leak-recovery` 51 (68 s) and 8 (18 s), `kv-store-grpc` 28 (34 s) and 8 (17 s), `largest-eigenval` 36 (29 s) and 48 (228 s), `multi-source-data-merger` 11 (6 s) and 7 (26 s), `pypi-server` 13 (17 s) and 8 (32 s), `pytorch-model-recovery` 5 (2 s) and 20 (120 s), `raman-fitting` none, the budget was spent before it started, and 21 (134 s). `overfull-hbox` started in neither.

The ledger of the forwarder counts every caller of the machine. In the minutes of the arm without a pace it has 206 answered and 263 refused requests of the model, so other runs of the machine were answered 40 times and refused 35 times beside it. In the minutes of the arm with the pace it has the arm's requests and no other. Its send times are at least 2.9 s apart.

**Where the pace did not help, and what it costs.**

- The arm with the pace was refused nothing for its first 173 answers, 12 minutes, and then 25 times in the 3 minutes after. Before each of those refusals the ledger has 6 to 17 answered requests of the model in the 60 s before, not 20: a caller that is not in this ledger was on the same account, as the entry on the route found before. A pace keeps a run under the number it is told and knows nothing of other callers. The same was there beside the arm without a pace: 81 of the 263 refusals of its minutes came with fewer than 15 answered in the 60 s before. So 0.12 is what this arm measured, above the 0.1 that was the aim, and the figure of an arm that has the model alone was not measured.
- Rows wait longer in all, 972 s against 228 s: a wait is 4.9 s on average where a pause after a refusal was 1.0 s, and a hold counts in the agent time of the row, as the pause does. The 7 rows that passed in both arms took 765 s of agent time against 670 s. One of them, `configure-git-webserver`, lost 32 s to a first request the forwarder answered `502`.
- That first request also made the first row look slow, 1 request in 32 s, so the run claimed 3 more rows within 35 s where the rule means the first row to run alone until it has asked and been answered. Their requests were then held about 6 s each.
- The demand of a row is the mean over every row of the model so far. From minute 9 to minute 12 three rows that wrote long answers were answered 5 times a minute together in two of those minutes, the mean stood at about 8 requests a minute for a row, so 3 rows were taken to feed the pace, and two rows stayed unclaimed beside a free slot for 3 min 25 s. The arm still was answered more often a minute than the one without a pace. A rule that claims one more row when the pace has held no request for a minute is the next step and is not in this change.

**Not verified.** krun slots and a deployed Worker. Sessions and a judge on a real route: their hold is tested in the lane only. Two paced models at once on a real route. A run of a provider whose idle sandboxes close while the pace holds its rows. An arm larger than 12 rows, and a pace above what the endpoint answers. What the provider charged.

## 2026-11-15: the loop is one command

**What was missing.** Setting six arms against each other on the tasks of `hourly`, with a line for each arm and a verdict against a baseline, took four commands, 14 options and a run id copied by hand, counted from the README before this change:

1. `nanoeval revision --eval terminal-bench-2.1 --subset hourly --attempts 3 --slots N --baseline previous --fail-on regression` and six `--agent`: 12 options. Left at its defaults it ran on 4 slots, and `--baseline previous` is refused in a lab whose first run this is.
2. `nanoeval revision --serve --port 8787 &`: 1 option, a Worker for reading.
3. `export NANOEVAL_URL=... NANOEVAL_TOKEN=$(cat LAB/token)`.
4. `nanoeval arms RUN`: the run id copied from the output of the first command, 1 option counted for it.

And nothing printed the time of the whole loop or its infrastructure errors over all arms, the two numbers a loop is judged by before its pass rates are read.

**The command.** `nanoeval loop` and one `--agent` for each arm: 1 command, 6 options for six arms. It is the path of `nanoeval revision`, which already was the engine: the Worker of a lab under local workerd, the import of what the lab lacks, one run with every agent, a runner, the wait, the summary, the comparison with a baseline, the gate and the Harbor job. `src/Loop.ts` adds what a loop does not have to choose, and the command says each in its first line:

- The eval `terminal-bench-2.1` and its subset `hourly`, unless `--eval`, `--task`, `--subset`, `--only`, `--only-file` or `--limit` name tasks, and 3 attempts a task: the list and the count the entry on the two task lists chose for loops.
- One slot for each hardware thread the command may run on (`availableParallelism`, so a command pinned to some threads takes those). The 4 slots of `run` are the same on every machine, and the 540 rows of six arms on `hourly` would run four at a time.
- `krun` slots where the machine has `/dev/kvm`, `ns` slots as root, as `doctor` reads a machine. A machine with neither is refused until `--backend dir` is named: directories have no isolation, and a loop that fell back to them silently would score arms on the state they leave each other.
- The baseline is the run before this one that holds these arms and tasks, and `--fail-on regression`. The first such run of a lab has no baseline: where `revision --baseline previous` is refused, a loop that took the baseline by itself says `baseline: none, so this run gets no verdict`, drops the gate and goes on. A baseline that was named and is missing is still refused.
- `--baseline NAME`: in a loop a word that is the `--name` of runs of the lab is the latest finished one of them, after the ids and revisions `revision` already reads. So `loop --name main` once and `loop --baseline main` afterwards hold later loops against a fixed line with no id copied.

`--build-only`, `--rerun` and `--serve` are refused, and so is a loop without `--agent` or `--oracle`: each in one line before anything is started.

**The scorecard** is printed after the summary and the comparison and written as `scorecard.json` beside the Harbor job. A row an arm: what `nanoeval arms` counts (`src/Arms.ts`, unchanged but for one function it now exports), pass@k for each k of the run, and the arm's verdict against the baseline with the tasks that moved down and up, from the changes `compare` works out. One line for the loop: its rows, the time from the start of the command to the scorecard, the time of the run from its first start to its last end with its slots, the infrastructure errors as a share of the rows, the agent and model errors. One verdict: a regression when any arm regressed, an improvement when one improved and none regressed, and an arm the baseline does not hold is named as such and judged by nothing. No new arithmetic: every figure is one `status`, `compare` or `arms` already had, put in one place.

**Counted.** Before: 4 commands, 14 options, a run id copied by hand, and no time or error rate of the loop. After: 1 command, 6 options, the six arms. A model whose endpoint names no cost adds one `--model-price`, and a fixed line adds `--baseline NAME`.

**Ran**, once each, on a machine with 5 cores and no KVM, by a user who is not root, on directory slots with the scripted model, on the change over `fa3176f`. No run failed.

- The lane `node test/revision.ts loop`: three loops of two arms on the three sample tasks at 2 attempts, 12 rows each: the first run of a lab (no baseline, no verdict, exit 0), the same arms on a model that fails every task against the run before (each arm `regression, 3 down and 0 up of 3`, exit 3), and the model that solves against the first run by its name (exit 0). 51.2 s for the three commands.
- Six scripted arms on 12 tasks at 2 attempts, 144 rows on 4 slots, which is what `availableParallelism` gave there. The tasks are stand-ins: copies of the three sample tasks under the names of the 12 tasks of `ten-minute`, so `--subset ten-minute` of `terminal-bench-2.1` resolved in the lab, and none of the benchmark's environments ran. They were imported by a loop of their solutions, 12 of 12 passed, 17 s from the command.

| Loop | Model | Baseline | From the command | The run on its slots | Passed by arm | Verdict | Exit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| First | Fails half the sessions of 2 tasks | None in the lab | 1 min 42 s | 1 min 27 s | 24, 20, 24, 20, 24, 20 of 24 | None, the run has no baseline | 0 |
| Seeded regression | And every session of 6 more tasks | The run before, taken by itself | 1 min 57 s (117.5 s to the exit) | 1 min 42 s | 12, 8, 12, 8, 12, 8 of 24 | Regression in all six arms, each 6 down and 0 up of 12 | 3 |
| Again | As the first | The first, by its `--name` | 1 min 57 s (118.1 s to the exit) | 1 min 39 s | 24, 20, 24, 20, 24, 20 of 24 | No change beyond noise in all six | 0 |

  0 infrastructure errors and 0 agent errors in the 432 rows. The 24 rows of an arm took 7 to 10 s of agent time and 48 to 59 s of attempt time together, so these times are the overhead of the command and of directory slots on 4 threads, not the time of a loop on a benchmark.
- Six changes to `src/Loop.ts`, one at a time, each failed `test/Loop.test.ts`: slots that are not the machine's, an improvement that outranks a regression, the error rate over arms instead of rows, a baseline by name that takes an unfinished run, directories that are not refused, and the time of the command dropped.
- Before it landed, from a fresh clone on main at `d68d7d6`, on a machine with 48 hardware threads and KVM, pinned to 4 of them: `npm ci`, `npm run lint`, `npm run check:types`, `npm run dry-run`, `npm test` with 456 tests, 451 passed, 5 skipped, 0 failed, and 1 of 1 each on directory slots: the lane of the loop (25.1 s for its three commands), the lane of `nanoeval revision` and the lane of `nanoeval watch` over it. The command of the quick start there, two scripted arms on the three sample tasks at 3 attempts, 18 rows on 4 slots: exit 0 after 8 s, 5/9 and 8/9 passed, 0 infrastructure errors, no baseline and no verdict. Main moved meanwhile to `705d8cc`: on the change rebased onto it, `npm run lint`, `npm run check:types` and `npm test` once more there, with 468 tests, 463 passed, 5 skipped, 0 failed. A second `npm test` there, with cargo in reach, ran four tests that the first had skipped for want of the launcher: 454 passed, 1 was skipped, and the one that builds a guest image failed where the registry answered 429 to an anonymous pull.

**Not run.** A loop with a model. A loop on krun or ns slots, so the backend taken from the machine was read by unit tests only. The tasks of `hourly` or `ten-minute` themselves, and so the wall time of a loop that means anything: the entry on the two lists puts six arms at three attempts at 27 to 58 minutes on 36 slots by a model of the slots. One slot a thread under six arms of real agents, on any machine: whether that is the right count was not measured. An import of the benchmark from nothing by the loop itself, and a loop with `--nanocode`.

**Limits.** Nothing bounds the wall time of a loop but the timeouts of its tasks. The arms share the slots of one run and the claim order of its rows, so no arm has slots of its own and an arm of slow rows holds the others up. The verdict of an arm is that of `compare`, all its tasks together, and at 3 attempts on `hourly` shows 6 to 12 points and nothing smaller. Two loops in one lab run one after the other, as two evaluations do.

## 2026-11-15: a runner that is given no slot count takes one slot for each hardware thread it may use

**The defect.** `run --slots` and `runner --slots` defaulted to 4 on every machine. The oracle arm of Terminal-Bench 2.1 in the entry on the claim order above, 89 tasks and three attempts each, took 2,203 s at 28 slots that were named by hand for 28 hardware threads. With no option the same arm is 7,920 s in the slot model of that entry, 2.2 hours and 3.6 times as long, on the same machine.

**Measured: where more slots stop helping.** One sweep, one run a point, before this change: the oracle on the 68 sound tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.1 whose oracle row is under 100 s, three attempts each, 204 rows a point, main at `ac039b7`, one bare-metal machine with KVM (24 cores, 48 hardware threads), one runner with krun slots pinned to 28 hardware threads, a local Worker. Each point ran beside the last 3 to 7 rows of a full arm on the same threads, the point at 14 slots also beside a model arm of 8 slots, and the point at 56 beside one of 16 slots from its third minute.

| Slots on 28 threads | Rows that ended | Wall | Rows a minute | Mean row | Rows that did not pass |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| 14 | 202 | 356 s | 34.0 | 21.1 s | 3 failed in the same minutes, all three fetch from one outside service; 2 cancelled, a verifier that hangs in its own tests |
| 28 | 204 | 283 s | 43.3 | 29.1 s | 1 failed: a verifier that measures speed |
| 56 | 203 | 271 s | 44.9 | 52.6 s | 1 failed: the same verifier; 1 cancelled, the verifier that hangs |

From 14 to 28 slots the rows a minute rise by 27 % and a row takes 1.38 times as long. From 28 to 56 they rise by 4 % and a row takes 1.8 times as long. At one slot a thread 23.4 of the 28 threads were busy. The point at 14 slots is a floor, since more other work ran beside it. One slot for each hardware thread is where the throughput of rows that compute stopped growing.

**What changed.**

- A run names a slot count or none. `Config.sandbox.slots` and the `slots` a runner is configured with are optional, `nanoeval run` on the local provider sends none unless `--slots` names one, and `nanoeval runner` takes the count of its run unless its own `--slots` names one.
- A runner with no count has one slot for each hardware thread it may use (`sandbox/Cpus.ts`, after `sandbox/Memory.ts`): the fewest of the threads that are online, the threads in the `Cpus_allowed_list` of its own status in `/proc`, which is its affinity as `taskset` or a cpuset left it, and the `cpu.max` of its control group and of every group above it, rounded down and never under one. That number is the `cpus` of the capabilities it says hello with, which were the threads online before. Its log says so: `N slots, one for each hardware thread this runner may use`.
- Admission is what it was. The count is a count of rows, a row takes one slot whatever CPUs its task declares, and memory is admitted as before. A count that is named is untouched.
- The run uses the count in two more places. `Config.lifetimeSec` sizes the life of a sandbox for one row at a time when no count is named, the longest it can be needed. The disks a runner is told to fetch ahead are as many as its slots: the count of the run, or the `cpus` the runner said hello with.

**What the default does to what already ran.**

- The lanes of this repository: none changes. `test/e2e.ts` puts a slot count in every run it creates (`NANOEVAL_E2E_SLOTS`, 4 in the test itself when the variable is not set) and passes `--slots` to every runner it attaches or stands, and `test/revision.ts` names `--slots` and `slots = 3` in its lab. The lane added here is the only one that names none. A runner of the workflow has 4 hardware threads, where the count is the 4 it was.
- A machine with fewer than 4 threads has fewer slots than before: 2 on 2 threads, where 4 ran. For rows that compute that is the measurement above. For rows that wait for a model it may end later than before, which was not measured: `--slots` names more.
- A machine with many threads and little memory: the count no longer limits the rows there and memory does, as it was built to. A runner admits rows by the memory their tasks declare into 80 % of the lower of its machine's memory and the limit of its control groups, so a runner of 16 threads and 16 GB admits 6 rows of 2 GB at once where its 16 slots would take 16 and the default before took 4, and a row that does not fit is passed over as before.
- `nanoeval loop` names a count of its own, the threads of the machine it runs on, and is unchanged. Its scorecard now takes that count from the loop and not from the configuration of the run, which may hold none.
- Two runners on one machine each take the count of the threads they may use: `--sandboxes 2` on the local provider, or two `nanoeval runner` processes that are not pinned apart, have twice as many slots as the machine has threads, where they had 8 before. Each also admits its own 80 % of the memory, as before. `--slots` for each, or an affinity for each, divides the machine.

**Not changed.** A run on `e2b` or `gateway` still takes 4 when `--slots` names none. The run buys such a sandbox for a life it computes from the count before a sandbox exists, and no run of this change was made on either. The constant is still there for them.

`Protocol.version` is not raised. A runner of an earlier commit works with a Worker of this one for every run that names a slot count, and for any run when the runner names its own (`runner --slots`). Handed a run that names none while it names none either, such a runner offers no slot and claims nothing, by the code and not run. Raising the number would refuse every runner of an earlier commit for every run, where one configuration fails. A Worker of an earlier commit refuses a run that names no count with its message about `sandbox.slots`.

**Built, modelled and held back: admitting rows by the CPUs their tasks declare.** The first version of this change also had a runner with no count admit rows against CPUs as against memory: a row took the CPUs its task declares out of the runner's threads, and a row that did not fit was passed over for the rows behind it. It ran in unit tests and in a lane on directory slots, and never in an arm. The slot model of the entry on the claim order (no contention between slots, a row takes the mean of the three attempts its task had in the arm at 28 named slots, the queue order of main), with the CPUs each task declares, 83 tasks one, 3 tasks two, 3 tasks four:

| Hardware threads | A count of that many, plain (this change) | Rows admitted by CPUs, passed over (held back) | Rows admitted by CPUs, claims stop at a row that waits (dropped) |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 4 | 7,920 s | 12,613 s | 14,748 s |
| 8 | 4,072 s | 6,431 s | 6,636 s |
| 14 | 2,826 s | 3,780 s | 4,254 s |
| 16 | 2,640 s | 3,408 s | 3,860 s |
| 20 | 2,418 s | 2,746 s | 3,365 s |
| 28 | 2,204 s | 2,122 s | 2,774 s |
| 36 | 2,038 s | 1,984 s | 2,485 s |
| 48 | 1,951 s | 1,920 s | 2,218 s |

The model has it 3.7 % sooner than the plain count on 28 threads, and 14 % later on 20, 29 % later on 16 and 59 % later on 4, where a task of four CPUs runs alone: the six tasks of several CPUs hold 2 or 4 threads for rows of 72 to 1,475 s, 16,700 thread-seconds more over the arm than a plain count gives them. The model cannot say what a plain count pays for the same rows in threads that are shared, since its durations were measured with 28 rows on 28 threads. So it is held back until one arm measures it: the oracle on the 89 tasks, three attempts, on 16 threads, with CPU admission against `--slots 16`. It lands if that arm ends within 5 % of the plain count, and is dropped with its numbers if not.

**Checked.** On one bare-metal machine with KVM (24 cores, 48 hardware threads), pinned with `taskset` to 4 of its threads, Node 24, from a fresh clone of main at `e5ccad0` with this change and without this entry, each once: `npm ci`, lint, both type checks, the dry run and `npm test`: 447 tests, 442 passed, 5 skipped, none failed, with the unit tests of the affinity list, of the quota, of the two together and of the whole threads (`test/Cpus.test.ts`), of a configuration that names no count, of the life of a sandbox without one and of a rerun of a run without one. Eleven directory lanes, 11 of 11 passed. The new lane (`NANOEVAL_E2E_SCENARIO=threads`) pins itself with `taskset` to one hardware thread fewer than it has rows, creates a run that names no slot count, and asks that its runner says hello with that many `cpus` and that as many rows ran at once: its runner had 2 threads and ran at most 2 of 3 rows at once, where the default before would have run all 3. The others: memory packing; three tasks with the scripted model; the oracle; two attached runners; a standing runner that two runs are handed to; a standing runner with the rows of two runs; a standing runner stopped during a run; a runner lost; a runner restarted; and the scripted gateway, which was cut off from outside together with the script that ran the lanes the first time, and passed when it was started again.

On krun slots on the same 4 threads, the oracle on the four tasks of the `smoke` subset of Terminal-Bench 2.1, three attempts, 12 rows a run, two runs each way in turn. With no `--slots` the runner said `4 slots, one for each hardware thread this runner may use` on the machine of 48, and the runs took 63 s, the first on that machine with the disks of the tasks still packed, and 36 s. With `--slots 4` they took 36 s and 34 s. 12 of 12 rows passed in each of the four.

Then the commit itself, with this entry, on main as it had moved, on the same threads: lint, both type checks, `npm test`, the new lane again and the loop lane of the workflow (`node test/revision.ts loop`).

**Not run.** An arm of the 89 tasks with no `--slots`: the count a runner takes for itself ran in the lane and in two runs of 12 rows, and an arm on a machine of N threads with no option is the arm with `--slots N` by the code. The krun and ns lanes of the workflow at this change. A run on `e2b` or `gateway`. A machine with fewer than 4 threads. A CPU quota that is not a whole number, outside the unit test.

## 2026-11-15: a run may bound the time of its agents, and every row says so

**The defect.** An arm cannot end sooner than its longest row, and the longest row of an arm with a model is an agent that does not stop. The tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.1 allow their agents 600 to 12,000 s: 50 of the 89 allow 900 s or less, 22 allow 1,200 or 1,800 s and 17 allow 2,400 s or more. Nothing in a run could shorten that, so no number of slots brought an arm under the longest timeout that one of its agents happened to run out.

Two arms of one harness on one open-weight model show it (fx 0.0.17 over chat completions, gpt-oss-120b, krun slots on one bare-metal machine with KVM, 24 cores and 48 hardware threads, main at `e5ccad0`). The 89 tasks once, on 20 slots: 88 rows had their verdict after 12 min 18 s, and the 89th, `crack-7z-hash`, whose agent had not stopped, was 27 minutes into the 1,800 s of its task when the run was cancelled. The 89 tasks three times, on 28 slots: 25.9 minutes, 264 of the 267 rows had ended after 20.5 minutes, and the last row to end was an agent that ran out the 900 s of `db-wal-recovery`, at 1,554 s. A row of that arm took 76 s at the median, 248 s at the ninth decile and 910 s at the longest.

**Measured: what a limit would have cost.** Eight recorded arms, each read once, no arm run for this: the two above; three arms of nanocode sessions and one of Claude Code on claude-haiku-5-5 and two arms of nanocode sessions on gpt-6-luna, 89 tasks once each, on other machines. A pass is lost to a limit of C when its agent took more than C seconds. That is an upper bound, since a row the limit ends is still verified.

| Arm | Rows | Passed | Agent seconds of its passes: median, ninth decile, longest | Rows that ran out their task's limit | Passes lost at 300 s | at 450 s | at 600 s | at 900 s |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| nanocode, haiku, through a gateway | 89 | 62 | 71, 609, 2,432 | 4 | 13 | 8 | 7 | 3 |
| nanocode, haiku, a later build | 89 | 57 | 67, 404, 1,715 | 2 | 6 | 5 | 3 | 1 |
| nanocode, haiku, a third arm | 89 | 61 | 88, 537, 2,400 | 6 | 11 | 8 | 6 | 4 |
| Claude Code, haiku | 89 | 64 | 87, 665, 2,256 | 5 | 12 | 10 | 7 | 4 |
| nanocode, luna, a later build | 89 | 33 | 54, 251, 863 | 1 | 3 | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| nanocode, luna, an earlier build | 89 | 39 | 73, 381, 946 | 0 | 4 | 3 | 2 | 2 |
| fx, gpt-oss-120b, once | 89 | 11 | 99, 168, 252 | 1, cancelled in it | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| fx, gpt-oss-120b, three times | 267 | 30 | 78, 236, 774 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 |

A pass takes about a minute at the median in every arm, and the rows that take longest are mostly not passes. A limit of 600 s costs the weak model 1 of its 30 passes, 0.4 points of its 267 rows, luna 1 to 2 of 33 to 39, 1.1 to 2.2 points, and haiku 3 to 7 of 57 to 64, 3.4 to 7.9 points. At 300 s haiku loses 6 to 13 passes, 6.7 to 14.6 points. So a limit is a different measurement for a strong arm and nearly the same one for a weak arm, and two arms are comparable only under the same limit.

**Measured: what a limit buys.** A model of the slots with no contention and the claim order of a run, each row its recorded setup, agent seconds cut at the limit and verifier (for the six arms of other machines the setup of the 48-thread machine), an arm of one attempt counted three times:

| Arm as 89 x 3 | Limit | Every row started at once | On 160 slots | On 96 slots | On 48 slots |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| fx, gpt-oss-120b, three times | none | 15.2 min | 15.2 min | 16.2 min | 19.0 min |
| | 900 s | 15.2 min | 15.2 min | 16.1 min | 19.0 min |
| | 600 s | 10.5 min | 10.9 min | 12.4 min | 16.5 min |
| | 300 s | 10.5 min | 10.9 min | 12.4 min | 16.5 min |
| fx, gpt-oss-120b, once, with the agent that did not stop at its 1,800 s | none | 30.0 min | 30.7 min | 32.7 min | 37.6 min |
| | 600 s | 10.3 min | 10.9 min | 12.9 min | 18.2 min |
| nanocode, haiku, through a gateway | none | 42.9 min | 43.6 min | 46.9 min | 59.1 min |
| | 900 s | 21.3 min | 21.9 min | 25.2 min | 37.2 min |
| | 600 s | 21.2 min | 21.7 min | 25.0 min | 35.2 min |
| | 300 s | 18.5 min | 19.6 min | 23.4 min | 31.1 min |
| nanocode, luna, a later build | none | 26.5 min | 27.5 min | 29.2 min | 34.5 min |
| | 600 s | 14.1 min | 15.1 min | 16.7 min | 21.9 min |

Without a limit the weak arm at one slot a row is 15 to 31 minutes, by whichever agents do not stop that time. With 600 s it is 10.9 minutes on 160 slots either way, and what is left is a verifier: under 600 s the row that ends last is `query-optimize`, whose verifier took 606 to 612 s after an agent of seconds. For haiku the limit halves the arm and then stops helping, at 21 minutes: its agents use the 600 s on the tasks whose verifiers are the slowest.

**The second floor: verifier and setup.** The largest verifier and setup seconds of each task in the 890 rows of that machine, two oracle arms of 89 x 3 and the two arms above: `torch-tensor-parallelism` 901 s (its verifier ran out its own 900 s in 2 of 6 oracle rows, and it is in `unsound.json`), `query-optimize` 694 s, `fix-ocaml-gc` 592 s, `regex-chess` 412 s, `filter-js-from-html` 310 s, and no other task over 180 s. On other machines `query-optimize` took 814 s and `fix-ocaml-gc` 675 s after a model's work.

So, by these counts: an arm of 89 x 3 in 15 minutes needs a slot for nearly every row and a limit of 600 s on the agent. The limit costs 1 pass of 30 for the weak model (0.4 points) and 3 to 7 of 57 to 64 for haiku (3.4 to 7.9 points). Five tasks cannot be promised to fit even so, because their verifier and setup leave the agent under 600 s of the 900: the five above. Two of them fit under 300 s, at twice the passes lost. An arm that keeps the five still ends in time when its agents are quick on them, as the weak model's were.

**What changed.**

- `run --agent-max-sec N` (`limits.agentMaxSec` of the configuration, a whole number of seconds, at least 1). The run reads every task with the smaller of its own agent timeout and N (`Config.bounded`, in the one place the run reads a task), so everything that follows from the agent timeout follows the limit: the deadline of a session's turn, the timeout a runner gives an installed agent and a solution, the wait of a runner for either, the worst case by which rows are claimed and admitted, and the life a sandbox is bought for. The task stored with the run is the task of the eval, unchanged. It applies to every agent of the run, the solutions of `--oracle` included.
- A row the limit ends is an agent timeout as before: the turn is cancelled, the verifier runs, the reward stands, and the row reads `failed after the agent timeout (the agent did not finish within N s)`.
- Every attempt of such a run carries `agentMaxSec` in its result, and so in the results of the run and what is read from them. A run without the option carries nothing new, and its results are what they were.
- `nanoeval arms` adds `agent time limit N s` to the line of such an arm, its JSON has `agentLimits` for every arm, and a table that holds one such arm has a column that says the limit of each, `the task's own` for the others. The scorecard of `nanoeval loop` has the same column on the same condition.
- A comparison of sides under different limits is a comparison of different things, as one of different payers is: `Compare.pairs` names it (`agent time limit the task's own in the baseline and 600 s in the run`), `compare`, `run --baseline` and `loop --baseline` refuse it until `--unlike`, which marks the comparison, and a baseline by rule (`latest`, `previous`, the name of a loop) passes over runs `under another limit on the agent's time`. An arm of solutions under a limit is not the arm without one either.
- A rerun keeps the limit of its run unless its command names one. Rows of one arm under two limits say both.
- `subsets.json` has `fifteen-minute`: the 84 tasks whose largest recorded verifier and setup on that machine are 300 s or less, the benchmark without the five above.

**Why the limit is one number and not a factor.** Harbor has both for a trial: a multiplier of each timeout and `max_timeout_sec`, the smaller of the task's timeout and a cap. A factor keeps the long tasks the longest, so the floor of an arm moves by the factor and a task of 12,000 s still decides it. A cap bounds the floor by itself, and leaves every task under it as it is.

**Why the verifier has no limit.** Harbor has the same cap for the verifier. It is not taken: an agent that is cut short has still left work that can be scored, and a verifier that is cut short has scored nothing, so its row is an error with no verdict and not a failure. A cap on the verifier would turn the slowest tasks of a deadline into errors of every arm. A task whose verifier does not fit is left out of the list, which is what `fifteen-minute` does, and a row whose verifier runs out its own limit is a verifier timeout as before.

**Checked.** Unit tests of the limit in a configuration (whole seconds, at least 1, absent when not named), of a task under it and of the worst case of a row and the life of a sandbox with it (`test/Config.test.ts`), of the line, the table and the JSON of `arms`, of the scorecard of a loop, of the sides `compare` names and refuses, a planned run and an arm of solutions among them, of the baseline a rule passes over, and of a rerun. Ten changes to the code of the limit, one at a time, each fail one of them. The lane `NANOEVAL_E2E_SCENARIO=bounded` on directory slots with the scripted model: a new fixture whose task allows its agent 300 s and whose scripted agent sleeps 30 s, beside `write-greeting`, in a run with `agentMaxSec` 10. The configuration of the run holds the limit, both attempts carry it, the long agent is ended after 10.0 s as an agent timeout that names 10 s, its verifier ran and its reward is 0, the other row passed, and the line of the arm says `agent time limit 10 s`.

On one bare-metal machine with KVM (24 cores, 48 hardware threads), on 4 of its threads, the change on main at `d01bb39`, each once: lint, both type checks, the dry run, `npm test` (477 tests, 472 passed, 5 skipped, none failed), the directory lanes `bounded`, `failures`, `tasks` and `threads` and the loop lane of the workflow, 5 of 5 passed. Then the commit itself, with this entry, on main as it had moved, from a fresh clone on a machine of 5 cores without KVM: `npm ci`, lint, both type checks, the dry run, `npm test` and the lanes `bounded`, `failures` and `tasks` and the loop lane.

**Run once with a model under the limit.** One arm, this change on main at `d01bb39`: fx 0.0.17 over chat completions on gpt-oss-120b, the 89 tasks three times, `--agent-max-sec 600`, 160 krun slots on 36 hardware threads of the machine above, beside the last rows of the same arm without the limit. 267 rows in 14.1 minutes, 845 s from the first start to the last end: half of the rows had ended after 207 s, nine in ten after 358 s and all but one after 733 s. The configuration of the run holds the limit and all 267 attempts carry `agentMaxSec` 600. 37 rows passed, 199 failed and 31 errored: 22 of the agent, which left with an error, and 9 of the verifier, 6 of them the package archive that answers 404 to the verifiers of two tasks and 3 a verifier that wrote no test report. The limit ended 3 agents, of `crack-7z-hash`, `mailman` and `make-doom-for-mips`, each after 600 s, each verified and failed. The longest pass took 475 s. The row that ended last was claimed 206 s after the first and ran out the limit: the runner admitted about 90 rows at once, by the memory their tasks declare, and not 160, which is why the arm took 14.1 minutes where the model above has 10.9. The three rows of `query-optimize` ended after 631 to 733 s, on a verifier of 556 to 601 s. 3,099 model calls, 33.0 million input and 0.75 million output tokens, 12.11 USD at list prices.

The same arm without the limit, started 15 minutes earlier on the same slots, had 260 of its 267 rows after 11 minutes and was 30 minutes old when this was written, with 30 rows passed and two agents still running, one of them in `crack-7z-hash` again. On 28 slots it had taken 25.9 minutes and passed 30. So the limit took the arm from more than 30 minutes to 14.1, and cost no pass that three attempts can show: 37 under it, 30 and 30 without.

**Not run.** The lane on krun or ns slots: the run bounds a task before a runner sees it, so the backends share the limit by the code. A session of nanocode with a model under the limit: the lane ran a scripted session and the arm an installed agent. The refusal of a Worker of an earlier nanoeval, which drops a limit it does not know: `nanoeval run` reads the configuration of the run it made, cancels the run and says so, by the code. `nanoeval loop` with the option, outside the unit test of its scorecard. A run through `--subset fifteen-minute`. An arm of a strong model under a limit: what it loses is the count above, not a measurement.

**Limits.** The costs are counted in arms that ran without a limit, by the seconds their agents took: an agent that knows nothing of the limit is cut where it would have gone on, and one that is slowed by a loaded machine or a slow route loses passes it would have made. No agent is told its limit. The times in the tables are a model of the slots with no contention: 160 slots ran in two arms, one of them under the limit, and about 90 rows ran at once in it, since a runner admits rows by the memory their tasks declare. `fifteen-minute` is chosen from verifier seconds of one machine after an oracle and after one weak model: a stronger agent leaves a verifier more to do, as the 814 s of `query-optimize` on another machine say. The promise of 900 s a row is not a promise for the arm unless every row has a slot at once. The list keeps 6 tasks of `unsound.json` and the tasks that fetch from outside services: it is the benchmark without what cannot fit, not a list chosen for what it tells.

The CPUs a task declares still size its microVM and nothing else. One arm in which 10 of 16 slots stood empty for 23 minutes beside rows that waited, and a model that has the plain count 29 % sooner on these threads, are not a reason to change a default, and code that no measurement supports does not go to main. **Not run.** Three attempts, which the rule named. More than 16 threads, where the model has the admission 2 to 4 % sooner than a plain count from 28 threads on. ## 2026-11-15: an error of a task whose dependency is gone is counted apart from infrastructure errors

**What was asked.** The first real arm of all 89 tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.1 three times had 5 infrastructure errors in 267 rows, 1.9%, over the line of 1% that an arm is held to. All five were the verifiers of `qemu-alpine-ssh` and `qemu-startup`, "the verifier could not install what its test.sh installs: its package archive answered 404 Not Found". No machine, slot or route can change that, so the number said nothing about the infrastructure.

**What is fetched, and why it is gone.** Both tasks build on `debian:bullseye-slim`. Their `tests/test.sh` begins with `apt-get update` and `apt-get install -y curl` (`qemu-startup` adds `expect`, `qemu-alpine-ssh` `sshpass`), then installs uv with curl and runs pytest through `uvx`. On 2026-11-15, with curl from the machine that holds the lanes, through its egress: `deb.debian.org/debian-security/dists/bullseye-security/InRelease` answers 200 and is dated 2026-09-12; its `Packages` lists `curl 7.74.0-1.3+deb11u16`; `pool/updates/main/c/curl/curl_7.74.0-1.3%2bdeb11u16_amd64.deb`, `libcurl4` of the same version and `pool/updates/main/n/nghttp2/libnghttp2-14_1.43.0-1%2bdeb11u3_amd64.deb` answer 404, and the directory of the pool holds only the packages of Debian 12 and 13; the same file answers 200 on `archive.debian.org`. The packages of `bullseye/main` that the same command installs answer 200. So it is not an index that moves under a pinned task: the index of the security archive of Debian 11 stopped moving after the end of its support and names packages that left the mirror. The entry of 2026-11-14 on verifiers that could not install found the same from another machine.

**Could the import have kept it.** No. An import converts the environment of a task, its image, and stores the tests as a blob: it runs no `test.sh`. The download is made by the verifier's own script when an attempt is verified, and from an index that the script refreshes first, so a package list kept in the image would be replaced as well. Keeping what a verifier downloads would mean running every verifier once at import behind a proxy that records, and answering from the record afterwards: `run --verifier-cache` keeps what uv downloads per task, and nothing does it for apt. It would not have helped here: the packages were already gone on 2026-11-10, when the 89 tasks first ran here with their own solutions. Pointing apt at `archive.debian.org` inside the slot would change what the task's verifier does, which this repository does not do: the fix is upstream's, and `unsound.json` names its report.

**The rule.** `Unsound.gone` says that an attempt errored because the dependency of its task is gone when three things hold: it ended as a `verifier` error; its message begins with the words that `src/Verdict.ts` writes when the verifier's output has the line of apt `E: Failed to fetch URL 404 Not Found`; and `unsound.json` lists the checksum of that version of the task, which is there because its own solution was shown to lose the same way, with the cause and the report. `src/Arms.ts` has a fourth class of errors, `task`, beside `infrastructure`, `agent` and `cancelled`, keyed by the name of the task: `nanoeval arms` prints `task dependency gone 5 or 1.9% of its rows (qemu-alpine-ssh 2, qemu-startup 3)` between the two classes when an arm has such rows, a table of arms gets a column when one of them does, and `--json` holds `errors.task`. The scorecard of `nanoeval loop` has the same column, `loop.taskErrors`, and the count after the infrastructure errors in its line; `infrastructureErrors` and `infrastructureRate` no longer count these rows. `status` and `run --wait` print one line under the lines of the unsound tasks. The verdict of the attempt, its retry rule and the exit status are unchanged: the row is an error, not retried, and `run --wait` and `loop` exit 1 on it.

**Why both proofs.** The 404 alone can be a mirror out of step with its index for an hour, which is the infrastructure of that hour: a task the list does not name keeps the error in the infrastructure class until `nanoeval oracle` loses the same row and somebody lists the task with its cause. The list alone is not enough either: five of its seven tasks have a solution that fails and a verifier that runs, and a `verifier` error on them is not explained by the entry. With `--unsound` of an empty list every count is what it was before this change, which is how the table below was made.

**Read over the recorded arms.** `nanoeval arms --results FILE --json` on the results of each arm, once with an empty list and once with `unsound.json` of this commit, on the machine that holds the lanes (5 cores, no KVM; reading results needs no slot):

| Arm | Rows | Infrastructure errors before | After | Task dependency gone |
| --- | ---: | --- | --- | --- |
| fx 0.0.17 on gpt-oss-120b, 89 x 1, 20 krun slots, cancelled with one row open | 89 | 2, 2.2% (verifier 2) | 0 | 2 (qemu-alpine-ssh 1, qemu-startup 1) |
| the same, 89 x 3, 28 krun slots: the arm of the question | 267 | 5, 1.9% (verifier 5) | 0 | 5 (qemu-alpine-ssh 2, qemu-startup 3) |
| the same, 89 x 3, 160 krun slots, cancelled with one row open | 267 | 7, 2.6% (verifier 6, verifier_timeout 1) | 1, 0.4% (verifier_timeout 1) | 6 (3 and 3) |
| the same, 89 x 3, 160 krun slots, agents bounded at 600 s | 267 | 9, 3.4% (verifier 9) | 3, 1.1% (verifier 3) | 6 (3 and 3) |

The oracle loses all six rows in both of its arms, each with the same three packages answered 404.
