The last arm of the table keeps its two rows: its Worker wrote "the verifier wrote reward 0 without the test report" for them, and the rule reads the verdict, not the log.

**Losses, and what the three rows of the bounded arm are.** That arm stays over the line, at 1.1%. Its three rows are verifiers that could not install curl because apt in the slot was broken when they started: `adaptive-rejection-sampler` #1 with `E: dpkg was interrupted, you must manually run 'dpkg --configure -a'`, and `build-pmars` #1 and #3 with `E: Type 'Types:' is not known on line 1 in source list /etc/apt/sources.list.d/debian-src.list`. Only the agent ran in those slots before the verifier, and the oracle passes both tasks in both of its arms. They are counted as infrastructure errors and are neither the infrastructure's nor the task's: a verdict for a verifier that an agent left unable to install is not decided here.

**Checked.** `test/Unsound.test.ts`: the rule needs the kind, the message and the listed version, each alone is refused, and the line of the summary. `test/Arms.test.ts`: an arm shaped like the one above, 5 rows apart and 2 left in infrastructure (a 404 on a task the list does not name, another verifier error on a listed task), its line, the column of the table, and the same arm without the list counted as before. `test/Loop.test.ts`: the scorecard, `taskErrors` and the line of the loop. `npm run lint`, `npm run check:types`, `npm test` (481 tests, 476 pass, 5 skipped where krun cannot run, 0 fail) and `npm run dry-run` pass from a fresh clone on the machine that holds the lanes, and so do the end-to-end lanes on directory slots that read these reports: `priced`, `unsound`, and `nanoeval loop` (`node test/revision.ts loop`). The other lanes of `ci.yml` were not run for this change.

**Not done.** No run was made for this change: the rule reads results, and the arms above are recorded. Leaving such tasks out of a run by a flag: the tasks of an eval are listed without their checksum, and a list by name would also leave out a version that upstream fixed; `--only` and `--subset` name the other 87 today. The rule knows one dependency, a package of apt answered 404: a wheel or a file that a verifier fetches and that is gone ends as a `verifier` error in the infrastructure class until its line is read the same way. A row of a Worker from before 2026-11-14 is not reclassified.

## 2026-11-15: a slot that frees ends the held claim of its runner, and one runner process is not what limits 160 slots

**The question.** An arm of 267 rows on 160 slots of one machine is driven by one runner process, one Node event loop for every slot, log, upload and claim, and by one local Worker, whose one object holds the ledger of the run and passes on every model request of every row. Whether either of the two limits such an arm was not known, and several runner processes for one run were the answer at hand. Both were read from arms that had run, then measured on two more. The answer is no, and the reading found a defect in the claim instead.

**Read from the arms that had run.** fx 0.0.17 over chat completions on `gpt-oss-120b`, Terminal-Bench 2.1 at three attempts, krun slots under a local Worker on a 48-thread bare-metal machine with KVM, 377 GB, each arm once. Each line is from the timeline of the run and the log of its runner.

| Arm | Rows at once, by minute while rows were claimed | A freed slot waits for the next claim | Claim to environment, mean | End of the verifier to the verdict, mean |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| 267 rows, 28 slots, main at `e5ccad0` | 28 | 0.32 s mean, 0.58 s ninth decile, 2.6 s longest, 239 rows | 0.43 s | 0.08 s |
| 267 rows, 160 slots, the same commit | 83 to 91 | 10.0 s mean, 17.5 s ninth decile, 19.6 s longest, 186 rows, 1,865 slot-seconds | 1.35 s, and 1.90 s at the longest for 91 rows claimed in one answer | 0.22 s, 2.5 s at the 99th percentile |
| 267 rows, 160 slots, agents bounded at 600 s, `d01bb39` with that change | 81 to 96 | 13.8 s median | 1.33 s | 0.14 s |
| The same on main at `86f0175`, alone on its 36 threads, the first arm of a machine that had no disk unpacked | 90 to 104 | 13.2 s median | 1.6 s median, 69 s for the rows that waited for a disk | 0.59 s |

On 160 slots a call of the runner to the Worker for a row took 9 to 97 ms at the median and 0.6 to 1.9 s at the 99th percentile, by the request log of the Worker. A row took 96 s at the median. Nothing the one process or the one Worker adds to a row is a hundredth of that, except the first column of waits.

**The defect.** On 160 slots the claims came in batches 20.05 to 20.45 s apart, in all three arms: 15 batches of 3 to 20 rows after the first 91. A runner asks for rows with what it has free, and the run holds that request until a row can be claimed, for a third of the lease at most, 20 s. On 28 slots a full runner has no free slot and asks nothing, so a slot that frees asks at once. On 160 slots the runner was short of memory, not of slots: it admits rows by the memory their tasks declare, 309,060 MB on that machine, about 95 rows. It still had free slots, so it asked, the run found no row that fit the memory it named, and held the request. A slot that freed meanwhile could not ask: its runner was already asking. The freed memory waited for the hold to run out, 10 s at the mean, and about 7 of the 90 rows that could have run were not running while rows were still unclaimed.

**What changed.** One line of `sandbox/Runner.ts`: when a slot of a runner is taken down, the runner ends the claim the run holds for it, with the request a standing runner already uses to pass its turn to another run, and asks again with what it has free now. A runner that holds no claim does nothing new. Each slot that frees under a held claim costs one request to end it and one new claim.

**Measured: the change.** On a 5-core machine without KVM, directory slots, each once, the two lanes with the scripted model:

- A unit test, `test/Runner.test.ts`, runs the runner against the endpoints of a run that the test answers itself: two slots and memory for one row, one row claimed, the next claim held as the run holds it, and the row then taken from the runner so that its slot goes down. With the change the runner ended the held claim and its next claim offered the memory it got back, in 1.5 s for the test. Without the line the claim was ended by its hold, 20 s later, and the test fails.
- The packing lane, three rows of which one waits for the memory of another: that row was claimed 20,042 ms after the first on main at `86f0175`, and 2,183 ms after it with the change. The lane now asserts that it is claimed before a hold would have run out, and fails without the line.
- An arm of 24 rows, the three sample tasks eight times, one runner with 4 slots and memory for two rows at once. Before: claims every 20.03 s, a freed slot waited 18.6 s at the mean, 225 s for the arm. After: 0.14 s at the mean, 0.23 s at the longest, 21 s for the arm. 12 of 24 rows passed in both, as the plan of the scripted model says, and every row was claimed once.

**Measured: the two processes.** The CPU time of every thread of the runner, of workerd and of the shim in front of the route was read from `/proc` every 5 s beside two arms on that 48-thread machine, main at `86f0175`, the processes and the microVMs on 36 of its threads. In percent of one hardware thread:

| Arm | Main thread of the runner | Busiest thread of workerd |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 267 rows on 160 slots, agents bounded at 600 s, about 100 rows at once, its first 775 s, from the totals of the processes | 7.8 % | 10.5 % |
| 252 rows on 252 slots with memory for all of them, so every row was claimed in the first answer and 252 microVMs were up 13 s in, by minute for five minutes | 11.5, 8.5, 8.8, 7.9, 7.3 %, and 37.6 % in the 5 s in which the slots came up | 35.0, 18.0, 17.3, 12.7, 10.5 %, 50.3 % at the ninth decile of the first minute, 62.5 % in its busiest 5 s |

In the second arm 232, 206, 189 and 174 microVMs ran in minutes one to four, the 36 threads were 32 to 50 % busy, and the Worker passed on about 650 model requests a minute. That arm was limited outside the repository: 1,505 of its first 3,588 model requests ended in a 502 that the forward between the machine and the model route made, and the answered ones took 22.9 s at the median at the Worker where the route itself counted 2 to 5 s. Neither process was near a full thread in either arm. The thread of workerd is the nearer one: at that rate of requests it would be full at roughly 400 rows at once.

**Several runner processes for one run: not built.** A run takes several runners already, and nothing had to change to try it. The same 24 rows on that 5-core machine, one runner with 4 slots and then two runner processes with 2 slots each, each pinned to two threads with half the memory: 12 of 24 passed both times, in 24 s each, and with two processes every row was claimed once and finished once, by the logs of the runners, the timeline and the claims the ledger counts, 12 rows by each. So `runner --processes` and a runner for each NUMA node would add a second way to do what attaching a runner does, for a process that uses a tenth of a thread. Neither was added. An arm on the 48-thread machine with four runner processes was prepared and not run: the two processes it would have relieved were idle.

**Not run.** The change on krun slots, and an arm with a model on 160 slots with it: what it gains there, about 7 % more rows at once while rows are unclaimed, is the wait above and not a measured arm. Several runner processes on krun slots at that size. A nanocode session at that size, whose harness runs in the Worker: on the 5-core machine 24 such rows on 4 slots kept the thread of workerd 22 to 27 % busy. More than 252 rows at once.

## 2026-11-15: a run may bound the time of its verifiers, and a verifier it ends is neither a fail nor an infrastructure error

**The defect.** The entry above on the time of the agents left the verifier alone: "a cap on the verifier would turn the slowest tasks of a deadline into errors of every arm", so a task whose verifier does not fit was to be left out of the list. One arm since shows what that leaves. With the agent bounded, a row is bounded by the limit of the run plus the verifier timeout of its task, and the 89 tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.1 allow their verifiers 360 s (1 task), 600 s (1), 900 s (48), 1,200 s (6), 1,800 s (17), 2,400 s (2), 3,600 s (12), 7,200 s (1) and 12,000 s (1). So under `--agent-max-sec 600` no row of 87 tasks is promised to end sooner than 25 minutes after it started, and a verifier that hangs, on any task, takes all of its task's limit.

The arm: fx 0.0.17 over chat completions on gpt-oss-120b, the 89 tasks three times under `--agent-max-sec 600`, 160 krun slots on 36 hardware threads of a bare-metal machine with KVM (24 cores, 48 hardware threads), alone on those threads, main at `86f0175`. It took 21.8 minutes, 1,310 s from the first claim to the last verdict, with 98.5 % of its 267 rows ended after 861 s. The last row was `torch-tensor-parallelism`: claimed at 337 s, its agent done in 71 s, and then its verifier ran out the 900 s of its task. The row before it in the tail was `large-scale-text-editing`, an agent of 415 s and a verifier of 606 s. The same arm an hour earlier, the one of the entry above, had ended in 14.1 minutes: its longest verifier was 601 s, of `query-optimize`, and no verifier hung. Without the limit on the agent, a third arm had a verifier of `headless-terminal` run out its 900 s. So the 14.1 minutes were the arm in which no verifier hung, and leaving five tasks out does not bound an arm either: of the two verifiers that ran out their 900 s, one was of `headless-terminal`, which is not among the five, and neither is `large-scale-text-editing`, whose verifier took 606 s here and 101 to 120 s after its solution.

**Measured: what a limit would have cost.** No arm was run for this table. Two arms of solutions (`--oracle`), the 89 tasks three times each on 28 krun slots of 28 threads of the machine above: 534 rows, 494 passed. Six tasks have no passing solution in them and are not counted (`build-cython-ext`, `crack-7z-hash`, `mcmc-sampling-stan`, `protein-assembly`, `qemu-alpine-ssh`, `qemu-startup`). A task "never verifies in time" under N when every passing verifier of its solution took longer than N: such a task cannot pass under that limit, whatever the agent does. Then nine recorded arms of models, by the seconds of each row's verifier: five arms of fx on gpt-oss-120b on that machine (89 x 1 on 20 slots, 89 x 3 on 28 slots, on 160 slots, and twice on 160 slots under `--agent-max-sec 600`: 1,157 rows, 145 passed), and four arms of nanocode sessions on other machines that recorded verifier seconds, two on claude-haiku-5-5 and two on gpt-6-luna, 89 x 1 each (356 rows, 191 passed).

| N | Tasks whose solution never verifies in time (the seconds its verifier took) | Passes of the solutions lost, of 494 | gpt-oss: passes lost of 145, rows ended of 1,157, verifier seconds saved | haiku and luna: passes lost of 191, rows ended of 356 |
| ---: | --- | ---: | --- | --- |
| 90 s | 9: `filter-js-from-html` (220 to 236), `fix-ocaml-gc` (512 to 580), `large-scale-text-editing` (101 to 120), `portfolio-optimization` (100 to 121), `query-optimize` (598 to 694), `regex-chess` (381 to 410), `reshard-c4-data` (132 to 146), `schemelike-metacircular-eval` (143 to 162), `torch-tensor-parallelism` (91 to 130); `torch-pipeline-parallelism` in 2 of 6 (102 at the longest) | 53 | 1, 48 (4.1 %), 10,743 s | 17, 32 |
| 120 s | 6: `filter-js-from-html`, `fix-ocaml-gc`, `query-optimize`, `regex-chess`, `reshard-c4-data`, `schemelike-metacircular-eval`; `large-scale-text-editing`, `portfolio-optimization` and `torch-tensor-parallelism` in 1 row each | 39 | 0, 31 (2.7 %), 9,665 s | 11, 19 |
| 180 s | 4: `filter-js-from-html`, `fix-ocaml-gc`, `query-optimize`, `regex-chess` | 24 | 0, 28 (2.4 %), 7,931 s | 6, 12 |
| 240 s | 3: `fix-ocaml-gc`, `query-optimize`, `regex-chess` | 18 | 0, 24 (2.1 %), 6,353 s | 3, 7 |
| 300 s | 3: the same | 18 | 0, 16 (1.4 %), 5,199 s | 3, 7 |
| 600 s | none; `query-optimize` in 5 of 6 (694 at the longest) | 5 | 0, 10 (0.9 %), 661 s | 2, 4 |

The weak model loses nothing to a limit of 120 s or more, because its passes are not on the tasks whose verifiers are slow: of the 24 rows that 240 s would have ended, 13 are `query-optimize`, whose verifier took 535 to 615 s in each of its 13 rows, none of which passed, 7 are `filter-js-from-html`, none of which passed, and the other 4 are one row each of `mcmc-sampling-stan` and `large-scale-text-editing` and the two verifiers that hung. The stronger models lose 3 passes of 191 at 240 s (`fix-ocaml-gc` twice, `mcmc-sampling-stan` once) and 17 at 90 s. So, as with the agent's limit, a limit is nearly the same measurement for a weak arm and a different one for a strong arm, and it removes whole tasks from what an arm can pass: 3 of 89 at 240 s, 9 at 90 s.

**What changed.**

- `run --verifier-max-sec N` (`limits.verifierMaxSec` of the configuration, a whole number of seconds, at least 1), and the same through `nanoeval loop`, which takes the options of a run. The run reads every task with the smaller of its own verifier timeout and N, in the place that bounds the agent (`Config.bounded`), so the timeout a slot gives the verifier, the wait of a runner for it, the wait for a judge, the worst case by which rows are claimed and admitted and the life a sandbox is bought for all follow the limit. The task stored with the run is the task of the eval, unchanged, and no file of a verifier is touched.
- A verifier whose time ran out under a run that allows it less than its task does (`Config.cuts`) ends its attempt with the new failure kind `verifier_limit`: `the limit of the run ended the verifier, which its task allows 900 s: the verifier did not finish within 240 s` (`Verdict.bounded`, applied where the run turns the facts of a verifier into a verdict and where a runner reports that a verifier or a judge did not answer in time). Where the task's own limit is the smaller one, the attempt is a `verifier_timeout` as before.
- Such an attempt is `errored` with no reward. It is not `failed`: no verifier failed it. It is not an infrastructure error: the run chose the limit, and an arm must not look broken, or be retried, for it. It is not claimed again.
- **It can never make a row pass.** The reward of a verifier that the limit ended is dropped even when the verifier had already written 1: a verdict is what a verifier says when it has finished. The limit only ever takes rows out of the scored ones. AGENTS.md says never to modify a task or its verifier to make an agent pass: this changes neither, bounds the time of both, and reports every row it cost.
- Every attempt of such a run carries `verifierMaxSec`. `nanoeval status` and `run --wait` add `verifier ended by the run's limit K` to the line of an agent that has such rows (`verifierLimited` in its summary). `nanoeval arms` adds `verifier time limit N s` to the line of an arm and ends its errors with `verifier ended by the run's limit K or P% of its rows`, its JSON has `verifierLimits` and the class `limit` beside `infrastructure`, `task`, `agent` and `cancelled`, and a table that holds one such arm has both columns. The scorecard of `nanoeval loop` has the same columns, and its line for the loop counts the rows apart from the infrastructure errors (`verifierLimited`).
- Such a row is no trial of the pass rate over scored attempts, as no errored row is, so that rate can move either way under a limit; the passes over all rows, which every line prints first, can only fall. This is why the limit is part of what two arms must share: `Compare.pairs` names sides under different limits (`verifier time limit the task's own in the baseline and 240 s in the run`), `compare`, `run --baseline` and `loop --baseline` refuse them until `--unlike`, and a baseline by rule passes over runs `under another limit on the verifier's time`.
- A rerun keeps the limit of its run unless its command names one. `nanoeval run` reads the configuration of the run it made and cancels it when a Worker of an earlier nanoeval dropped the limit, as for the agent's.
- The exit status is unchanged: a row the limit ended is a row that errored, so `run --wait` and `loop` exit 1 for it as for any other.

**Why the earlier choice is reversed.** That entry was right about the cost and wrong that a list bounds an arm. A list of tasks bounds the verifiers that are slow every time. It does not bound the one that hangs once, and the two arms above differ by exactly that. With a limit the bound is the run's: a row has ended `--agent-max-sec` plus `--verifier-max-sec` seconds after its agent started, and the 10 s a verifier is given to stop, whatever its task allows and whatever hangs. What the earlier entry feared is answered by the class: the rows are not errors of the infrastructure, they are printed under their own name with their share, and the tasks that cannot pass under a limit are named above.

**Why its own kind.** A `verifier_timeout` says the verifier ran out the time its task gives it: the task or the machine is at fault, and it counts as infrastructure. A fail says the verifier judged the work. A row the run's limit ended is neither, and counted as either it would bend a number that is read: the infrastructure share of an arm, which decides whether its numbers are trusted, or its failures.

**Checked.** Unit tests: the limit in a configuration (whole seconds, at least 1, absent when not named), a task under it, with the agent's limit and without, and the worst case of its row (`test/Config.test.ts`); the verdict for both exit codes of a timeout, with a reward of 1 already written, at the limit of the run and at the task's own, a verifier that ended in time scored as without the limit, an agent timeout kept, and no retry (`test/Verdict.test.ts`); the summary (`test/Result.test.ts`); the classes, the line, the table and the pass rate of an arm (`test/Arms.test.ts`); the scorecard and the line of a loop (`test/Loop.test.ts`); the sides `compare` names and refuses and a planned run (`test/Compare.test.ts`); the baseline a rule passes over (`test/Baseline.test.ts`); a rerun (`test/Rerun.test.ts`). Fifteen changes to the code of the limit, one at a time, each fail one of them. The lane `NANOEVAL_E2E_SCENARIO=bounded` on directory slots with the scripted model now has a third task, a new fixture whose verifier writes its reward and then sleeps 60 s and whose task allows it 120 s, in a run with `agentMaxSec` 10 and `verifierMaxSec` 10: the configuration holds both limits and all three attempts carry both; the agent solved the task and its verifier wrote 1, and the verifier was ended after 10.5 s; the attempt is `errored` with reward null and the message above, was claimed once, the summary of its agent counts 1, and the arm reads `agent time limit 10 s, verifier time limit 10 s, errors: infrastructure 0, agent or model 0, verifier ended by the run's limit 1 or 33.3% of its rows`; the two other rows are what they were, an agent timeout that is verified and a pass.

On a machine of 5 cores without KVM, each once: `npm run lint`, both type checks, `npm run dry-run`, `npm test` (489 tests, 484 passed, 5 skipped where krun cannot run, none failed) and the directory lanes `bounded`, `failures` and `tasks`, on this change on main at `6659815`; then the commit itself from a fresh clone of main as it had moved, the same steps.

**Not run.** An arm with a model under the limit: the costs above are counted in arms that had none. The lane on krun or ns slots: the run bounds a task before a runner sees it, and the slot applies the number it is given as it applies a task's own, so the backends share the limit by the code. A task with a judge under the limit: the wait for the judge and each of its two verifier passes get the limit, by the code. `nanoeval loop` with the option outside the unit test of its scorecard. The refusal of a Worker that drops the limit, by the code.

**Limits.** The seconds are of verifiers on 28 slots of 28 threads after solutions, and after one weak model on up to 160 slots of 36 threads: a verifier that computes is slower on a machine with more rows than threads, and a stronger agent leaves a verifier more to do (`query-optimize` took 814 s on another machine), so more rows than these can be ended, and the count of each arm is the measurement. Two further recorded arms on other machines carry no verifier seconds and are not in the table. The bound of a row runs from its claim: a row that is claimed late, or claimed again after an error of its agent, ends late, so the bound of an arm is the bound of a row after its last claim. No verifier is told its limit, and one that is ended has used its slot for all of the limit.

## 2026-11-15: the retry of a row counts within its claims, so a run of one claim a row ends inside its time limits

**The defect.** With `--agent-max-sec` and `--verifier-max-sec` a row was to be bounded by the two limits. It was not, because a row could be claimed twice and its second claim had both limits again. `run --claims 1` did not stop that. The retry of an attempt that the machine or the way to the model failed (the entry of 2026-11-13: a slot out of disk, an `agent` failure of a claim in which a model request was answered `502` or `530`, an agent that never started, and the `environment` errors added since) was a counter of its own. `finish` asked only whether a claim of the row had ended `retried`, and gave the row back with a limit of its claims plus one, so `limits.claims` was not read at all. Two things followed. A run of `--claims 1` claimed rows twice. And a row of any run could be claimed `--claims` plus one times, where the help of `run` and the README say `at most --claims times in all`: a row lost twice whose third claim then failed in that way was claimed a fourth time.

**Measured.** Three arms of one harness on one open-weight model (fx 0.0.17 over chat completions, gpt-oss-120b, krun slots, main at `86f0175`, a 48-thread bare-metal machine, each arm once), read from their timelines and results, no arm run for this:

| Arm | Rows | Limit on the agent | Rows claimed a second time | Their second claims began, seconds after the first claim of the arm | How those rows ended | The arm ended at | The last row that was claimed once ended at |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| The 89 tasks three times, 160 slots, on 36 threads | 267 | 600 s | 12 | 168 to 660 | 3 passed, 5 failed, 4 agent errors | 1,310 s | 1,310 s |
| The 84 tasks of `fifteen-minute` three times, every row claimed at once, on 36 threads, 12 of them shared from minute 6 | 252 | 600 s | 29 | 121 to 600 | 2 passed, 16 failed, 7 agent errors, 4 open when the arm was cancelled | cancelled at 799 s | 697 s |
| 77 tasks three times, every row claimed at once, `--claims 1`, on 24 threads | 231 | 180 s | 11 | 43 to 191 | 1 passed, 6 failed, 3 agent errors, 1 `environment` error | 411 s | 328 s |

In the first arm the row claimed again at 660 s ran its agent for the whole 600 s once more and ended at 1,265 s. That arm ended later still, on a verifier that ran out the 900 s of its task, which is what `--verifier-max-sec` is for. The second arm could not have ended before 1,200 s and a verifier, and was cancelled. The third was to end inside 300 s: 218 of its 220 rows that were claimed once did, the last at 328 s, and its last retried row at 411 s. Its one `environment` error read `the attempt lost its runner 2 times, the limit of the run` under a limit of 1. The model requests of those arms went through one forwarded connection that answered `502` by the hundred in a minute, which is the answer the rule retries. Which cause each of the 52 retried claims named was not read: it is in the claims of each run, and the files kept of the arms hold timelines and results only.

So the retry bought 6 passes of the 74 of the three arms (3 of 37, 2 of 26, 1 of 11) and 27 fails, and cost the bound of every arm it happened in.

**What changed.**

- The retry counts within `--claims`. `Ledger.retriable` says whether a row may be retried: it has claims left in the run and no claim of it ended `retried`. `finish` asks it where it asked `Ledger.retried`, and a claim that ends `retried` goes back to the ledger with the limit of the run, as every other ending does.
- A row that is not retried ends as the error it had, as the second such failure of a row always did: an `environment` error that names the cause where the run made it one (a model endpoint that never answered, a provider that limited the agent, an agent that never started), or the error of its agent. Nothing is added to it and nothing is scored.
- So under `run --claims 1` no row is claimed twice, whatever ended its claim, and with the two time limits a row has ended its setup, `--agent-max-sec`, `--verifier-max-sec` and the 10 s a verifier is given to stop after its one claim. The price is the price `--claims 1` always had: a row whose runner or slot is lost ends as an `environment` error at its first loss. Such rows are what `run --rerun RUN --errored` is for, which gives each its whole limits in a run of its own.
- The default changes in one corner. With `--claims 3` a row is still retried once, on its first or second claim. A row on its third claim is not claimed a fourth time: it ends as the error it had. That was the defect against `at most --claims times in all`.
- The help of `run` says it.

**Why the second claim does not get what is left of the limit.** The other way to bound a row is to give a second claim only the seconds its row has left of `--agent-max-sec` since its first claim. In the three arms that was 180 to 505 s for the 12 rows (median 401 s), 0 to 479 s for the 29 (median 221 s), and nothing for 5 of the 11 under the limit of 180 s (median 20 s). Of the 6 second claims that passed, 4 took no longer than what was left (3 of 3, 1 of 2, 0 of 1), and 13 second agents ran longer than it (2, 4 and 7). It is not taken, for what it would make of a row: an agent ended at 137 s in a run that says its agents have 600 s is scored under a limit the row does not name, or its timeout has to become the error of the first claim after its verifier ran, which is a rule in the deadline of a session, the timeout a runner gives an installed agent, and the verdict. It would keep 4 passes of 74. One claim a row is a line of the ledger and a pass rate that means what the limits say. A run that wants the retry keeps it by leaving `--claims` at 2 or more, and then its rows are bounded by twice the limits.

**Why the rule that names a cause is left as it is.** An `agent` failure is retried when any model request of its claim was answered `502` or `530`, not only its last: an agent that asked again by itself, went on for minutes and failed on something else is retried too, and that is how a second claim began 660 s into an arm. Narrowing it to the last request would change which rows of a run without limits are retried, on no measurement of how many of them the endpoint failed. It is not changed here.

**Checked.** Unit tests of the ledger (`test/Ledger.test.ts`): a row with no claim left is not retried and the ledger does not give it back, a row retried once is not retried again while it has claims left, and no row is claimed more often than the run allows. Four changes to `Ledger.retriable`, one at a time, each fail that test: the claims of the row not read, the earlier retry not read, a row at its limit let through, and a row that does not exist let through. The lane `NANOEVAL_E2E_SCENARIO=unreached` on directory slots, installed agents with a scripted command and a model endpoint that answers `530` to the first request of every row: every row of the first run is retried once and none ends as an error, as before, and a second run of the same rows under `limits.claims` 1 ends every row after one claim as an `environment` error that begins `the model endpoint never answered the agent`, with no `attempt.retried` in its timeline and no lost claim.

On a machine of 5 cores without KVM, from a fresh clone of the commit with this entry, on main as it had moved, each once: `npm ci`, lint, both type checks, the dry run, `npm test` (491 tests, 486 passed, 5 skipped, none failed), and the directory lanes `unreached`, `bounded`, `failures`, `tasks` and `lost`, 5 of 5 passed.

**Not run.** An arm with a model under `--claims 1` with this change, on any backend: the bound of such an arm is read from the rule and from the rows of the three arms that were claimed once. krun and ns slots. A deployed Worker.

## 2026-11-15: a run serves an installed agent the models a session falls back to, and a model it refuses is an error of the run

**The defect.** The endpoint of a run served an installed agent one model, the one it was declared with (`worker/Run.ts`, `model`): a request that named another was answered `400`, "model X is not served in this run". A nanocode session never passes that check. Its requests leave through the egress of its own object (`worker/Sessions.ts`), which reads no model name, and since nanocode `f85fd5a04` (in the pinned `455d4e724`) the session sends a response that Claude stopped for safety again to another model: from `claude-opus-5-5` to `claude-opus-5` for the categories `bio` and `frontier_llm` and to `claude-opus-4-8` for `cyber`, from `claude-opus-5` to `claude-opus-4-8` for `cyber`, from `claude-sonnet-5-5` to `claude-sonnet-5` for `cyber` and `frontier_llm`, and from any other model to `claude-opus-5` or `claude-opus-4-8` (`refusal_fallback` in `crates/backends/claude/src/agent.rs`). Claude Code falls back the same way by itself. So in a pair of a session and Claude Code on one model, the run served the fallback to one side and refused it to the other, and the row of Claude Code ended as an `agent` error that its agent did not cause.

**Measured.** One run, nanoeval `b48388c` on a deployed Worker, the 89 tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.1 three times for a nanocode session and for Claude Code 2.1.318, both on `claude-opus-5-5` at high effort through a Claude plan login, krun slots of one bare-metal machine with KVM (24 cores, 48 hardware threads), read when 489 of its 534 rows had ended. 30 rows had errored: 26 of Claude Code and 4 of the session. 18 of the 26 were this refusal, on 6 tasks: 9 asked for `claude-opus-5` (`dna-assembly`, `dna-insert`, `protein-assembly`, three attempts each) and 9 for `claude-opus-4-8` (`break-filter-js-from-html`, `crack-7z-hash`, `vulnerable-secret`). Each made 2 or 3 requests to `claude-opus-5-5`, all answered `200`, the last two with 0 output tokens, reported `safety_stops 2`, asked for the other model, was answered `400` and exited with 1 within a minute of its start. On the 5 of those tasks whose session rows had ended, all 14 session rows made their first request to `claude-opus-5-5`, then 6 to 21 requests to `claude-opus-5` or `claude-opus-4-8`, every one answered `200`, and reached the verifier: 8 passed, 6 failed. The other 12 errors were the same for both sides or no refusal: 9 verifier errors of `qemu-alpine-ssh` and `qemu-startup`, whose package archive is gone (5 of Claude Code, 4 of the session), 2 verifiers of Claude Code rows that wrote a reward without their report, and 1 DNS failure in a slot. Over those rows `arms` read the arm of Claude Code as `infrastructure 2 (verifier 2), task dependency gone 5, agent or model 19 (agent 19)`; with this change it reads `infrastructure 20 or 8.1% of its rows (model not served 18, verifier 2), task dependency gone 5, agent or model 1 (agent 1)`.

**What changed.**

- `src/Fallback.ts` holds the table of the pinned nanocode and follows it to its end: `Fallback.served` is the declared model and every model a session can reach from it, for the Claude provider only. For `claude-opus-5-5` that is `claude-opus-5` and `claude-opus-4-8`. The endpoint serves those and refuses every other model as before, so an installed agent is served what a session is and nothing wider. The table is a copy: a pin of a nanocode that changes `refusal_fallback` changes this file with it.
- A refused request is now kept with the model requests of its row, status `400` and refusal `model`, where before only the agent's own output held it.
- An agent that ends as an `agent` error right after such a refusal ends as an `environment` error instead, "the run refused a model that the agent asked for: ..." (`Retry.unserved`): the run made the choice, not the agent. It is not retried, since the same request would be refused again, and it is no trial of a pass rate, as no errored row is. An agent that was refused and went on keeps its own verdict.
- `nanoeval arms` counts these rows under infrastructure as `model not served`, and `nanoeval status` and `run --wait` add one line for them. ## 2026-11-15: a package that the mirror of a distribution dropped reaches a verifier from the distribution's archive

**The failure.** The verifiers of `qemu-alpine-ssh` and `qemu-startup` run `apt-get update` and `apt-get install -y curl` in a Debian 11 image when an attempt is verified. The index of `bullseye-security` on `deb.debian.org` is signed, dated 2026-09-12, and lists `curl 7.74.0-1.3+deb11u16`. The three files apt then asks for answer 404 there and on `security.debian.org`: `http://deb.debian.org/debian-security/pool/updates/main/c/curl/curl_7.74.0-1.3+deb11u16_amd64.deb`, `libcurl4_7.74.0-1.3+deb11u16_amd64.deb` beside it, and `http://deb.debian.org/debian-security/pool/updates/main/n/nghttp2/libnghttp2-14_1.43.0-1+deb11u3_amd64.deb`. `http://archive.debian.org/debian-security/` answers 200 for the same three paths. So every attempt at the two tasks ended as a `verifier` error, the solution's too: 12 of 12 in one paired run of two agents, three attempts each.

**Why this is the environment and not the task.** The task is run as it was imported: its image, its `test.sh` and their checksums are untouched, and so is what the verifier does. The index it reads is the mirror's own, unchanged and signed, and apt checks every package against the SHA-256 that index lists, whichever host sent the bytes. What changed after the task was written is where Debian keeps the file: off its mirrors, in its own archive. Which host answers a name is the network of the slot, which the sandbox already owns: it writes `/etc/hosts` and the resolver of every slot. An index is never taken from the archive, so the verifier installs exactly the versions its mirror lists or fails as before.

**What was implemented.** `runner --package-archive` (`sandboxd --package-archive`, `NANOEVAL_PACKAGE_ARCHIVE`), off by default, for krun and ns slots. When the verifier of a row starts, the runner listens on a loopback address of that row's own, port 80 (`sandbox/Archive.ts`), and writes the address and the names it answers for into the slot's directory. `slot.sh verify` appends one line with them to `/etc/hosts` of the guest, and on a private network adds the address to the slot's allow list and gives it to the verifier's command as a forward, so the guest listens there for that command only and the relay carries each connection to the runner. The listener passes every request to the host it names, with its headers, and returns the answer as it came. Only a `GET` or `HEAD` whose path holds `/pool/` and that the mirror answers 404 is asked again of the archive of that mirror, at the same path, and served from there when the archive answers 200 or 206. The table is `deb.debian.org` and `security.debian.org` to `archive.debian.org`. Each file that came from the archive is a line of `archive.log` in the slot, and the row keeps them as the artifact `verifier-archive.txt`, whose first line is `verifier package served from the distribution's archive: N files`. The runner logs the same line. Nothing changes for the agent: the line in `/etc/hosts` and the listener exist from the start of the verifier, and a verifier whose task closes its network gets neither.

**What the first run on microVM slots showed.** A line for `deb.debian.org` alone is not read: apt asks the service record `_http._tcp.deb.debian.org` first and connects to the host that record names, so the six verifiers of the first run still reached the mirror's own address and ended on the 404. The names a slot is given are therefore each mirror and the hosts its service record names, which the runner resolves when the verifier starts.

**Why it is an option.** The runner listens on port 80, so it runs as root or on a machine whose `net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start` is 80 or lower, and it refuses to start otherwise. While the verifier runs, port 80 of one loopback address of the guest is taken, and the names above resolve to it there.

**Ran,** each once. On a machine without KVM: the listener against the Debian mirror, the three files above asked with the `Host` of the mirror: 200, 271,568, 347,388 and 77,576 bytes, each with the SHA-256 the mirror's signed `Packages` lists; the index and a file the mirror has came from the mirror. On a machine with 48 hardware threads and KVM, the runner pinned to 4 of them, krun slots on the private network, a local Worker with the two tasks imported, the solutions as the agent: without the option 2 attempts, 2 `verifier` errors on the 404; with it 6 attempts, 0 errors, 5 passed and 1 failed, each with `verifier-archive.txt` naming the three files. The failed attempt is of `qemu-alpine-ssh`: its test ran and its `ssh` into the nested machine ended with status 255. `npm test`: 502 tests, 497 pass, 5 skipped, 0 fail, 8 of them new in `test/Archive.test.ts`.

**Not run.** ns slots, krun slots on the host network, a remote sandbox, a verifier that asks for a range of a file, a mirror of another distribution. No end-to-end lane holds it: the lanes have no mirror to lose a file.

## 2026-11-15: what the rows of an arm write to the home of their runner, and an ns slot no longer flushes the disk of its machine

**The finding.** One arm, nanoeval `c767cdd`: fx 0.0.17 on `@cf/zai-org/glm-4.7-flash` over chat completions, 84 tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.1 three times, 252 rows claimed in the first 30 s, krun slots of one bare-metal machine with KVM (24 cores, 48 hardware threads, 377 GB), 36 threads for the arm, a 600 s limit on the agent and 240 s on the verifier. The runner's home and the local Worker's state were on the disks the system boots from, a mirror of two 480 GB disks. Read while it ran: 224 microVM processes wrote 673 MB/s by their own counters over 6 s in the eighth minute, four of them 82 to 175 MB/s each; the runner's home held 66 GB after six minutes, 260 MB a row; the mirror took 230 to 440 MB/s, the machine waited on I/O 24 to 55 % of the time while its CPUs were 36 to 69 % busy and 229 GB of memory were free. The Worker took 25 to 34 s for a stored artifact and 14.3 s at the median for a model request that its upstream answered in 7.6 s, the runner logged 188 stores that were answered `500`, the median verifier took 125 s, 179 of the 252 agents ran into their limit, and 14 rows passed.

The same arm again on a second machine of the same kind, nanoeval `5ab804b`, with two things changed: the runner's home on an NVMe disk nothing else used and the Worker's state on a second one, and `--claims 1`. I/O wait 0 to 1 % with up to 596 MB/s written, no store answered `500`, the median verifier took 34 s, 157 agents ran into their limit, 25 rows passed, and the last verdict came 701 s after the first claim where the rows claimed once had taken 855 s. One arm each way, so the pass counts say which way, not how much.

**What a row writes.** Read in `sandbox/slot.sh` and `krun/guest/src/boot.rs`, then measured.

- No copy of the task's disk. A krun or ns slot attaches the environment disk of its row read-only and formats a sparse ext4 of the task's `storage_mb` beside it (`truncate`, then `mke2fs` without a journal), which the guest or the slot's namespace mounts as the upper layer of an overlay. A filesystem without reflinks changes nothing here, since nothing is cloned. Only a slot that forks (`:branches=N`) copies an upper disk, with `cp --reflink=auto --sparse=always`. Formatting a 10 GB upper disk allocates 4.2 MB.
- What the attempt writes, which is everything else: the packages that the agent and the verifier install, builds, downloads, and the files that overlayfs copies up before a change. Six tasks with their own solutions and verifiers, four rows each on ns slots: `fix-code-vulnerability` 1 MB, `cancel-async-tasks` and `openssl-selfsigned-cert` 17 MB in 13 rows of 16 and 88 to 106 MB in 3, `fix-git` 32 MB, `git-leak-recovery` 35 to 172 MB, `pypi-server` 680 to 753 MB. The mean was 142 to 172 MB a row over the four arms below. The arm above, with an agent that also installs and builds, had 260 MB a row after six minutes.
- Logs and artifacts are small beside that: the Worker's state grew to 36 MB over 60 such rows. Rows with an agent keep its events and model requests too, which was not measured here.

**Why a disk waits on it.** The upper disk dies with its slot: taking a slot down deletes the file, and a row whose slot is lost starts again from nothing. But both backends treated it as a disk whose writes must survive a power cut. libkrun at the pinned commit attaches a disk with buffered I/O and full sync (`krun_add_disk`), and answers the guest's `VIRTIO_BLK_T_FLUSH` with an `fsync` of the image. In an ns slot the loop device does the same for the file behind it. So every `fsync` in a slot, and `dpkg`, `apt`, `pip` and `git` call it often, became an `fsync` of the whole upper disk in the runner's home: every dirty page of that file written now, a commit of the journal of the machine's filesystem, and a cache flush of the device. Without it the same bytes are ordinary buffered writes: the kernel writes them when it chooses, and what a slot wrote in its last seconds is dropped with the file.

**What changed.** `slot.sh` mounts the upper disk of an ns slot `nobarrier`, so ext4 sends no flush for it. The option is the whole change. Nothing reads an upper disk after its machine went down, and a fork is unaffected: it runs `sync` in the slot and copies the file through the page cache of the same machine. The slot test of ns slots reads the options of the mounted disk and expects `nobarrier`.

**Measured.** A machine of 5 cores and 14 GB with root and no KVM, one virtual disk, nanoeval `f3998bd` against the same with this change.

- A real `dpkg --unpack` of nine packages (28 MB of archives, 168 MB and 7,452 files unpacked) into an upper disk made and mounted as `slot.sh` does, read from the counters of the loop device and of the machine's disk. One slot, which is then removed: 134 flushes and 182.5 MB on the disk before, no flush and 8.1 MB after. Eight at once, twice each way: 1,561 and 1,615 flushes of the disk before the slots were removed, 6 and 8 after the change; 1,387 and 1,392 MB written before, 823 and 1,375 MB after, because eight slots dirty more memory than this machine lets wait. The unpack took 15.8 and 16.0 s before, 15.9 and 19.2 s after.
- Rows: the six tasks above twice, 12 rows on 3 ns slots, their own solutions and verifiers, a local Worker, four arms in the order before, after, before, after. Every loop device of a slot was read five times a second, from the counters it had before the slot attached. Before: the slots sent 8,836 and 8,836 flushes, 20 to 3,393 a row, and the machine's disk took 3,057 and 3,042 MB in 48,641 and 49,230 writes with 17,610 and 17,680 flushes. After: no flush from a slot, 1,435 and 1,468 MB in 9,020 and 9,262 writes with 2,863 and 2,928 flushes, which are the Worker's and the runner's own. The kernel counted 4.9 and 5.7 s in which some task waited on I/O before, 2.6 and 2.6 s after. All 48 rows passed. The arms took 125 and 121 s before, 122 and 127 s after. The same disk in 120 s with the Worker up and no arm: 1.4 MB, 146 writes, 31 flushes.

So on this machine a row puts about half the bytes and a fifth of the writes on the disk, and no row is faster for it: the disk here answers a flush in 0.3 ms and the rows wait on the CPU.

**Not run.**

- krun slots. The same option for the microVM's upper disk is one line in `krun/guest/src/boot.rs` and builds, but it has not booted a microVM, so it is not in this commit: a guest that failed to mount its disk would fail every row of every arm. Until it has run, a microVM passes each flush of its guest on as before.
- The arm it is for: 252 rows at once with the runner's home on a slow mirror, with and without the option. What is measured is fewer flushes and fewer bytes on a small machine. Rows of ten minutes still reach the disk, since the kernel writes a dirty page after 30 s whatever the slot does, so the option removes the waits of `fsync` and not the volume. Whether that alone keeps a mirror from stalling is not known.
- `test/Ns.test.ts` with the new assertion: it converts a Dockerfile, which this machine cannot do without KVM. The command of the assertion was run by hand against an upper disk mounted both ways, and printed the option only for the one mounted with it.

**Not done, and why.**

- The upper disk in memory. A slot may write up to its `storage_mb`, 10 GB for most tasks, and pages of a tmpfs can only be dropped with the slot. Admission counts the memory a row declares, not what its disk would hold, and 252 rows at 260 MB are 66 GB that no rule here accounts for.
- A runner that measures its home and refuses a slow one. The speed is easy to measure, but the number to hold it against is not there: one arm gives 260 MB a row in six minutes and peaks of 82 to 175 MB/s from single rows, and nothing says what a different model or eval writes.

**For the next machine.** Before an arm with many slots, give the runner's home a disk that holds nothing else, and keep the Worker's state off it. On the machine above that was two commands, a filesystem on an unused disk and `--home` there, and it is what moved the arm. The README says so where it lists what goes where.

## 2026-11-15: the release of an installed agent is copied into a home on another filesystem than the cache

**The defect.** `slot.sh agents` keeps each release of an installed agent once in the cache and gives every home a tree of hard links to it, `cp -al`, with `cp -a` behind it for when the links fail. They always fail when the home is on another filesystem than the cache. `cp -al` has made the directory by then and leaves it, so the fallback found the directory there and copied the release inside it: `agents/fx/any/any/fx`, where the slot runs `agents/fx/any/fx`. The entry above tells an operator to give the runner's home a disk of its own, which is exactly this layout.

**Measured.** One probe on a bare-metal machine with KVM (48 hardware threads), nanoeval `5ab804b`, the runner's home on an NVMe disk of its own and the cache on the disks the system boots from: 4 rows of fx 0.0.17 on 4 krun slots, and 4 of 4 ended `fx exited with 127: /opt/nanoeval/agents/fx/any/fx: not found`. With the cache's `agents` directory moved to the filesystem of the home, the same 4 rows ran their agent: 82 model requests, no such error. On a machine of 5 cores without KVM the same call with the cache on a tmpfs and the home on its disk left `gnu/gnu/claude` for `gnu/claude`.

**What changed.** When the links fail, `slot.sh` removes what they left and then copies. Nothing else: a home on the filesystem of the cache still gets hard links.

**Checked.** Two unit tests call `slot.sh agents` with a release in a file: one with the cache on a tmpfs and the home on the disk, skipped on a machine that has no second filesystem to write to, and one with a `cp` in front of the machine's that makes the directory and fails when asked for links, so that the case is tested where there is one filesystem only. Both failed before the change, the entry not found, and pass after it. From a fresh clone of main with this commit, on the machine of 5 cores: `npm run lint`, both type checks, `npm run dry-run` and `npm test`.

**Not run.** The fix on the machine that showed the defect, and an end-to-end lane: the lanes of installed agents name their command as a file of the machine, which is copied and never linked, so no lane reaches this line.

## 2026-11-15: a runner may admit rows by the memory its machine uses

**The defect.** A runner admits rows by the memory their tasks declare, into 80 % of the memory it may use. The 89 tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.1 declare 68 x 2,048, 13 x 4,096 and 8 x 8,192 MB, 2,899 MB a row on average and 774,144 MB for three attempts of each, so a machine of 386,452 MB admits about 106 rows at once and fewer at the start of an arm, where the longer tasks come first. One arm: fx on gpt-oss-120b, the 89 tasks three times under `--agent-max-sec 600`, main at `86f0175`, one bare-metal machine with KVM (48 hardware threads, 377 GB), one runner with `--slots 160` pinned to 36 threads and alone on them, a local Worker. It had 85 to 110 microVMs at once, by the minute. Its last row was claimed 660 s after its first and the arm ended at 1,310 s, because a row that is claimed at 660 s still has its 600 s. `MemAvailable` never fell under 319,008 MB. Every arm of that size since was run with `runner --memory-mb 774144`, the sum the rows declare, written by hand: every row is then claimed in the first answer, and the runner has no limit left at all.

**Measured: what rows use.** No figure for a row exists. The results of a run carry no memory of a slot, and the log of the machine has `MemAvailable` and the count of microVMs every 5 s, for the machine as a whole. From that log of two arms of 160 slots, 95 to 113 microVMs at once: `MemAvailable` fell by at most 82,433 MB in one and 75,137 MB in the other from where it stood before the arm. That is 608 MB for each running microVM at the median of the samples with 60 microVMs or more and 1,179 MB at the most, against the 2,899 MB a row declares: 21 to 41 %. The figure counts the Worker, the runner and the VMMs with the guests.

**What changed.** `runner --memory-overcommit`, for a runner of a run and for a standing one.

- The limit is what it was: `--memory-mb`, or 80 % of the memory the runner may use.
- What is counted against it changes (`Admission.held`): the memory the machine uses, which is the memory the runner may use less `MemAvailable` and less the headroom of its control groups, as for a row that runs alone, and the declared memory of the rows whose environment has not started yet, which the machine cannot show. A row then starts while the machine has free what the row declares beside what the limit leaves unused.
- An empty runner offers its whole limit as before, so a row that asks for the whole machine still starts there and only there.
- When the environment of a row has started, the runner ends the claim that the run may be holding and claims again, as it does since `bb82fdc` when a slot frees. The run holds a claim that found nothing for up to a third of the lease, with the offer it was sent, and the declared memory of a row that has started is on offer at once.
- A runner on a machine that does not say what memory it has free refuses the option when it starts.
- No constant was added. What rows fill after they started is not reserved: the option is a bet that the rows which run do not fill what they declare at the same time. Each slot keeps its own limit and its `oom_score_adj` of 1000, so when the machine runs out the kernel ends a slot and not the runner, and the row of that slot goes back to the run.

**What it is not.** A measure of each row. The count is the machine's, so it includes whatever else runs there, and two runners on one machine read the same figure. It does not claim every row in the first answer either: the first answer is filled by what rows declare, into the whole limit, and the rest are claimed as environments start. The declared count stays the default.

**Measured: one arm on microVMs, beside its twin.** fx 0.0.17 over chat completions on `gemma-4-26b-a4b-it`, the 84 tasks of `--subset fifteen-minute` three times, 252 rows, `--agent-max-sec 600 --verifier-max-sec 240 --claims 1` and a model budget, one runner with 252 krun slots under a local Worker, main at `5ab804b`, a 48-thread bare-metal machine with KVM and 386,452 MB, the runner and its microVMs on 36 of its threads with the slot disks on a disk of their own. Each arm once, 34 minutes apart. The twin had `runner --memory-mb 774144`. The arm had `runner --memory-overcommit` in its place, on that commit with this change, and its runner said a limit of 309,161 MB. **The arm was cancelled 185 s after its first claim, when its machine was given to other work**, so the two are compared over those 185 s and no further.

A machine on which the count binds: here it stood at a third of the limit. The option on a runner that a provider starts, which `run` does not pass. Two runners on one machine. ns slots.

## 2026-11-15: a session turn carries the agent deadline of its attempt

**What.** A run that asks a session for its first turn sends `deadline: { at_ms, limit_ms }` with it: `limit_ms` is the task's agent timeout (`task.agent.timeoutSec` times 1000) and `at_ms` is the time of the ask plus that limit. The ledger's `deadline_at`, at which the run cancels the turn, is set after the ask returns, so the deadline the agent gets is never later than the one the run enforces. The value is host policy and nothing else: the run adds no text to the prompt. nanocode-ts 6f43bb6 keeps it with the turn and passes it to the Claude harness of nanocode 9cc200cfe, which tells the model the time remaining at 50%, 75% and 90% of the limit and caps a Bash timeout or an exec or wait yield at the time remaining. A nanocode-ts build without that change ignores the field, so the pinned `build-1d71a9d` runs as before. The Codex harness ignores it.

**Why.** In one run of the 89 tasks three times the nanocode session had no idea of its limit. Two attempts of train-fasttext (3600 s) had a passing model 13 to 18 minutes before the cancel and never copied it to `/app/model.bin`, one of extract-moves (1800 s) had its transcript at 1466 s and never wrote `/app/solution.txt`, and two of make-doom (900 s) were cancelled inside 300 s steps they started at 682 s and 647 s. The fractions and their measurements are in nanocode's DECISIONS.md.

**Checked.** `npm run lint`, `npm run check:types`, and `node --test test/Turn.test.ts test/Preflight.test.ts` (the new body test passes; the preflight probe test fails on macOS before and after this change). The Worker is not deployed and `package.json` still pins nanocode-ts `build-1d71a9d`: a release of nanocode-ts 6f43bb6 or later is needed before a run sees the deadline.

## 2026-11-15: a claude agent with direct tools

The harness `claude-direct` names a nanocode `claude` session whose model gets the hand's Claude Code tools directly. `Config.parse` takes `orchestration: "direct"` for a `claude` agent and refuses `jobs` for it, `parseAgent` and `agentText` read and write `claude-direct`, and `Turn.body` sends `claude_orchestration` for a claude turn and `codex_orchestration` only for a codex turn. The claude session keeps its subagents and web search, as the plain `claude` agent does, so the arm differs from `claude` only in how the model calls its tools.

Why: on the Codex pair direct tools beat Code Mode by 6.4 points (one run of each), and the Claude arm could only run Code Mode. In 39 nanocode attempts of one run of the 89 tasks three times (the 13 tasks with misses, 3 attempts each, claude-opus-5-5 high), Code Mode took 700 exec and 80 wait calls for 1,449 nested calls. 11 cells failed: 4 TypeError, 2 SyntaxError, 2 thrown tool errors, and 3 refusals of a leading sleep that only cells get. 79 of 83 yields returned no output, which is 3,439 s of cell time and 405 s of model calls that only sent the next wait. 25 cells finished with nested output but printed none of it, and 8 cells were cancelled.

The sessions need nanocode-ts d56a177 (`claude_orchestration`) and nanocode 498e20459 (direct Claude tools on a hand, and background job notices returned with direct calls). Checked: `npm run check:types`, `vp check` on the changed files, and `node --test` of the Installed, Turn, Config, Compare, Preflight and Baseline tests on one Linux machine (67 tests, 63 pass). The 4 failures (the Claude Code and opencode image commands, the release checksum and the probe) fail the same way on main on that machine. A run with a model was not made.

## 2026-11-15: wave 7 release set: nanocode-ts `build-d56a177` and the hand of nanocode-cli-498e204

**What changed.** `package` pins nanocode-ts `build-d56a177` (nanocode-ts d56a177, SDK 498e20459, which holds 6f43bb6, the turn deadline passed to the Claude harness, afa77dc, `git_repository` in the hand environment, and d56a177, `claude_orchestration`, since `build-1d71a9d`) and `Slot.runtime` the hand `nanocode-cli-498e204` (nanocode 498e20459, Linux x86_64, gz SHA-256 ea77c90f8a195da1574d04d1fa229d599519a76afaadefb8d4dc49607ff24b37). Both come from the same nanocode commit, which holds 3c5dcd582 (an exec yields at once for a session notice pending at its start), 9cc200cfe (deadline reminders and capped waits in Claude sessions), 6e55490e2 (the environment section of a Claude session comes from its hand), 799d10d5b and 2e9b41d4d (the bypass permissions note and Bash text of Claude Code 2.1.325), 379ffb760 (Claude Code's tools offered directly in sessions whose tools run on a hand) and 498e20459 (background job notices returned with direct tool calls). With these pins the two entries above take effect: a run's first turn carries the agent deadline to a build that reads it, and `claude-direct` names a session whose build reads `claude_orchestration`. Defaults in this repository are unchanged.

**The hand build.** As for wave 6: `cargo fetch --locked`, then `cargo zigbuild --locked --offline --profile dist --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.2.31 -p nanocode-cli --bin nanocode`, zig 0.13.0, cargo-zigbuild 0.24.1, Rust 1.100.0, with `CC` set to a wrapper of the zig target compiler that names no libgcc_eh.a: 47,182,384 bytes, GNU_STACK RW, newest symbol GLIBC_2.30, NEEDED libc.so.6, libpthread.so.0 and libdl.so.2. It took 372 s on 8 hardware threads of a bare-metal machine.

**The package build.** `node scripts/release.mjs` of nanocode-ts at d56a177, WebAssembly build `5e26d8ce3124374bfbc7`. The Python module's C sources need a clang that targets wasm32: on a machine whose clang is not on the path, `NANOCODE_CC` names it.

**What the lanes found, and two fixes.** The first pass of `ci.yml` on this set (the pins with the two entries above, on eec8b2d) was red in four steps. Three were the lane `branches`, on directory, krun and ns slots: nanocode-ts binds the deadline of a turn into the key its session opens with, so a second turn with another deadline, or with none after a first turn that had one, opens the session again, and the requests of that turn then declare no hand tools in `exec` (the cells still list them, and the row passed). The self-check of a branch is such a second turn. The sessions of a branched attempt are now sent no deadline; a session that is asked one turn, which is every other session of a run, keeps it. Sending the self-check the deadline of the first turn would keep the key, and needs the first deadline kept with the attempt: not done. The fourth was the lane `priced` on directory slots, red on main since the errors of an arm gained the class `limit`: its expectation now names the class. That lane fails the same way on main at eec8b2d with the pins before these.

**Checked.** Every `run` step of `ci.yml` (`if: failure()` steps left out), three times, its six jobs side by side on 16 hardware threads of one bare-metal machine with KVM (24 cores, 48 hardware threads; the directory lanes as two halves, each with its own `npm ci`). On eec8b2d with the pins and the two entries above: 120 of 124 steps passed in 706 s, the four red ones above, each red again when run alone. With the two fixes, still on eec8b2d (the branch `wave7` at 844571c): all 124 passed in 508 s, check 5, krun 3, e2e-dir 32 and 32, e2e-krun 34, e2e-ns 14, e2e-revision 4. Rebased onto e737a96, which is the parent of this commit: all 125 passed in 495 s, the lane `overcommit` among them. On a machine with 5 cores and no KVM, from a fresh clone of each of the three: the check job, 5 of 5, `npm test` 504 tests (499 pass, 5 skipped, 0 fail) on the first two and 507 (502 pass, 5 skipped, 0 fail) on the third. This commit adds only DECISIONS.md and README.md to the third.

**Not verified.** A deployed Worker, a model on the new hand and package, a `claude-direct` session end to end (it has unit tests and no lane of its own), a model that reaches its deadline, and a branched attempt with a deadline.

**Wave 7b: headless sessions.** The App of `worker/Sessions.ts` now sets `headless: true`, so every eval session, Claude and Codex, opens headless. For Codex this turns on the guard that does not end a turn while its work is not persisted and the delivery of held job results within the turn; for Claude, from nanocode-ts af7b1a8 (nanocode 8131a9e31), one finish-check message at the first end of a root turn, unless the last deadline reminder has passed. Both are meant for runs that no person watches, as evals are. The Claude half needs a nanocode-ts pin at af7b1a8 or later: the pin stays at d56a177 here, and the releasing lane moves it.

**Wave 7b: branched attempts send their deadline again.** This reverts the change to `worker/Run.ts` of a5c5670. nanocode-ts af7b1a8 opens a session with the hands already attached to its scope and selects the turn's hand before the agent opens, so a session opened again for a turn with another deadline still declares the hand tools in `exec`: its output/wave7b/reopen.ts reproduces the loss on a Codex session at d56a177 (turn 2 declares no `exec_command`) and shows it kept with the change. Every session of an attempt, branched or not, now gets the deadline of the agent again, and the self-check turn of a branch opens its session again with the new deadline. This needs the nanocode-ts pin at af7b1a8 or later: on d56a177 the `branches` lane fails as it did before a5c5670.

## 2026-11-15: a task list `five-minute`, and the one arm with a model that ended inside five minutes

**What changed.** `subsets.json` has `five-minute`: 73 of the 89 tasks of `terminal-bench-2.1`, `fifteen-minute` without eleven more. No code changed. A unit test now reads the lists of this checkout: each names a task once, in order, and `five-minute` holds 73 tasks, all of them tasks of `fifteen-minute`, which holds 84.

**What the list is for.** With `--agent-max-sec A --verifier-max-sec V --claims 1` a row has ended its setup, A, V and the 10 s a verifier is given to stop after its claim (the entry on the retry of a row), and an arm whose rows are all claimed at once ends that long after it started. For 300 s that is A 180 and V 90, with 20 s left for the setup of a row. A limit on the verifier ends a verdict and not only a wait, so a task whose verifier does not fit in 90 s would be an error in every arm, or would lose its passes: such a task is left out, as `fifteen-minute` leaves out what does not fit its limits.

**The tasks left out, and why.** 16 of the 89, 18 % of the benchmark. Five are those `fifteen-minute` leaves out (`filter-js-from-html`, `fix-ocaml-gc`, `query-optimize`, `regex-chess`, `torch-tensor-parallelism`). The other eleven each had a verifier of more than 90 s in a recorded row. The list was fixed from fewer rows before the arm below ran. The counts here were read once afterwards from nine arms on bare-metal machines of one kind (24 cores, 48 hardware threads, KVM): the tasks' own solutions once, under limits of 150 s and 90 s, and eight arms of fx on three open models at three attempts, 77 to 89 tasks each.

| Task | Its verifiers of more than 90 s in those arms |
| --- | --- |
| `headless-terminal` | 900 s, the limit of its task, after the work of a model, in 1 of 21 rows |
| `large-scale-text-editing` | Ended by the limit of 90 s after its own solution; 95, 103 and 606 s after a model |
| `mailman` | 91, 100 and 127 s |
| `mcmc-sampling-stan` | 143 and 188 s |
| `overfull-hbox` | 91, 95 and 131 s |
| `portfolio-optimization` | 92 to 123 s in 7 of 20 rows, all 7 of them passes |
| `pytorch-model-cli` | 137 to 161 s in 4 of 24 rows |
| `reshard-c4-data` | Ended by the limit of 90 s after its own solution; 93, 93 and 126 s after a model |
| `schemelike-metacircular-eval` | Ended by the limit of 90 s after its own solution |
| `torch-pipeline-parallelism` | 92, 119 and 143 s |
| `train-fasttext` | 138 s |

The 73 tasks that are kept had a verifier in 2,131 rows of those nine arms and the arm below, and one of them took more than 90 s: `git-multibranch`, 98 s, in an arm of 267 rows at once.

**Run once.** fx 0.0.17 over chat completions on `gemma-4-26b-a4b-it`, the 73 tasks three times, 219 rows, `--agent-max-sec 180 --verifier-max-sec 90 --claims 1` and a model budget, the tasks named in a file with `--only-file` and not through `--subset`. One runner with 219 krun slots and `--memory-mb 583680`, three times what the tasks declare, under a local Worker, main at `5ab804b`, one bare-metal machine with KVM (24 cores, 48 hardware threads, 386,452 MB), the runner and its microVMs alone on 36 of its threads, with the slot disks on a disk of their own and the state of the Worker on another, a build of another job on the other 12 threads. It started 34 s after an arm of all 89 tasks had ended there, so every image had run on the machine before.

- 259 s from the first claim to the last verdict. All 219 rows were claimed in the first 10 s and none twice. Half of the rows had ended after 216 s and nine in ten after 232 s. The last was a row of `make-doom-for-mips`: 4 s of setup, an agent ended at 184 s, a verifier of 71 s.
- 29 rows passed, 13.2 % of the 219 and 13.9 % of the 208 that were scored, in 15 of the 73 tasks. 179 failed.
- The limit of 180 s ended the agents of 152 rows, 69 %, and 9 of those passed. The limit of 90 s ended no verifier: the longest took 71 s, the median 31 s, and the setup of a row 3.2 s at the median.
- 11 rows errored. 4 are infrastructure errors, 1.8 % of the rows and over the line of 1 %: 2 whose last model requests the provider answered `429`, which a run of more than one claim would have run again, and 2 whose verifier wrote no test report. 6 are the rows of `qemu-alpine-ssh` and `qemu-startup`, whose package archive answered 404, counted as a dependency that is gone; the entry on the archive of a distribution is later than the commit of this arm. 1 is an error of the agent.
- 2,876 model calls, 36.1 million input and 1.10 million output tokens, 3.94 USD at a list price of 0.10 and 0.30 USD a million. The provider answered `429` to 125 of 3,038 requests. The 36 threads were 64, 80, 53 and 87 % busy by minute, and the machine never had less than 280,312 MB available.

**What it loses.** The same model on the same machine and commit, under `--agent-max-sec 600 --verifier-max-sec 240 --claims 1`, passed 50 of these 219 rows in an arm of 84 tasks and 51 in an arm of all 89, each once: 22.8 and 23.3 %, in 27 and 24 of the 73 tasks. So this arm kept 29 of about 50 passes. In both of those arms 25 of the passes had an agent of more than 180 s: a limit of 180 s cuts this model at the middle of its passes on this route. The 16 tasks that are left out passed 6 of their 48 rows in the arm of 89. The tasks' own solutions do not all fit either: in their one arm under limits of 150 s and 90 s, 64 of the 73 passed, no verifier of the 73 was ended, and the solutions of 5 ran out the 150 s (`caffe-cifar-10`, `compile-compcert`, `crack-7z-hash`, `install-windows-3.11`, `rstan-to-pystan`); the other 4 are 2 tasks of `unsound.json` that failed and the 2 whose package archive was gone. A pass rate on `five-minute` under these limits is what a model does in its first three minutes on four fifths of the benchmark. The list keeps five tasks of `unsound.json` (`build-cython-ext`, `crack-7z-hash`, `protein-assembly`, `qemu-alpine-ssh`, `qemu-startup`) and the tasks that fetch from outside services: like `fifteen-minute` it is the benchmark without what cannot fit, not a list chosen for what it tells.

**What the 300 s need besides the list.** A slot and the memory for every row at once, a machine the arm has alone, images that are already there, and no row claimed twice. The entry on the retry of a row has the arm that lacked them: 77 tasks three times under a limit of 180 s on 24 threads beside another run ended at 411 s and passed 11 of 231 rows, its last row claimed once at 328 s behind a verifier of 137 s, of `pytorch-model-cli`. Four of its tasks went over 90 s there or in the arms after it and are among the eleven above.

**Checked.** The list resolves with `src/Subset.ts` against the 89 task names of an import, 73 of 73, as the five lists before it do. The unit test fails for a task of `five-minute` that is not in `fifteen-minute`, for a task named twice and for a task dropped, each tried once. The tasks' own solutions under a limit of 180 s on the agent.

## 2026-11-15: an attempt whose time ends while the run asks a limited provider again is not an error of the provider

**Found** in the errors of three real arms of an installed agent, one run each: fx 0.0.17 on `@cf/google/gemma-4-26b-a4b-it` behind a chat completions route, microVM slots, one slot a row, on one bare-metal machine with 48 hardware threads and KVM, main at 5ab804b, `--claims 1`. The arms had 267 rows with `--agent-max-sec 600`, 252 rows with the same limit, and 219 rows with `--agent-max-sec 180`. The route answered `429` without `Retry-After` to about one request in twenty of the first arm (297 of 5,852, each within 2.3 s), and the run waited each out and asked again, as the entry on limited providers says. 2, 4 and 2 rows of the three arms ended as `environment: the model provider limited the agent: its last 1 model requests were answered 429, and the run waited 0 s before it asked again: the agent did not finish within 600 s` (one of the eight names 2 answers and 1 s). Those eight rows had 3 to 58 answered model requests each, and the run had waited 1 to 8 times and 0.25 to 3.25 s for each of them over the whole attempt. The agent limit ended more than 100 rows of each arm, most of them while a model request was unanswered. These eight were ended while the unanswered request was one that the run had asked again a quarter of a second after a `429`. They were 2 of the 10 infrastructure errors of the first arm (3.7 % of its rows) and 4 of the 10 of the second (4.0 %), and with the default of two claims each would have been run a second time.

**The rule before.** `Retry.throttled` made an attempt an error of the provider when it ended as an agent error, or at its agent timeout without a pass, and the last answers to its model requests were all limited. It read the status of the answers and not who had been given them. An installed agent is not given a limited answer while its attempt has time for the next pause: the run asks again, and the agent sees a request that takes longer. An attempt that is ended by its time limit during such an ask ended as every other row that the limit ends, waiting for its model.

**What changed.**

- **The relay says which answers it asked again.** A limited answer that the run waits out is settled with `again` (`worker/Meter.ts`), kept in a column `again` of `model_requests` and written on its line of `agent/model-requests.jsonl`. An answer that goes to the agent has none: the one for which the attempt has no time left, and every answer to a session, which the run does not wait for.
- **The rule reads it.** At an agent timeout, `Retry.throttled` makes the attempt an error of the provider only when one of its last limited answers went to the agent. When all of them were asked again, the failure stays `agent_timeout`: the verifier's reward stands, the row is scored, and it is not claimed again. An attempt that ends as an agent error after limited answers is an error of the provider as before, whoever asked again: an agent that gives up while the run waits was ended by the wait.

**Why a provider that limits to the end is still an error.** The pause doubles from `--poll-ms` and is never started when it would pass the deadline of the attempt: that answer goes to the agent. A provider that keeps limiting therefore hands the agent a limited answer before the time limit, and the last answers then hold one that was not asked again. The one case the rule does not tell apart is a time limit that falls inside an ask of the run, between a pause and its answer, when no limited answer has gone to the agent since the last reply. For an attempt limited for minutes, whose pauses have grown to tens of seconds around asks that are answered in about a second, that is a small share. An attempt limited only in its last seconds lost those seconds. Both are scored as rows that their time limit ended. Nothing in the row says what that ask would have been answered.

**Checked**, on a machine with 5 cores and no KVM, by a user who is not root.

- Unit tests: the rule, with the answers asked again and with one that went to the agent (`test/Retry.test.ts`), and the relay marking the three answers it asks again and none of the two it passes on (`test/Meter.test.ts`).
- A lane, "installed agents whose time ends while the run asks a provider again that limited them", a step of the job `e2e-dir`: 2 tasks, 2 installed agents, 4 rows on one directory slot, `agentMaxSec` 10. The scripted provider answers the one request of each row `429` and holds the second ask until the agent is gone. The lane asks that no row errored, that no row was claimed again, that the provider was asked twice for each row, and that each row is `failed` with reward 0 and `agent_timeout`, has `modelWaits` of 1 wait and `--poll-ms`, and has one line in its request log: `429`, `again`, a wait of `--poll-ms`. 2 of 2 runs passed, in 51 and 62 s. One slot, because the first model request of a run with a model budget goes alone until a response is priced, and this provider prices none.
- Broken by hand, one run: with the rule removed the lane failed after 97 s, `the provider was asked again once for the one request of a row`, 3 where it asks 2. All 4 rows had been claimed twice: the first claim of each had ended as the error of the provider and was retried.
- The lane of the entry on limited providers (3 tasks, 6 rows, `429` with `Retry-After`, `429`, then the reply) passed once with the change, in 12 s.
- From a fresh clone of the change on main at d493592: `npm ci`, `npm run lint`, `npm run check:types`, `npm test` (508 tests, 503 passed, 5 skipped, 0 failed) and `npm run dry-run` pass.

**Not run.** The other lanes of the workflow at this change, a deployed Worker, microVM slots, and a real arm. Read from their results, the eight rows above fall under the new rule (each of their last limited answers carries a wait of the run), which would leave the first arm 8 infrastructure errors in 267 rows and the second 6 in 252.

**What the other infrastructure errors of those arms were**, none of them changed here. In the first arm: 4 rows whose every model request was answered `502` by the route after 235 s, on three tasks whose requests that model does not finish in that time; 3 rows whose verifier ran out of the disk their task declares while it downloaded a package of 167 MiB, reported as a verifier without a test report because the installer wraps `No space left on device` over two lines; 1 row whose verifier could not resolve a host name. In the second: 1, 3 and 2 such rows, the last two as timeouts of a package index.
